turns: made dal in my dorm with an instant pot. red lentils 1 cup, water 2 cups, 8 min high pressure. got the BURN error and the bottom is scorched. what happened

Red lentils are starchy and sink to the bottom, where they stick and scorch before the pot builds enough pressure. With only 2 cups water, there isn't enough thin liquid at the base, so the sensor detects overheating and throws BURN.

Fixes:

- **More water:** use about 3 cups for 1 cup red lentils.
- **Water first, lentils on top,** and don't stir them down.
- **Deglaze** if you sauté onions or spices first. Scrape the bottom with a splash of water before adding everything else.
- **Add tomatoes on top**, not at the bottom. Tomato is a common burn cause.
- **Rinse lentils well** to remove extra starch.

Also 8 minutes is more than red lentils need. 5 minutes on high pressure with natural release is plenty.
i did sauté onion garlic and spices first. didnt deglaze

That's probably the main cause. Sautéed onions, garlic and spices leave browned bits stuck to the bottom, and those bits trigger the BURN sensor almost every time.

Next time:

1. Sauté onion, garlic, spices.
2. Add 1/4 cup water and scrape the bottom thoroughly with a wooden spoon until nothing's stuck.
3. Add the remaining water, then the rinsed lentils on top. Don't stir.
4. 5 min high pressure, 10 min natural release.

For the scorched pot: soak with water and a spoon of baking soda, then scrub.
ok did that and no burn this time. but its kinda watery now

Easy fix. Red lentils keep thickening as they sit, but you can speed it up:

- **Use the sauté function** after opening, simmering and stirring for 3–5 minutes until it thickens.
- **Mash or whisk** some of the lentils to make it creamier.
- **Reduce water to 2.5 cups next time.** With the deglazing step, 2.5 cups won't burn.

It'll also thicken a lot in the fridge, so slightly watery is actually ideal if you're saving leftovers.

brainstorm: im an undergrad with a part time job and some freelance income, total around 4 lakh a year. trying to figure out new regime or old regime for income tax planning in FY 2026-27. i have a small PPF and a health insurance policy. what should i be thinking about to decide

Here are the main things to weigh when choosing between the two regimes:

- Deductions you'll actually claim. The old regime allows deductions like 80C (PPF, life insurance, some savings), 80D (health insurance premiums) and HRA if you pay rent. The new regime gives up most of these in exchange for lower slab rates.
- Your total taxable income. At around 4 lakh, the new regime's rebate under section 87A can bring your tax to zero, and the standard deduction helps too. Check the current slab and rebate limits on the Income Tax department site, since they've changed recently.
- The size of your deductions. A PPF contribution plus health insurance premiums might add up to less than the gap in slab rates, so run the numbers for both.
- Freelance income and expenses. If you're self-employed, you may have business expenses to deduct, which can change the comparison.
- Whether you need to file. Even with no tax, filing can help you claim refunds and build a record, so don't skip it just because the tax is low.

The easiest check is to compute your tax under both regimes with the same income and deductions, then pick the lower one.

ok thanks. btw making chicken tikka masala for a potluck sat, 10 ppl. heres my plan

2 lb chicken breast
marinate in yogurt + tikka masala powder 1 hr
pan fry
sauce: 1 onion, 1 can tomato sauce, 1 cup heavy cream, 2 tbsp garam masala
serve w rice

enough? anything off

Mostly fine, but a few things to adjust for 10 people:

- **Quantity:** 2 lb chicken is light for 10. Plan about 1/3 lb per person, so 3.5–4 lb.
- **Thighs over breast.** Much more forgiving, stay juicy, and reheat better for a potluck.
- **Marinate longer.** Overnight is ideal; at least 4 hours. Add lemon juice, salt, ginger and garlic to the marinade.
- **Sauce is thin on flavor.** Add ginger and garlic, cook the onion until golden, use crushed tomatoes or puree instead of tomato sauce, and add cumin and Kashmiri chili or paprika. Garam masala: 2 tsp, not 2 tbsp, added near the end.
- **Double the sauce** for 10 people: 2 onions, 2 cans tomatoes, 1.5–2 cups cream.
- **Rice:** about 4 cups dry for 10.

Pan-frying 4 lb in batches is slow. Broiling on a sheet pan for 10–12 min is faster and gets nice char.
ok switched to 4 lb thighs, overnight marinade. sauce now 2 onions, ginger garlic, 2 cans crushed tomato, cumin, paprika, 2 tsp garam masala, 1.5 cups cream. broiling chicken. good?

That's a solid plan now. Two small additions:

- **Salt the sauce properly.** About 2 tsp total for that volume, added gradually. Under-salted sauce is the most common reason it tastes flat.
- **A spoon of butter and a pinch of sugar** at the end round it out. Kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves) crushed in at the end gives that restaurant taste if you can find it.

Cook the sauce at least 20 minutes after adding the tomatoes, until the oil starts to separate. Then add the broiled chicken and simmer 10 minutes before the cream.
can i make it fri night and reheat sat

Yes, it's actually better the next day. The flavors settle in.

- Cool it quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours.
- Reheat gently on the stove over medium-low, stirring, until it's steaming hot throughout. Add a splash of water or cream if it's too thick.
- Avoid boiling hard after the cream is in, since it can split.
- Make the rice fresh on Saturday if you can; it's quick, and reheated rice dries out.

If you need to keep it warm at the potluck, a slow cooker on low or warm works great.

turns: just adopted a 4 month old rescue pup (beagle mix, named Pickles) and i work from home as a freelancer so i have flexible hours. can you help me plan out a training schedule for the first month? she pulls on the leash, has accidents inside, and barks when i leave the room

Yes. With a flexible schedule you can do lots of short sessions, which is the best way to train a puppy. Here's a framework for the first month:

**Daily routine:**
- Potty breaks: first thing in the morning, after meals, after naps, after play, and every 1 to 2 hours in between. Reward immediately outside with a treat.
- 3 to 4 training sessions of 5 minutes each (morning, midday, afternoon, evening).
- Crate time or a pen for short stretches while you're home, building up gradually.

**Week 1:** potty routine, name recognition, 'sit', and getting comfortable in the crate for 5 to 10 minutes.
**Week 2:** 'down', 'come', and loose-leash basics indoors.
**Week 3:** leash walking in the yard and quiet streets, and short separation practice.
**Week 4:** add distractions, longer separations, and 'stay'.
the barking when i leave the room is the worst. how do i do the separation thing

Start with very small separations and build up, so she never gets to the point of panic.

1. Give her something to do, like a stuffed Kong or chew toy, in her crate or pen.
2. Step out of sight for 2 to 3 seconds, then come back before she barks. Reward calm behavior.
3. Gradually increase: 5 seconds, 10, 30, 1 minute, 5 minutes. If she barks, you went too fast; go back to an easier step.
4. Don't make arrivals and departures a big deal. Stay calm and ignore her for a minute when you come back.
5. Practice several times a day, even when you're working at home.

Beagles are vocal and prone to separation distress, so this will take a few weeks. If she is panicking, drooling or destroying things, talk to your vet or a trainer.
what do i do about the leash pulling? she is a rocket

Beagles follow their noses, so pulling is expected. Two methods that work:

**Stop and go:** the moment the leash goes tight, stop walking and stand still. When she turns back or the leash slackens, say 'yes' and move forward. She learns that pulling stops progress.

**Reward position:** keep treats at your side and reward her whenever she's next to you with a loose leash.

Start in the house or yard, not in a high-distraction spot. Use a front-clip harness to reduce pulling in the meantime, and plan walks where she can sniff for part of the time. Sniffing tires her out and satisfies her instincts.
ok and accidents inside, still happening like once a day

Once a day at 4 months means the schedule needs tightening, not that she's failing.

- Take her out more often: every 1 to 2 hours while awake, plus after eating, drinking, playing and waking up.
- Use the same spot and a cue word like 'go potty', and reward with a treat within 3 seconds of finishing.
- Watch for signs: sniffing in circles, whining or going to the door. If she has an accident, interrupt calmly and take her outside, and clean the spot with an enzymatic cleaner so it doesn't smell like a toilet.
- Don't punish after the fact. She won't connect it.
- Limit freedom indoors by using a pen or keeping her in the room with you.

Most puppies are reliable by 5 to 6 months.
can i fit all this into my work day? i have calls

Yes. Many freelancers do this. A rough day:

- **7:30 am:** potty, breakfast, potty, 5-minute training
- **9:00:** work block, with her in a pen with a chew; potty break at 10:30
- **12:00:** potty, lunch, a short walk and a training session
- **1:30 to 3:30:** nap in the crate (puppies sleep a lot), with a potty break after
- **3:30:** play and training
- **5:30:** dinner, potty, walk
- **evening:** relaxed time, last potty at bedtime

For calls, put her in the pen with a stuffed Kong, or take her out right before. Schedule important calls during her naps. Training sessions can be tucked into 5-minute gaps between tasks.
last thing, how do i know if shes making progress. what should i track

Keep a simple log, maybe in your phone's notes, once a day:

- **Accidents:** how many per day. This should trend downward week to week.
- **Separation:** the longest time she stayed calm while you were out of sight.
- **Leash:** how many steps or how long before the first pull, or minutes of loose-leash walking.
- **Commands:** which she does reliably (3 out of 5 tries) and in which locations.

After 2 weeks, check the numbers. Progress is often uneven: puppies regress during growth spurts and when something changes in the home. If a number stays flat or gets worse for two weeks, change something or ask a trainer. A puppy class is also worth considering.
random q. so i have like 6200 on a card at 24.99% apr and my plan is to just throw all my extra money at it every month instead of splitting it up w my savings. thats the right move yeah?

Mostly yes. At nearly 25% APR, every dollar you put toward the card is effectively a guaranteed 25% return, which beats anything a savings account or the market will reliably give you.

One caveat: keep a small emergency cushion, even $500 to $1,000, so a surprise expense doesn't end up back on the card. After that, send everything extra to the debt. Do you have any other cards or loans, or is it just this one?
just this one. i do have about 1500 in savings tho, should i use that too

I'd put maybe $500 to $1,000 of it toward the card and keep the rest as your buffer. As a freelancer your income can be lumpy, so having a month of bare-bones expenses set aside matters more than it would for someone on a salary.

If you drop $500 on it now and then add, say, $400 a month, you'd be done in roughly 14 to 15 months and pay somewhere around $1,100 in interest. Paying only the minimum would take years and cost several times that.
ok thats not as bad as i thought. also someone told me to open a 0% balance transfer card, is that dumb

Not dumb at all, it's often the best tool for this. If you can get approved for a card with 0% for 15 to 21 months, you'd pay a one-time transfer fee (usually 3 to 5%, so about $190 to $310 on $6,200) but skip nearly all the interest.

The catch is you need a plan to pay it off before the promo ends, because the rate jumps after. And don't run up the old card again. With the fee you'd likely still come out ahead by several hundred dollars compared to staying at 24.99%. Check your credit score first, since you usually need good credit to qualify.
need ideas, im a freelance designer from india and want to work in the US for a bit. what visa options are even there for me

The realistic options depend on how you want to work:

- **H-1B**: needs a US employer to sponsor you and win the lottery. Hard to do as a freelancer.
- **O-1**: for people with extraordinary ability, which can include strong design portfolios, awards, press, and high-paying work. You need an agent or sponsor, but it's flexible.
- **L-1**: only if you work for a company abroad that has a US office.
- **B-1/B-2**: short visits for meetings or conferences, but you can't do paid work.
- **J-1 or training programs**: sometimes used for internships and exchange roles.
- **E-2 or EB-2 NIW**: more of a business or long-term route.

Do you want to work for US clients while living there, or work for an Indian employer or yourself and just visit?
mostly us clients, i want to move for like 2 years maybe. no employer

Then O-1 is probably the one to look at first, since it doesn't tie you to a single employer the way H-1B does. You can use a US agent as your petitioner and list your different clients as your itinerary.

You need to meet at least 3 of 8 criteria, such as awards, published work about you, judging others' work, high pay, or a critical role at known companies. A strong design portfolio with named brands can help.

The other route is forming a US company and going for an E-2 if your country has the treaty (India doesn't), so that's out. Alternatively, a long-shot H-1B through a staffing arrangement. O-1 is the most practical.
idk if i qualify tho. i won a couple design awards and was on a few blogs

That could already count for two criteria, if the awards are nationally or internationally recognized and the blog coverage is about you and your work, not just a mention. You'd need a third.

Things that often fill the gap:
- Evidence of high pay or rates compared to others in your field
- Letters from industry experts or past clients
- Being a judge on a design competition or portfolio review
- Work for well-known brands or agencies

It's worth a consult with an immigration lawyer, since an O-1 has to be built as a package. Many offer a flat-fee evaluation.
how much does that cost all in, lawyer and fees

Rough numbers for 2026, and they vary:

- Lawyer fees: about $3,000 to $8,000 for an O-1 petition
- USCIS filing fee: around $1,000 plus the asylum program fee ($600 for most employers, less for small ones)
- Premium processing (optional): about $2,800 for a 15-day decision
- Agent fee if you use one: varies a lot, sometimes a percentage of your income
- Visa application fee at the consulate: around $185

So budget $6,000 to $12,000 total. Check current USCIS fees before you commit, since they change.
ugh ok. any cheaper way to just test the waters first

A few ideas:

- Get a B-1 visa and attend a US design conference or meet clients in person. You can't work there, but you can network and scope things out.
- Do a free or low-cost initial consultation with an immigration attorney to find out whether your profile is strong enough before paying for a full petition.
- Start collecting O-1 evidence now: ask clients for letters, enter more awards, apply to judge something, and save press links.
- Look at remote contracts with US firms that have an Indian entity, which could lead to an L-1 or sponsored route later.

That way you spend a few hundred dollars finding out where you stand rather than thousands.
ok ill think about it. another thing, my puppy is 14 weeks and i think the best way to housebreak is to just take her out every 2 hours and give a treat when she goes. right?

Yes, that's the core of it. At 14 weeks a 2-hour schedule is sensible, plus take her out right after waking up, after meals, after play, and before bed. Reward immediately, within a couple of seconds, and do it outside so she connects the treat to the location. Adding a cue word like 'go potty' helps later.
she keeps having accidents inside tho even with that

That's normal at 14 weeks. A few things to check:

- Are you staying outside long enough, 5 to 10 minutes? Some pups just sniff and then go the moment they're back in.
- Are you supervising her indoors? When she can't be watched, use a crate or a gated area.
- Clean accident spots with an enzymatic cleaner, since regular cleaners leave a smell that tells her to go there again.

Punishing after the fact won't help, she won't connect it.
ok i dont yell or anything. is crate training good for her or is it kinda mean

It's not mean when done well. Dogs naturally like a small den-like space, and it's one of the fastest ways to housebreak, since puppies avoid soiling where they sleep.

The crate should be just big enough to stand up and turn around in. Make it pleasant with treats and a chew toy, never use it as punishment, and don't leave her in too long. A general guide is about one hour per month of age during the day, so around 3 hours max at her age, and not all day.
she cries at night in it, i was gonna just ignore it so she learns

Ignoring is fine for a pup who's just protesting, but at 14 weeks she may actually need to go out. Most puppies this age can't hold it more than 4 to 5 hours overnight.

So I'd do a quiet potty trip once in the night, no play, no talking, straight back in. If she cries between trips and you know she's emptied out, then waiting it out is reasonable. If you respond to a long meltdown, she learns that crying works. Put the crate near your bed for now so she feels less alone.
should i be doing sit and stay too or wait till shes older

Start now with short, fun sessions. Puppies can learn sit, down, name recognition and come at 8 weeks or younger. Keep each session to 3 to 5 minutes, a few times a day, with tiny treats.

Sit is easy to teach by luring with a treat over her nose. Stay is better to build slowly: begin with one second and add time and distance gradually. Don't expect solid reliability until she's several months old.
cool so basically housebreak first, rest later is wrong, do both at once

Right, they don't compete. Potty training is mostly about schedule and management, and the short training sessions are just a few minutes of fun. Doing both builds focus and the habit of working with you. Just keep expectations realistic: accidents will still happen for another month or two, and that's normal.

turns: I'm 31, working as a PM in Bangalore, and I've finally got about ₹40,000 a month I can invest consistently. I currently have an emergency fund of 6 months' expenses in an FD and nothing else apart from my EPF. I keep reading about SIPs but there are thousands of funds. Could you help me brainstorm some ways to structure this, rather than just naming specific funds?

Good starting point: emergency fund done, steady monthly amount. A few ways people structure ₹40k/month:

1. **Simple core:** one Nifty 50 index fund (or a Nifty 50 + Nifty Next 50 combo). Very low cost, easy to stick with.
2. **Core + satellite:** 60–70% in an index or flexi-cap fund as the core, 30–40% split between a mid-cap or small-cap fund for growth.
3. **Three-fund approach:** large-cap index, flexi-cap active fund, small-cap fund, roughly 50/30/20.
4. **Goal buckets:** separate SIPs for different goals, e.g. retirement (equity-heavy), house down payment in 5 years (more hybrid or debt), travel (short-term debt fund).
5. **Equity + debt balance:** add a debt or hybrid component, especially if you want lower volatility. Your EPF already acts as a debt-like component.
6. **Tax angle:** ELSS for 80C, only relevant if you're on the old regime.

What are you investing for, mainly long-term wealth or specific goals?
Mostly long-term wealth, but I'd also like to buy a flat in maybe 6–7 years. I'm on the new tax regime.

Then the goal buckets idea fits well. Two separate pools:

**Long-term wealth (15+ years):** this can be fully equity. Options:
- Nifty 50 index + flexi-cap + small-cap
- Or simpler: Nifty 50 index + a flexi-cap

**Flat down payment (6–7 years):** medium horizon, so some equity but not all:
- A balanced advantage or aggressive hybrid fund
- Or an equity index fund now, gradually shifting to debt/liquid funds in the last 2–3 years

Possible split of ₹40k:
- ₹25k for long-term (e.g. 15k index, 10k flexi-cap or small-cap)
- ₹15k for the flat (e.g. hybrid fund)

Since you're on the new regime, skip ELSS; there's no tax benefit and it has a 3-year lock-in.
That makes sense. What other ideas are there for the flat money specifically?

Some options for a 6–7 year goal:

- **Balanced advantage fund:** shifts between equity and debt automatically based on valuations. Lower volatility than pure equity.
- **Aggressive hybrid fund:** ~65–80% equity, rest debt. Higher growth, more swings.
- **Multi-asset fund:** equity, debt, plus some gold. Diversified in one fund.
- **Equity index + glide path:** invest in a Nifty 50 index fund for the first 3–4 years, then move gradually into a short-duration debt fund or liquid fund as you get close.
- **Equity savings fund:** much lower equity, more conservative.
- **RD or FD ladder:** if you'd rather have certainty for part of it.

A practical combo: half in a balanced advantage fund, half in an index fund, with a plan to shift into debt starting around year 4.
The glide path idea is interesting. How would I actually do that in practice?

A simple way to do it:

**Years 1–4:** SIP the full ₹15k into an equity index fund (or a hybrid fund).

**Year 5:** stop the equity SIP, start a new SIP into a short-duration debt fund or a liquid fund. Also move about a third of the accumulated equity into debt via an STP (systematic transfer plan) over 6–12 months.

**Year 6:** move another third.

**Year 7 (purchase year):** remaining equity into liquid fund, so the down payment isn't exposed to a market fall right before you need it.

Notes:

- Moving from equity to debt is a redemption, so long-term capital gains tax applies above the annual exemption (₹1.25 lakh currently). Spreading switches across financial years helps use the exemption each year.
- If the market is down when you're supposed to shift, you can delay slightly, but don't wait too long.
Okay. For the long-term part, I'm torn between including small caps or not. Can you brainstorm the case for and against?

**For small caps:**
- Historically higher long-term returns in India, as smaller companies grow.
- Over 15+ years, the volatility tends to even out.
- Adds diversification beyond the large companies in Nifty 50.
- At 31, you have time to ride out downturns.

**Against:**
- Very volatile: falls of 40–60% have happened (2008, 2018–2020). Many investors panic and sell at the bottom.
- Valuations have been high recently after a big run-up.
- Active small-cap funds have varying quality and some have restricted inflows during frothy periods.
- Flexi-cap funds already hold some small and mid caps.

**Middle grounds:**
- Limit small-cap to 10–20% of the long-term pool.
- Use a Nifty Midcap 150 or a Nifty 500 index fund for broader exposure without picking a small-cap fund.
- Use a flexi-cap fund and skip a dedicated small-cap fund.

The real question is whether you'd stay invested through a 50% drop.
Honestly, I'm not sure I would. I've never seen a big crash with my own money.

That's a very honest answer, and it's an important one. Then it makes sense to start more conservatively:

- **Skip a dedicated small-cap fund for now.** Use Nifty 50 index + flexi-cap, which gives some small/mid exposure inside a managed fund.
- **Or add a small slice**, ₹3–5k a month, to see how it feels during market swings. If you find you can stay calm, increase later.

You can always add small caps later once you've experienced a correction. Starting with a portfolio you'll stick with is better than an aggressive one you abandon at the worst time.
So putting it all together, what would the options look like for the full ₹40k?

Here are three versions, from simplest to more diversified:

**Option A: Simple**
- ₹25k: Nifty 50 index fund (long-term)
- ₹15k: Nifty 50 index fund in a separate folio (flat, with glide path)

**Option B: Balanced (probably the best fit for you)**
- ₹15k: Nifty 50 index fund (long-term)
- ₹10k: Flexi-cap fund (long-term)
- ₹15k: Balanced advantage fund (flat)

**Option C: Growth tilt**
- ₹12k: Nifty 50 index
- ₹8k: Flexi-cap
- ₹5k: Small-cap or Midcap 150 index
- ₹15k: Index fund with glide path (flat)

All use direct plans, not regular, to save on expense ratios. Review once a year, and increase SIPs when your salary rises.
Option B feels right. Is there anything I should do before starting?

A few things:

- **KYC:** make sure your KYC is complete and validated (via any platform or KRA). Most apps handle this.
- **Pick a platform** that offers direct plans: Zerodha Coin, Groww, Kuvera, or the AMC/MF Central sites directly.
- **Choose specific funds:** compare expense ratio, fund house, consistency and the manager's track record. For index funds, lowest expense ratio and tracking error.
- **Add nominees** to every folio.
- **SIP dates:** a few days after your salary credit.
- **Set a step-up:** many platforms let you increase SIPs by 10% a year automatically.
- **Write down the plan** (goal, allocation, glide path for the flat) so you stick to it during market drops.

Then start, and resist checking it daily.
Thanks, that's helpful. Unrelated question: how long does cooked rice last in the fridge? I'm planning to batch-cook a week's worth on Sunday.

Cooked rice is generally safe for **3–4 days** in the fridge, as long as it's cooled quickly and stored properly. A full week is pushing it.

The concern with rice specifically is *Bacillus cereus*, a bacterium whose spores survive cooking. If rice sits at room temperature too long, they can grow and produce toxins that reheating doesn't destroy.

So for a 5–7 day plan: refrigerate what you'll eat by Wednesday, and freeze the rest.
How quickly do I need to cool it?

Ideally get it into the fridge within **1 hour** of cooking, and definitely within 2 hours.

To cool it fast:

- Spread it out in a thin layer on a tray or large plate.
- Let it steam off for 10–15 minutes.
- Then portion into containers and refrigerate, or freeze.

Don't leave a big pot of rice on the stove to cool for a few hours; the center stays warm for a long time.
And how long does it last in the freezer?

Cooked rice keeps well in the freezer for about **1 month** for best quality, and it's safe longer than that if kept frozen. Texture is the main thing that declines over time.

Freeze it in flat, portion-sized bags or containers so it freezes and thaws evenly.
What's the best way to reheat it from frozen?

The microwave is easiest:

- Put the frozen rice in a microwave-safe bowl, sprinkle a tablespoon of water over it, and cover loosely.
- Microwave 2–3 minutes on high, stir, then another 1–2 minutes until steaming hot all the way through.

No need to thaw first. You can also reheat in a pan with a splash of water over medium heat, stirring, which works well for fried rice.

Only reheat rice once. Don't refreeze after reheating.
Does the same 3–4 day rule apply to cooked chicken?

Yes. Cooked chicken is also good for **3–4 days** in the fridge, and up to 2–4 months in the freezer for best quality.

Same cooling principle applies: get it into the fridge within 2 hours, and slice or portion large pieces so they cool faster.
What about roasted vegetables?

Roasted vegetables last about **3–5 days** in the fridge. Sturdy ones like carrots, sweet potatoes, peppers and squash hold up best. Broccoli, zucchini and mushrooms get soft and watery faster, so eat those earlier in the week.

They freeze okay, but the texture gets softer. Fine for soups, stews or blending into sauces, less great as a side.
So if I cook everything on Sunday, which day should I start using the frozen portions?

With a 3–4 day fridge window, a simple schedule:

- **Sunday:** cook, cool, portion.
- **Monday–Wednesday:** eat from the fridge.
- **Wednesday evening:** move Thursday's portions from freezer to fridge to thaw.
- **Thursday evening:** move Friday's portions.

So the frozen portions are for **Thursday onward**. If you also eat these meals on the weekend, freeze those too and pull them the night before.
Is it fine to thaw the rice and chicken together in the same container?

Yes, that's fine as long as both were cooked, cooled and frozen properly. Thaw the container in the fridge overnight, not on the counter, and eat it within 24 hours of thawing.

If the chicken is in a sauce, the rice will soak some of it up and get softer. If that bothers you, use divided containers or freeze them separately.

I'm a PM and I occasionally edit docs in our repo. I made some changes on main by mistake, then tried to switch to a new branch with `git checkout -b docs-update`, but now when I run `git status` it shows my changes on the new branch and also says main is 'ahead of origin/main by 1 commit'. I'm confused about what state I'm in and I don't want to push something broken to main.

No need to panic. Here's what likely happened:

- You made changes and **committed** one of them on `main` (hence 'ahead of origin/main by 1 commit').
- You may have other changes that are **not committed**.
- When you ran `git checkout -b docs-update`, Git created a new branch from your current position and carried the uncommitted changes with it. The new branch also contains that commit.

So right now:

- `docs-update` has the commit and your uncommitted changes. That's what you want.
- Your local `main` also has the commit, which you don't want.

Nothing has been pushed, so nothing is broken on the remote. To confirm, run:

```
git log --oneline -3 main
git log --oneline -3 origin/main
```

The first should show one extra commit compared to the second.
Yes, main has one extra commit, 'update onboarding doc', which is the one I made by mistake. How do I remove it from main without losing it?

Since the commit is also on `docs-update`, you won't lose it. You just need to reset `main` back to match the remote.

1. Make sure you're on `docs-update` and commit or stash any uncommitted changes there:
   ```
   git add .
   git commit -m "More docs changes"
   ```
2. Switch to main:
   ```
   git checkout main
   ```
3. Reset main to match the remote:
   ```
   git reset --hard origin/main
   ```
4. Switch back to your branch:
   ```
   git checkout docs-update
   ```

After this, `main` matches the remote, and `docs-update` has both of your commits. Run `git log --oneline -3` on each to confirm.

I did all of that. Now `git status` on main says 'up to date with origin/main', which is good. But when I try to push docs-update, I get 'fatal: The current branch docs-update has no upstream branch'.

That's expected. The branch only exists locally, so Git doesn't know where to push it yet. Push it and set the upstream in one step:

```
git push -u origin docs-update
```

The `-u` links your local branch to the remote one, so future `git push` and `git pull` on this branch work without extra arguments.

After that, Git usually prints a link to open a pull request.
That worked, and I opened a PR. However, the PR shows a file I didn't mean to change: package-lock.json. I never touched it.

That usually happens if you (or a tool) ran `npm install` locally, which can rewrite `package-lock.json` even without you editing it. You can remove it from the branch:

```
git checkout origin/main -- package-lock.json
git commit -m "Revert unintended package-lock change"
git push
```

The first command restores the file to the version on `main`. After pushing, the PR will update and the file should disappear from the diff.

To avoid it in the future, check `git status` before committing and only stage the files you meant to change, e.g. `git add docs/onboarding.md` instead of `git add .`.
That fixed it, the PR now only shows the docs file. Is there anything I should do to avoid committing to main by accident again?

A few simple habits and safeguards:

- **Create a branch first, every time:** `git checkout -b my-change` before editing anything.
- **Show the current branch in your terminal prompt.** Tools like Oh My Zsh or Starship do this, or check with `git branch --show-current`.
- **Ask your team about branch protection** on GitHub/GitLab for `main`. That blocks direct pushes, so even if you commit to main locally, it can't be pushed.
- **Use `git status` before committing.** It shows the branch name at the top.
- **Stage specific files** rather than `git add .`.

If you mostly edit docs, GitHub's web editor is also an option. It automatically offers to create a new branch and PR when you edit a file.
Quick question: is there a real difference between direct and regular mutual fund plans, and does it matter for a SIP of 5,000 a month?

Yes, there's a real difference. Both plans invest in the same portfolio, but a regular plan includes a distributor commission that's built into a higher expense ratio. A direct plan skips that commission, so its expense ratio is usually lower, often by about 0.5 to 1 percentage point.

Over a long SIP, that adds up. On 5,000 a month for 15 years at a 10 percent return, the final value is roughly 1.4 lakh rupees higher with a direct plan, on a corpus of about 21 lakh. It matters more the longer you hold and the more you invest. The main trade-off is that with a direct plan you do the research yourself, since you don't have a distributor to help.
so if i invest directly do i need to file anything extra or is it just the app

Usually it's just the app or the fund house website. Once you set up a direct plan, your SIPs run automatically from your bank account, and your holdings show up in your account statements. You don't need to file anything extra for the investment itself.

The main things to keep track of are your statements and the capital gains when you sell. Your broker or the registrar will send consolidated statements each month or quarter. Keep those, because you'll need the purchase dates and amounts when you calculate tax on redemptions.
what if i stop the sip for a year, is that bad

It isn't a disaster, but it's not ideal. Stopping a SIP doesn't create a penalty on its own. You just stop buying units for that year, so you lose the compounding on the money you would have invested and you buy fewer units if the market dips.

If you can, pause rather than stop. Many fund houses let you pause or skip a SIP installment for a few months. If you need to restart later, you can do it through the app or your bank mandate. Make sure you don't redeem the existing units by accident, since that can trigger tax and an exit load.
what's an exit load and how do i avoid it

An exit load is a fee the fund charges when you sell units within a set period after buying them. For many equity funds it's 1 percent if you redeem within 12 months, and it drops to zero after that. The exact terms are in the scheme document, so check that for your fund.

To avoid it, don't redeem units bought in the last year or so, or wait until the holding period passes. With a monthly SIP, each installment has its own date, so only the most recent few months will have the exit load. Your app usually shows which units are still under the exit load period, and you can choose to redeem only the older ones.

turns: got a bunch of sourdough discard in the fridge, like 400g+, sick of pancakes. what else can i do with it

Plenty of options:

- **Crackers**: mix discard with flour, oil, salt and herbs, roll thin, bake. Very easy and keeps well.
- **Flatbreads or naan-style**: discard plus flour and a bit of baking powder, cooked in a skillet.
- **Waffles or crumpets**
- **Pizza dough**: use it with some added flour and a long cold rest.
- **English muffins**
- **Focaccia** with a pinch of yeast for lift
- **Pretzels or soft pretzel bites**

Crackers and flatbreads use the most discard with the least effort.
crackers sound good. is there like a ratio

A simple starting point: 200g discard, 60g olive oil or melted butter, 100g flour, and 5g salt, plus rosemary, seeds or cheese if you like. Mix into a dough, rest 30 minutes if it's sticky, roll as thin as you can between parchment, score, and bake at 175C for 20 to 25 minutes, until crisp and golden. Thinner means crunchier. The exact flour amount depends on how wet your discard is.
nice. also is it ok if the discard is like 3 weeks old and has hooch on top

Yes, it's fine. Hooch is just alcohol the yeast makes when it's hungry. Stir it in or pour it off. The flavor will be tangier, which actually works well for crackers.

Throw it out if you see fuzzy mold or pink or orange streaks, or if it smells really off, like nail polish remover. Three weeks in the fridge is normally fine.

cool. ok totally different thing, im a phd student, been running maybe 3x a week, 25-30km total, mostly easy 8-10k loops. a labmate talked me into signing up for a half in may (bristol). i was gonna try one of those free plans online but theres like a million and idk which to pick. hal higdon? runna? something else? i have like zero time flexibility during the week bc of experiments

With your base (25–30 km/week, comfortable 8–10k runs), you're in a good spot for a May half. The plan matters less than picking one that fits your schedule.

Options:

- **Hal Higdon Novice 2 or Intermediate 1:** free, simple, 4–5 runs/week. Very well tested. Fixed schedule though, which might clash with experiments.
- **Runna:** app-based, adapts to your pace and preferred days, includes workouts. Paid subscription (~£10–20/month), but flexible scheduling might suit you.
- **NHS / Couch-to-half type plans:** too basic for you.
- **Build your own from a template:** 3–4 runs/week (one long run, one workout, 1–2 easy).

Given your limited weekday flexibility, I'd go with a **3–4 day plan** where the long run is on the weekend. How many days could you realistically commit?
3 is realistic. 4 on a good week. long run def has to be sat or sun

Then I'd recommend a 3-day plan with an optional 4th:

- **Weekday 1:** workout (tempo or intervals), 40–50 min
- **Weekday 2:** easy run, 30–45 min
- **Weekend:** long run, building from 12 km to 18–19 km
- **Optional 4th:** another easy run or cross-training

Good ready-made fits:

- **Hal Higdon's 'Novice 1'** uses 3–4 runs a week and is free, but very easy for you.
- **The FIRST method ('Run Less, Run Faster')** is literally 3 runs a week: one interval, one tempo, one long. It's quite intense, but designed for people with limited time.
- **Runna** can generate a 3-day plan with your weekdays chosen.

For a first half with a decent base, I'd lean toward Runna or a custom 3-day plan rather than FIRST, since FIRST's intensity can lead to injury if you're not used to speedwork.
runna costs money tho and im on a phd stipend lol. whats the custom version look like

Fair, here's a free custom version for ~20 weeks to the Bristol Half in May:

**Weeks 1–6 (base):**
- Tue: easy 6–8 km, last 1 km a bit faster
- Thu: easy 6–8 km with 6 x 20s strides
- Sat/Sun: long run 12 → 15 km, +1 km/week, cutback in week 4

**Weeks 7–14 (build):**
- Tue: tempo, e.g. 2 km easy, 4–6 km at comfortably hard pace, 1–2 km easy
- Thu: easy 7–8 km or intervals (5 x 1 km at 10k pace)
- Sat/Sun: long run 15 → 19 km, cutback every 4th week

**Weeks 15–18 (peak):** keep the structure, long runs 18–20 km, some at goal pace.

**Weeks 19–20 (taper):** cut volume by 30–50%, keep a bit of pace.

Add a 4th easy run when you can, but don't make up for missed days.
how fast should the tempo be? i dont really know my paces, i run by feel

Running by feel works fine. Tempo pace is 'comfortably hard': you could say a few words but not hold a conversation. Roughly 7 out of 10 effort.

If you want a number, you can estimate from a recent race or hard effort:

- If you've done a 5k or 10k recently, put it into a calculator like the VDOT (Jack Daniels) or McMillan calculator. They give tempo, interval and easy paces.
- Or run a time trial: 5k as hard as you can on a flat route, then plug it in.

Roughly, tempo pace is close to what you could race for an hour, usually 15–25 seconds per km slower than your 5k pace.

Keep easy runs truly easy, at full conversation pace. Most amateurs run easy days too fast.
did a parkrun last week in 26:10. is that useful

Yes, that's perfect. A 26:10 5k suggests roughly:

- **Easy pace:** ~6:15–6:50 /km
- **Tempo:** ~5:30–5:40 /km
- **Intervals (1 km reps):** ~5:05–5:15 /km
- **Half marathon prediction:** around 2:00–2:05, with good training possibly under 2:00.

These are estimates, so use them as a guide alongside feel. If a tempo at 5:35 feels like an all-out effort, slow down a bit. Run another parkrun mid-way through training to update the numbers.
sub 2 would be sick tbh. is that realistic or am i getting ahead of myself

It's realistic, not guaranteed. A 26:10 5k predicts roughly 2:00–2:05 today, and you have ~20 weeks to train. Many people with your base improve their 5k by 1–2 minutes with consistent training, which would put sub-2 well within reach.

The key factors:

- **Consistency over 20 weeks** more than any single workout.
- **Long runs up to 18–20 km**, so the distance doesn't surprise you.
- **Some running at goal pace** (5:40/km for sub-2) in the later long runs.

A good check: if your parkrun gets to around 25:00 by March, sub-2 is very likely. Set it as an 'A' goal, with 'finish strong and enjoy it' as the baseline.
ok so custom 3 day plan, parkrun as a checkpoint in march, sub 2 as the stretch goal. sound right?

Sounds right. That's a sensible, realistic plan for your schedule.

A couple of last things:

- **Parkrun as a workout:** you can swap a weekday tempo for a parkrun now and then, if a Saturday run doesn't clash with your long run. Or do the long run on Sunday.
- **Don't skip easy days** when you're busy and try to squeeze extra intensity in. If you miss a run, just carry on with the plan.
- **Add 15–20 min of strength work** once or twice a week if you can (squats, lunges, calf raises). Great for injury prevention.

Enjoy the Bristol Half, and good luck with the sub-2.
so we just got a 5 month old rescue (beagle mix) and she pulls like crazy on the leash. harness or head halter or just keep working on loose leash with the regular collar?

For a strong puller I'd start with a front-clip harness. It redirects her forward momentum sideways when she pulls, which cuts the pulling right away, with little risk to her neck. A head halter works well too but many dogs hate wearing one at first and you'll need to condition her to it.

A regular flat collar is fine for ID but not great for a puller, since pulling against it can strain her throat. Pair the harness with loose leash training either way: stop when she pulls, move when the leash is slack, and reward her for being beside you.
do the harness's actually train anything or just mask it

Mostly they manage it. A front-clip harness reduces how much she can pull, but the dog doesn't learn what you want on its own. The training comes from rewards and consistency, like treating at your side and stopping or turning when the leash goes tight.

Think of the harness as a tool that makes the training work easier. Over weeks, you can often switch to a regular harness or collar once she understands.
ok going with front clip + treats. any specific one you'd say

Common well-reviewed ones are the Ruffwear Front Range, the 2 Hounds Design Freedom harness, and the PetSafe Easy Walk, which is cheaper. Whichever you choose, fit matters most: check that you can fit two fingers under the straps and that it doesn't rub her armpits. Beagles can be escape artists, so one with a four-point adjustment (neck, chest, and so on) tends to stay on better. Start with high-value treats, like small bits of chicken, since beagle noses are distracted by everything.

thanks. separate question, do i go with a B2 tourist visa for a conference or should i apply for a J-1? im a PhD student invited to speak at a 4-day conference in Chicago. the conference won't pay for travel up front, just reimburses after, and my advisor said J-1 might be better. i'm thinking tourist/visitor since i'm not being paid for the talk. which should i do

For attending a conference and giving a talk, the B-1/B-2 visitor visa is usually the right category, not J-1. J-1 is for exchange programs like research scholars or training positions with a sponsor, and a four-day conference doesn't fit that.

A few points to check:

- Conference attendance and a talk are generally allowed on a B-1 business visitor visa. Tourist (B-2) is the general category, and many people apply for B-1/B-2 together.
- Being paid is the key issue. Reimbursement for documented travel and reasonable expenses is usually fine, but an honorarium or payment for the talk can create problems, so ask the conference for a letter stating what is and isn't covered.
- Ask your university's international student office before you book. They can confirm the category and check your current status, since your current visa or F-1 status affects the answer.
- Keep the conference invitation letter, your registration confirmation, and your accepted abstract with you at the border or interview.

If you're already on an F-1 visa, travel for a conference is often possible without a new visa, but confirm with your office first.
I'm on an F-1 right now and i already have a valid visa stamp. so i dont need a new one for a conference?

If your F-1 visa stamp is still valid and you're maintaining status, you usually don't need a new visa to attend a short conference in the US. The visa stamp only matters for re-entering the country after travel abroad. Since you're already in the US, you're not applying for a new visa for this trip.

Two things to confirm before you go:

- Your status: make sure your SEVIS record and your enrollment are current, and that you have a signed travel signature on your I-20 if you've been out of the country before.
- Your reimbursement: the same rule applies. Reimbursement for documented expenses is usually fine, but ask the international student office about any payment for the talk.

The international student office can confirm both quickly, so it's worth a short email before you book the flights.
im fitting a model on about 800 samples with 2000 features (gene expression), what should i pick, random forest, lasso logistic reg, or a small neural net? binary outcome

With n much smaller than p, I'd start with regularized logistic regression, either lasso or elastic net. It handles p >> n well, does feature selection, and is easy to interpret, which matters for gene expression. Random forest is a solid second option and good for non-linear effects, but can be noisy with so many irrelevant features. A neural net is the weakest choice here: 800 samples isn't enough to train it reliably, and it will overfit unless heavily regularized.

Whichever you use, use nested cross-validation so your performance estimate isn't optimistic.
elastic net vs lasso then? genes are correlated

Elastic net, then. Lasso tends to pick one gene out of a correlated group arbitrarily, and which one it picks can change between resamples, so your selected set is unstable. Elastic net's L2 part lets correlated genes share weight, which gives more stable selection and often better prediction.

Tune both alpha (L1/L2 mix) and lambda by cross-validation. Try alpha values like 0.1, 0.5, 0.9 as a coarse grid.
ok and should i standardize before? and do it inside cv folds right

Yes to both. Standardize features, since the penalty is scale-sensitive, and fit the scaler on the training fold only, then apply it to the validation fold. Same goes for any feature filtering or batch correction. Doing those steps on the full data before splitting leaks information and inflates your scores. In scikit-learn, put the scaler and the model in a Pipeline and run cross-validation on the pipeline, and it handles this automatically.

turns: ok so I've been running a basic 5x5 for about 7 weeks, 3 days a week, and my squat has completely stalled at 85kg. I already tried deloading to 75 and building back up like the program says and I got stuck at 85 AGAIN. same rep, rep 4 of set 3 just dies every time. what am I doing wrong

Stalling twice at the same weight after a deload usually means the deload fixed fatigue but not the actual limiter. A few common culprits:

1. **Recovery outside the gym.** Sleep under 7 hours or eating at maintenance (or below) will cap linear progression fast. If your bodyweight hasn't gone up at all in 7 weeks, that's a strong suspect.
2. **Squatting heavy 3x a week.** Linear 5x5 has you squatting every session. Past the beginner phase, that's often too much volume at too high an intensity.
3. **Technique breaking down under load.** Failing on the same rep of the same set is often a bracing or depth issue. If the bar drifts forward or your hips shoot up first, that's where reps die.

Quick things to try: film a set from the side, check your sleep and bodyweight trend, and consider switching one of the three squat days to a lighter day (around 80% of your working weight). How's your food and sleep been?
sleep is like 6 hrs on a good night, client deadlines. weight is basically flat. but honestly I don't want to eat a ton more, I sit at a desk all day and don't want to get soft

That pretty much explains it. Six hours of sleep with flat bodyweight is a tough combination for adding weight to the bar every session. Linear progression depends on recovering fully between workouts, and right now you aren't.

You don't have to bulk hard. Options:

- **Small surplus.** Around 200 to 300 kcal over maintenance, aiming for maybe 0.25 kg gain a month. That's very little fat if protein is high (roughly 1.6 to 2 g per kg).
- **Accept slower progression.** Stay at maintenance but switch to a program that progresses weekly instead of every session, like Texas Method or a simple heavy/light/medium split. Gains come slower but they keep coming.
- **Protect sleep where you can.** Even getting 6 hours up to 7 on training nights helps more than most supplements.

If you'd rather not touch your diet, the second option is the realistic one.
fine. so heavy light medium, what would that actually look like for squat with me stuck at 85

Something like this, using 85 kg as your current top:

**Monday (heavy):** 5x5 at 80 kg, building up over weeks. Once you hit all 25 reps, add 2.5 kg the next week.

**Wednesday (light):** 2x5 at about 65 kg. Move the bar fast and keep your technique sharp. This should feel easy.

**Friday (medium):** 3x5 at around 72.5 kg, or one top set of 5 that you push a little harder.

Only Monday's weight drives progression. The light and medium days just let you practice the movement without burying your recovery.

Start Monday at 80 rather than 85. Hitting clean reps for a couple of weeks will get you past 85 faster than grinding failed sets. Expect to add around 2.5 kg every week or two instead of every session. And film the heavy day, because if rep 4 still dies at the same spot it's more likely technique than fatigue.

Switching gears a bit. I got two months behind on my Visa card after a client paid late and now I'm stressing. how do I set up a payment plan with the card company? I want to call them tomorrow morning and I've never done this before so please walk me through what to say and do

Here's a step-by-step approach for the call:

1. Have your account number, your last few statements, and your income and expenses in front of you.
2. Call the number on the back of the card and ask for the hardship or payment assistance department. Some issuers route you there if you say you're struggling to make payments.
3. Explain briefly what happened: a client paid late, you're behind by two payments, and you want to get back on track. You don't need to over-explain.
4. Ask what options they have. Common ones are a temporary lower APR, a reduced monthly payment for a set number of months, or waiving late fees.
5. Get the terms in writing, or in the app, before you agree. Check the new monthly amount, how long it lasts, and what happens to the interest.
6. Ask them to stop late fees while the plan is active, and ask whether they'll report the account as current to the credit bureaus.
7. Set up autopay for the new amount, so you don't fall behind again.

If they say no to everything, ask to speak to a supervisor, and ask whether a nonprofit credit counselling service is an option for your situation.

thanks, that helps a lot. different thing: can someone explain why my bench went DOWN when I added more sets. I went from 3x8 to 5x8 at 60kg thinking more volume = more growth and after 3 weeks I can barely get 60 for 6 reps. that makes zero sense to me

It makes sense once you separate fitness from fatigue. Every session does two things: it builds a training adaptation and it piles on fatigue. What you can lift on any given day is roughly your underlying strength minus the fatigue you're carrying.

Going from 3 to 5 sets at the same load raised your volume by about 67% in one go. Your body couldn't recover from that between sessions, so fatigue built up faster than strength. The strength is probably still there; it's just masked.

Some signs this is what's going on:
- Bar feels heavy from the warmups
- Shoulders or elbows feel achy
- Reps slow down earlier than they used to

Take a lighter week (3x8 at around 50 kg) and then test again. Most people bounce back above where they were before. When you add volume, add one set at a time every couple of weeks.
but every article says volume is the main driver of hypertrophy. so is that just wrong?

It's not wrong, but people leave out the condition that comes with it: volume drives growth **only as far as you can recover from it**. The research looking at weekly sets shows more sets usually means more growth, up to a point. Past that point the extra sets mostly add fatigue.

That ceiling is different for everyone. It depends on your training age, sleep, food, stress, and how hard each set is. Five sets of 8 taken close to failure is very different from five sets left with 3 reps in the tank.

Think of volume as something you build up to, not a dial you crank all at once. Studies showing higher volume works usually ramp people up over weeks, or they use trained subjects who already tolerate it.

So the articles are right in general, but a jump like yours skipped the adaptation part.
ok how do I actually know when I've hit my ceiling then, without wrecking myself again

There's no blood test for it, but you can watch for a few practical signals:

1. **Performance trend.** If reps or load at the same effort stall or drop for two sessions in a row, you're probably at or past what you can recover from.
2. **Reps in reserve.** Track how many reps you think you had left on each set. If the same weight starts feeling like 1 RIR when it used to feel like 3, fatigue is building.
3. **Soreness and joints.** Muscle soreness that lasts into the next session, or achy elbows and shoulders, are early warnings.
4. **Motivation and sleep.** Dreading sessions or sleeping worse can be a sign too, though that's noisier.

A simple way to do it: go back to 3 sets, then add one set every 2 weeks while performance keeps climbing. The first time it stalls, drop back one set. That's roughly your working ceiling for now, and it tends to rise as you get more trained.

I've rewritten my resume twice now and still getting zero callbacks for in-house design roles. 40 applications. I'm a freelance product/brand designer, 6 yrs. trying to decide between three formats: (a) classic reverse chronological with each client listed as its own job, (b) one entry 'Freelance Designer 2019-present' with bullets per client, or (c) skills-based/functional. which one actually works for freelancers going in-house

Go with (b), and avoid (c).

**(a) Each client as its own job** makes you look like a job-hopper. Ten three-month "roles" get read as instability, especially by ATS and by recruiters skimming in six seconds.

**(b) One umbrella entry** reads as six years of continuous experience, which is what you actually have. Put "Independent Product & Brand Designer, 2019 to present" on top, then 4 to 6 bullets, each naming a client and an outcome: "Redesigned onboarding for [fintech client], cutting drop-off 18%." You can group by type (product work / brand work) if you have lots of clients.

**(c) Functional** resumes are a known red flag. Recruiters assume you're hiding gaps, and many ATS parse them badly.

At 40 applications with no callbacks, the format might not be the only problem, though. Are you tailoring the summary and bullets to each posting, and does your portfolio link sit at the very top?

portfolio is at the top. I wasn't tailoring much, honestly. but my current version is basically (a) so maybe that's it. with (b) how do I handle the 2 big retainer clients I had for like 2 years each? feels wrong to bury them in bullets

Good point. Long retainers are your strongest evidence that you can work like an in-house designer, so don't flatten them.

A hybrid works well:

**Independent Product & Brand Designer** | 2019 to present
- *Retainer: Acme Health (2020 to 2022).* Embedded with the product team as sole designer; shipped redesigned patient app used by 40k users.
- *Retainer: Northwind Logistics (2022 to 2024).* Owned design system across 3 products; cut handoff time for engineering.
- Selected projects: brand identity for X, landing page for Y, ...

The retainers get their own sub-headings and 2 to 3 bullets each, and the shorter gigs get condensed into one line. A recruiter sees continuity plus two long, team-embedded engagements, which is basically in-house experience.

Use words like "embedded," "collaborated with PMs and engineers," and "stakeholders" in those bullets. They signal you already know how to work inside a team.
that's way better than what I had. so (b) with the retainers pulled out, not (a). you're sure ATS doesn't choke on the sub-headings?

Yes, with the retainers pulled out like that. ATS handles it fine as long as you keep the formatting simple:

- Use normal text for the sub-headings (bold or italic is fine). Don't use tables, text boxes, or columns for that section.
- Keep the main entry in a standard pattern: title, "company" (you can write "Self-employed" or your studio name), dates.
- Submit as .docx or a text-based PDF, not an exported image or a heavily designed InDesign file. Designers get caught by this a lot.

If you want to check, paste the resume into a plain text editor. If the order and text come through cleanly, an ATS will read it.

Then add the tailoring: swap 2 or 3 bullets and the summary line to mirror each posting's language. That plus the format change should move your callback rate.

title: I'm doing a part-time online MA…
