title: how do i teach my 1…

question_types: how-to: wants step-by-step instructions to do something

turns: how do i teach my 1 yr old lab to stop jumping on ppl when they come in the door, kids friends come over and its chaos

The simplest method is to reward the behavior you want and remove the reward for jumping, which is attention.

1. Teach a solid 'sit' first, away from the door.
2. Practice a 'go to your spot' cue, like a mat or bed a few feet from the door.
3. When someone comes in, ask her to sit or go to the mat before anyone greets her.
4. If she jumps, everyone turns away, goes silent and avoids eye contact. The moment all four paws are on the floor, give calm attention or a treat.
5. Keep her on a leash at first so you can guide her.
she does sit fine but not when shes excited lol

That's common, since excitement overrides her training. Practice in steps by building up the arousal level.

- Start with a boring setup: you open and close the door with no one there, and treat her for staying seated.
- Next, have someone knock or ring the bell, and reward her for sitting.
- Then a family member comes in, then a friend.

Keep her on a leash or behind a baby gate until she's reliable. Also exercise her before guests arrive, since a tired lab is far easier. Use really tasty treats, like chicken, only for these practice runs.
can i get the kids friends to help or will they mess it up

They can help if you give them one clear job. Tell them: 'don't talk to her or touch her until she sits, then you can pet her.' Kids usually love having a rule. It helps to practice with one friend at a time, and with your own kids first, before a whole group arrives.

If the friends get over-excited, just keep the dog behind a gate or in another room until things calm down, and then let her in. Don't punish her if it goes wrong. That's just a rehearsal that needs more practice.
ok how long till she stops completely

With daily practice, expect noticeable improvement in 2 to 3 weeks, and fairly reliable behavior in 6 to 8 weeks. Labs at a year old are still adolescent, so some backsliding is normal, especially with new people. The biggest factor is consistency: if even one person lets her jump sometimes, the behavior stays alive. Making sure everyone follows the same rule matters more than the number of sessions.

title: So I started running in July…

question_types: troubleshooting: something is broken or not working and they describe what they see
feedback: pastes or describes their own draft, numbers or idea and asks for review
planning: wants help putting together a plan or schedule

turns: So I started running in July to get away from the desk (I'm a freelance designer, basically sit 9 hours a day). Doing a couch-to-5k type thing, 3 runs a week. Got up to about 4km continuous. But for the past two weeks the outside of my right knee starts hurting around 2km in, gets sharp enough that I have to walk. Fine when I walk, fine the next day. What's going on?

Pain on the outside of the knee that starts at a predictable point into a run, eases when you stop, and is fine the next day is a classic pattern for **IT band syndrome** (ITBS). It's very common in newer runners who ramp up mileage.

The IT band runs along the outside of your thigh to just below the knee. Irritation usually comes from:
- Increasing distance or frequency faster than your tissues adapt
- Weak hip muscles (especially glute medius), so the knee drifts inward
- Running on cambered roads, always on the same side
- Worn-out shoes, or a big overstride

Lots of sitting can play a part too, since tight hip flexors and underused glutes are common with desk work.

I can't diagnose it, so if there's swelling, locking, or pain at rest, see a physio or sports doctor. But if it matches what I described, it's usually very manageable. Did anything change in the last few weeks: route, shoes, distance?
I did switch to running along the river path which has kind of a slope toward the water. And I've been on the same old trainers I've had for years, not running shoes really

Both of those are likely contributors.

**The sloped path:** if you always run the same direction, one leg is effectively always on the lower side, which changes how your hip and knee move. Your right knee could be taking the brunt of that. Try running out-and-back and switching sides of the path, or find a flatter route for a couple of weeks.

**Old trainers:** casual trainers often have little support and are worn unevenly after years. That can affect how your foot lands and loads the knee. It's worth getting a proper running shoe. A running store can watch you on a treadmill and suggest a neutral or stability shoe.

In the meantime:
- Cut back to a distance that's pain-free, maybe 2km or run/walk intervals.
- Start some hip strengthening (clamshells, side-lying leg raises, glute bridges) 3 times a week.
- Foam roll the outer thigh and glutes if it feels good, though the evidence that rolling fixes ITBS is mixed.

Give it 2 to 3 weeks with these changes.
bought shoes, flat route now, did the hip stuff for 10 days. pain now comes at like 3km instead of 2 which is better but it's still there. kind of discouraging

That's actually real progress. Going from 2km to 3km before pain in 10 days shows things are moving in the right direction. ITBS often takes 4 to 8 weeks to settle fully, so this is about what you'd expect.

A few things to adjust now:

1. **Stop runs before the pain**, not at it. If it starts at 3km, run 2.5km and stop, or switch to run/walk. Running into pain keeps irritating it.
2. **Make the hip work harder.** If clamshells feel easy, add a resistance band, or progress to side planks, single-leg glute bridges, and lateral band walks.
3. **Shorten your stride a bit.** Aim for slightly quicker, lighter steps. Increasing cadence by 5 to 10% reduces load on the knee and hip for many runners.
4. **Break up sitting.** Stand or walk for a few minutes each hour, and stretch hip flexors at the desk.

If it isn't continuing to improve after another 3 to 4 weeks, a physio visit is worth it. They can check your movement and give you targeted exercises.
how do I know my cadence? I have an old apple watch

Your Apple Watch tracks it. In the Workout app, during an outdoor run, you can add cadence to the workout view: open the Watch app on your iPhone, go to Workout, then Workout View, choose Outdoor Run, and add the Cadence metric. After a run, it also shows in the Fitness app under the workout details, as steps per minute.

If your watch or watchOS version doesn't show cadence, count manually: count right-foot strikes for 30 seconds and multiply by 4.

For beginners running easy, cadence is commonly around 150 to 165. There's no magic number like 180; that comes from elite runners at race pace. Just take your current number and aim 5 to 10% higher. If you're at 155, try about 165.

A metronome app or a playlist at that BPM helps a lot. It feels short and choppy at first, which is normal.
I'm at 152. ok 165 it is, will try the metronome. anything else or just wait it out

That's most of it. A few more things to keep it moving in the right direction:

- **Progress slowly once it's pain-free.** When you can do 3 runs in a row with no pain, add about 10% distance per week, no more. Don't jump straight back to where you were.
- **Keep the hip strength work going** even after the pain is gone. Most ITBS comes back when people stop.
- **Warm up.** 5 minutes of brisk walking plus leg swings and a few bodyweight squats before running.
- **Ice after** if it's sore. Not required, but can help with discomfort.
- **Watch for warning signs:** pain at rest, swelling, pain that comes on earlier instead of later. Those mean see a physio.

So: new shoes, flat route, shorter stride at 165 cadence, hip work, and stopping before it hurts. That's a solid plan. Give it a few weeks before judging it.

I work from home as a freelance designer and I've been living on toast and takeout for months, so I decided to start meal prepping on Sundays. I'm cooking for just me, budget around 60 euros a week, I have a small kitchen with two burners and an oven, and I don't love eating the exact same thing every day. Here's my first attempt at a plan, can you tell me if it's realistic or where it falls apart?

Sunday prep:
- big pot of chickpea curry (4 portions)
- tray of roasted veg (peppers, courgette, red onion, sweet potato)
- 6 chicken breasts baked with paprika
- pot of quinoa
- 6 hard-boiled eggs

Week:
- lunches: quinoa + roasted veg + chicken, Mon-Fri
- dinners: chickpea curry Mon-Thu, Friday takeout
- breakfast: 2 eggs + toast
- snacks: whatever

I'm guessing it'll take 2 hours on Sunday.

It's a solid first plan. The components are good, prep for a two-burner kitchen is feasible, and 60 euros a week should cover it comfortably. A few places it might fall apart:

**1. Repetition.** Five identical lunches plus four identical dinners is the most common reason people quit meal prep, and you already said you dislike sameness. Fix: keep the same base components but change how they're served. For example, Mon/Tue quinoa bowl, Wed chicken and veg in a wrap with hummus, Thu chicken and veg over pasta, Fri a grain salad with feta and lemon.

**2. Chicken by Friday.** Cooked chicken keeps 3 to 4 days in the fridge. Freeze 2 breasts on Sunday and move them to the fridge Wednesday night.

**3. Six eggs isn't enough.** Two a day for breakfast is 14 a week. Either boil 10 to 12, or boil 6 and fry eggs fresh some mornings.

**4. The curry for four nights straight.** Freeze two portions and rotate in something quick on other nights, like an omelette with leftover veg or pasta with the roasted veg blended into a sauce.

**5. Two hours is realistic** if you overlap: chicken and veg share the oven, curry and quinoa go on the two burners, eggs go into the quinoa pot's spare time or a kettle trick afterwards. Expect 2.5 hours the first time.

**6. "Snacks: whatever"** is where takeout sneaks back. Plan two or three: yogurt, fruit, nuts, hummus with carrots.

So it's realistic. The main changes are more variety in how you serve things, freezing some portions, and planning snacks.

Okay, thanks. On another note, I'm a freelance designer, so my week is unpredictable. Some weeks I have client calls in the morning, some weeks I'm free. I'm training for a 5k personal best in 6 weeks and I'm currently running three times a week at about 5k each. How do I plan this when my schedule keeps changing?

A flexible plan works better than a fixed one for a freelancer. Here's a setup that adapts to your week:

- Keep three runs per week as the core, but don't assign them to specific days. Pick two or three windows you can usually protect, like early morning or the lunch hour.
- Make one run a quality session, such as 4 x 800 m at a hard but controlled pace with 90 seconds of easy jogging between reps. It doesn't need a fixed day, just a slot in the week.
- Keep the other two runs easy, around 5 km at a conversational pace.
- Taper for the final week: two short runs and one easy 3 km with a few strides.

When a week gets busy, do the quality session first, since that's the one that moves your 5k time most.
what if i miss a session because of a client deadline, do i just skip it or move it

Skip it, don't try to make it up. Moving it to a day when you're already tired adds fatigue, and that's the thing that actually breaks a training block.

A simple rule:

- If you miss the quality session, do the easy runs that week as planned and get the quality session back the next week.
- If you miss an easy run, leave it out entirely.
- If you miss two or more sessions in a week, don't double up the next week. Just resume the normal plan.

With 6 weeks to go, a missed session is a small loss. Focus on the sessions you can get in, and make sure the last two or three quality runs are done well.

title: I'm about to redesign the database…

question_types: planning: wants help putting together a plan or schedule
explanation: wants to understand why or how something works
explanation: wants to understand why or how something works

turns: I'm about to redesign the database for our internal booking system (Postgres 15, about 40 tables, grown messy over 5 years) and I'd like to put together a migration plan that won't cause downtime. Where would you start?

I'd split it into phases so each step is reversible:

1. **Inventory and baseline**: document current tables, FKs, indexes, and the queries that hit them (pg_stat_statements helps). Find out which tables are hot and which are rarely touched.
2. **Define the target schema**: draw the new model, normalize where it matters, and list every change as a delta from today.
3. **Expand/contract migrations**: add new tables and columns alongside the old ones, backfill, dual-write, switch reads, and only then drop the old stuff.
4. **Cutover and cleanup** once you've verified parity.

Do you have a staging environment with a recent copy of production data?
Yes, staging gets a nightly restore from prod. We also have a pretty thin test suite, which worries me. What do I do about that?

Thin tests plus a schema change is the riskiest combination, so I'd put test work in the plan before any migrations:

- Add characterization tests around the 10 to 15 most important queries and endpoints, capturing current outputs from staging.
- Write data consistency checks as SQL, such as row counts and sums between old and new tables, that you can run repeatedly during the migration.
- Add a shadow-read step: for a while, query both old and new structures and log any differences without affecting users.

Budget a week or so for this. It pays back quickly when you're doing backfills.
Makes sense. How should I sequence the actual table changes? I have a few big ones, like splitting a bookings table that holds customer info inline.

Start with the lowest-risk, highest-value changes, and keep the big splits for later when your tooling is proven.

For the bookings split specifically:
1. Create a new customers table (nullable FK on bookings, no constraint enforcement yet).
2. Deploy code that writes to both places on new bookings.
3. Backfill existing rows in batches of, say, 10,000, with pauses so you don't overload replication.
4. Add the FK as NOT VALID, then run VALIDATE CONSTRAINT separately, which avoids a long lock.
5. Switch reads to the new table, watch shadow-read diffs.
6. Drop the old inline columns a release or two later.

Index creation should use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
Good. How long should I give the whole thing? I need to give my manager a timeline.

For 40 tables with a thin test suite, I'd estimate something like 10 to 14 weeks if one or two people are on it part-time, and you can state it as a range with milestones:

- Weeks 1-2: inventory, target schema, review
- Weeks 3-4: test and consistency-check scaffolding
- Weeks 5-9: migrations in order of risk, with the bookings split around weeks 7-9
- Weeks 10-12: cleanup, dropping old columns, index tuning
- Weeks 13-14: buffer

Say the buffer explicitly. Managers tend to respond well to a plan where the uncertain parts are labeled.
What would you flag as the main risks I should mention?

I'd list these:

- **Backfill load** slowing production or lagging replicas. Mitigation: batch, throttle, run off-peak.
- **Long locks** from ALTER TABLE or constraint validation. Mitigation: NOT VALID plus VALIDATE, lock_timeout settings.
- **Hidden consumers** such as reports, BI tools, or cron scripts that read the old tables directly. Mitigation: check pg_stat_user_tables and query logs, and keep compatibility views for a while.
- **Dual-write drift**, where the two copies get out of sync. Mitigation: the consistency checks.
- **Scope creep**, because every redesign tempts people to fix more. Mitigation: freeze the target schema after review.
Hidden consumers is a good point, we definitely have some analyst queries I don't know about. Any tip on finding them?

A few ways to find them:

- Turn on log_min_duration_statement (or temporarily log all statements) with application_name and user in the log prefix, then group by role and query text.
- Check pg_stat_statements joined with pg_roles to see which roles hit which tables.
- List database roles and connections: anything not from your app's service account is suspect. pg_stat_activity shows live ones.
- Ask the analysts directly and send a short heads-up message with the table names that will change.

As a safety net, create views with the old table names that map to the new structure, so older queries keep working during a transition period.

Thanks, I'll try that. Unrelated: can you explain why my 10 week old puppy bites harder when she's excited, and why 'gentle' redirection sometimes makes it worse? I want to understand the mechanism before I start trying things, because the advice online contradicts itself.

Puppy biting when excited is mostly about arousal and play. Puppies explore the world with their mouths, and when they're worked up, their bite inhibition hasn't developed yet. They haven't learned how hard is too hard, because they're learning that from their littermates and from people reacting to them. Excitement also raises their heart rate and energy, so they stop controlling their jaws as well as they will later.

Why gentle redirection can make it worse: if you redirect a very aroused puppy with a soft, drawn-out voice or slow hand movements, the calm signal may not register. The slow movement can look like a game, so she grabs harder. Quick, short cues tend to work better than long explanations.

The contradictory advice usually comes from different stages. Calm redirection can work when the puppy is only mildly excited. When she's at full speed, it's often better to stop the play for a few seconds, so the game ends and she learns that rough mouthing makes the fun stop. Consistency matters more than any one technique, since the aim is for her to learn that gentle mouthing keeps play going and hard biting ends it.

Could you explain why we normalise to third normal form for a typical orders and customers schema, and when it's sensible to denormalise? I'm building a reporting table for a dashboard and I want to understand the reasoning, not just the rule. We're on Postgres.

Normalising to third normal form (3NF) is about avoiding update anomalies. If a customer's address is stored on every order row, changing the address means updating many rows, and if you miss one, the data disagrees with itself. 3NF says each fact lives in one place. Customers go in a customers table, orders reference them by customer_id, and order items reference products.

Denormalising makes sense when reads dominate and the duplication is controlled. For a reporting table, you usually don't need the strict rules, because the table is rebuilt or appended to on a schedule, not edited row by row.

A reasonable approach for your dashboard:

- Keep the normalised tables as the source of truth.
- Build a reporting table that pre-joins what the dashboard needs, such as order date, customer segment and product category.
- Refresh it from the source tables on a schedule, or with a materialized view in Postgres.
- Don't write to the reporting table directly, so there's only one place where the logic lives.

That gives you fast queries without losing the integrity of the main data.

title: first half marathon is in march.…

question_types: comparison: deciding between two or three specific options

turns: first half marathon is in march. deciding between hal higdon novice 1, nike run club plan, or runna. which one

All three can get you to the finish. They differ in structure and flexibility:

**Hal Higdon Novice 1**
- 12 weeks, 4 runs a week, long run builds to 10 miles.
- Free, simple, very proven. Mostly easy runs, no speed work.
- Best if you want a simple, low-injury-risk plan.

**Nike Run Club**
- Free app, guided audio runs with coaches.
- Includes intervals and tempo runs, adapts lightly.
- Best if you like motivation in your ears.

**Runna**
- Paid (~$20/month), builds a personalized plan from your current pace and goal time.
- Mix of easy, intervals, tempo, long runs. Syncs to watches.
- Best if you have a time goal and want structure.

What's your current running level and do you have a goal time or just finishing?
running 3x a week, 5k in about 29 min. goal is under 2:15

Your 5k pace suggests a half around 2:12 to 2:18 with proper training, so 2:15 is realistic.

For a time goal like that:

- **Higdon Novice 1** is focused on finishing. You'd likely get there, but it doesn't really target a time.
- **Higdon Novice 2** adds a bit of pace work. A better fit if you like Higdon.
- **Runna** is the most goal-oriented. It sets paces for each run based on your 5k time and the 2:15 target.
- **NRC** has some speed work but less precise pacing.

When is the race exactly? That affects which plan length fits.
march 15

That's about 22 weeks from now. More time than any of these plans need.

Options:
- **Base building first.** Spend 8 to 10 weeks just running 3 to 4 times a week easy, getting your long run to 8 to 10k. Then start a 12-week plan in mid-December.
- **Runna** lets you set the race date and it builds the full timeline, including base phase.
- **Higdon** you'd just start in mid-December.

The extra time is good. Most first-half injuries come from building too fast, so a long runway lowers that risk.
runna vs higdon novice 2 then. is runna worth paying

Depends what you'd use it for.

**Runna is worth it if:**
- You want specific paces for each session and don't want to calculate them.
- You like plans that adjust when you miss a run or get faster.
- You'll use the watch sync (Garmin, Apple Watch, Coros) so workouts load automatically.

**Higdon Novice 2 is enough if:**
- You're fine with "easy pace" and "race pace" without exact numbers.
- You'd rather not pay ~$20/month for 5 months (~$100).
- You like a simple PDF on the fridge.

Price-wise, Runna often has a free trial. You could try it for a week or two and see if you actually follow the sessions.
does runna push too hard? read some reddit stuff saying people got injured

That's a known criticism. Some users report Runna's plans being aggressive, especially:

- **Speed work** that's fast relative to the runner's actual easy fitness, often because the starting 5k time entered was optimistic or old.
- **Mileage jumps** that can be steep for newer runners.
- **Too much intensity overall.** Some weeks have 2 hard sessions out of 3 to 4 runs.

To reduce the risk if you use it:
- Enter a **recent, honest** 5k time.
- Pick the more conservative plan options and fewer sessions per week.
- Run easy days actually easy. If you can't talk in sentences, slow down.
- Skip or soften a session if anything hurts.

Higdon is gentler by design, which is why it's often recommended for first half marathons.
what about combining. higdon base, add one runna-style interval session

That's a reasonable middle ground. Something like:

- Follow Higdon Novice 2 as the backbone.
- Replace one of the shorter midweek runs with an interval or tempo session.
- Keep the long run and the other easy runs as written.

Example interval sessions to rotate:
- 6 x 400m at 5k pace (~5:45/km), 90 sec jog between
- 4 x 1km at half marathon goal pace (~6:20/km), 2 min jog
- 20 min tempo at a comfortably hard pace

Don't add it on top of the plan, swap it in. Total running stays the same, just one session is harder.

And don't do intervals the day before the long run.
what pace should easy runs be

For your fitness, roughly **7:00 to 7:45 per km** (about 11:15 to 12:30 per mile).

That probably feels slow, which is the point. Easy runs build aerobic base and let you recover for the harder sessions.

Simple checks:
- You can talk in full sentences.
- Heart rate is in the low-to-mid zone 2, roughly 65 to 75% of max if you track it.
- You finish feeling like you could do more.

Most newer runners do easy runs too fast, which makes everything feel medium and increases injury risk.
ok going with higdon novice 2 + 1 interval day. starting dec 1 with base till then

That's a solid plan. Quick recap:

**Now to Nov 30 (base)**
- 3 to 4 runs a week, all easy (7:00 to 7:45/km).
- Build long run gradually from 5k to 8 to 10k.
- Increase total weekly distance by about 10% max.

**Dec 1 to Mar 15 (race plan)**
- Higdon Novice 2, 12 weeks. That ends around Feb 22, so you have about 3 extra weeks. Either repeat some mid-plan weeks or start the 12-week plan around Dec 22 instead.
- Swap one midweek run for intervals or tempo.
- Long runs stay easy.

**Extras**
- Do one practice race or 10k in Jan/Feb to test goal pace.
- Practice fueling on long runs over 75 min.

If you want, start the plan Dec 22 and use December to extend base and get used to the interval session.

title: got a panel interview thursday for…

question_types: quick fact: a short factual question, then a follow-up or two
explanation: wants to understand why or how something works
troubleshooting: something is broken or not working and they describe what they see
explanation: wants to understand why or how something works

turns: got a panel interview thursday for a project coordinator job at a freight company. im a working parent so i can only prep after the kids are in bed, like 9-10pm. quick one: how long should each answer be? mine keep running like 5 minutes and i think i lose them

Aim for roughly 60 to 90 seconds per answer, and two minutes is about the ceiling for a big behavioral question. Panels usually have three to five people and a set list of questions, so a five-minute answer eats the time for everyone else's questions and they start tuning out. A quick check: time yourself reading the answer out loud. If you're past two minutes, cut the background and the 'why this happened' part and get to what you did and what changed. Keep the result specific, something like 'the shipment was three days late, I rerouted two pallets, and the client didn't lose the order.'
ok that helps. so what's the STAR thing everyone keeps saying

STAR is a structure for behavioral answers. Situation is one or two sentences of context. Task is what you were responsible for. Action is what you specifically did, and it's the biggest part. Result is what happened, with a number if you have one. Most people spend too long on Situation and too little on Action, which is what interviewers are scoring. For a project coordinator role, your Actions might cover scheduling, chasing vendors, or clearing blockers. Write one story per STAR, then practice telling each in about 90 seconds.
that didn't work for me last time tbh, i kept forgetting the result part

That's really common, and it usually means the result got tacked on at the end when you were already tired. Try writing the result first. Finish the sentence 'because of what I did, ___ happened.' If you can't fill that blank with something concrete, the story probably needs a different example. A rough number is fine too: 'cut onboarding from two weeks to one' works. Then practice telling the story backwards from the result so you always land on it.
ok wait what if i don't have a good result. like the project just kinda ended

Then say what changed afterward and be honest about the outcome. 'The project was shelved after two quarters, but the vendor checklist I built was still in use a year later' is a real result. Interviewers mostly want to see how you think about outcomes. Don't invent a metric you can't defend, because the follow-up questions will find it. If the outcome is truly empty, pick a different story. Have at least three ready for different themes: conflict, deadline pressure, and a mistake you made.
and if i only have like 3 evenings before thursday, what do i actually do

Evening one: write four or five stories in STAR form as bullet points, and don't polish them. Evening two: say each one out loud, timed, and cut anything past two minutes. Evening three: do a full mock with a friend, or record yourself on your phone and watch it once. Also skim the company's recent news and the job posting, and pick two questions to ask them at the end. Forty-five focused minutes a night will get you further than rereading notes for hours.
perfect. one more thing, what if they ask why i left my last job, which was because my old boss was awful. how do i say that without sounding bitter

Keep it to one sentence about the reason, then pivot to what you're looking for. Something like: 'I was ready for more ownership, and my last role had limited room for that. I'm looking for a place where coordinators run projects end to end.' Don't name the boss or describe what happened, even if it was bad, because interviewers hear that as a red flag about you. If they press, say you'd rather focus on the role ahead, then give a positive example of what you want next.

ok switching gears. my sister is getting married in november and i'm supposed to give the maid of honor speech. im a working parent with two kids so i have basically no time. why do people say the speech should be short? like what's the actual reason, not just 'keep it brief'

The main reason is attention. Wedding guests have been through the ceremony, cocktails and dinner, often after a long day of travel, and the room's patience drops off sharply after about three minutes. A short speech also makes the good moments land harder. A sharp story and a clear closing line hit better than a long run of memories. There's a practical side too: long speeches drift into inside jokes that only you and the bride understand, and the rest of the room checks out. Most good maid of honor speeches run four to five minutes, roughly 500 to 650 words spoken at a relaxed pace.
that makes sense. wait so is the 5 min thing a hard rule or can i go longer if the story is good

It's not a hard rule. If the story is strong, a bit longer is fine, but most rooms start to fidget somewhere around six or seven minutes. Length matters less than whether each part earns its place. If you're unsure, read it aloud once with a timer. If you're over six minutes, look for a story that repeats a point you already made and cut it. Also speak slower than feels natural, because nerves make people talk faster, and that alone can add a minute.

Okay, thank you. Different topic now. I'm a working mum with two kids, and I've started making dal on Sunday nights so we have something healthy for weekday lunches. My mother-in-law makes this amazing dal and I'm trying to recreate it. I use masoor dal, boil it with turmeric and salt, then do a tadka of cumin seeds, garlic, dried red chillies and ghee. But mine tastes flat and kind of watery even though I follow what I think she does. What am I missing?

Flat and watery usually points to a few things:

1. **Dal not cooked down enough.** Masoor should break down completely and get creamy. After it's soft, whisk it or mash it with the back of a spoon and simmer uncovered for 5 to 10 minutes to thicken. Watery dal often just needs more cooking or less water to start (about 1:3 dal to water).
2. **Salt.** Dal needs more salt than people expect. Taste and add more at the end.
3. **Missing aromatics.** Many home dals include onion, tomato, ginger, or green chilli cooked into the dal itself, not just the tadka. Even half a chopped tomato boiled with the dal adds a lot of depth.
4. **Tadka technique.** The ghee must be hot enough that cumin seeds sizzle immediately. Garlic should turn golden, not pale. Then pour it into the dal straight away and cover for a minute so the aroma stays in.
5. **Acid at the end.** A squeeze of lemon or a bit of tamarind brightens flat flavor dramatically.

Does your mother-in-law use onion or tomato anywhere?

I asked her and she said she adds a tomato and some ginger when boiling, and a pinch of hing in the tadka. Also she uses a pressure cooker, I just use a pot. I made it again with all that and it's better, but still not quite the same and it got really thick the next day

Good progress. The tomato, ginger and hing are a big part of the flavor. For what's left:

**Thickening the next day** is normal. Dal keeps absorbing water as it cools, especially masoor. When reheating for lunches, add a splash of hot water and stir until it's the consistency you like. For packed lunches, you can also cook it slightly thinner on Sunday so it's right by Tuesday.

**Still not quite the same:**
- **Pressure cooker vs pot.** Pressure cooking breaks the dal down more evenly and gives a silkier texture. In a pot, cook longer and whisk well.
- **Ghee quantity.** Home cooks often use more ghee than they'd admit. Try 1.5 to 2 tablespoons in the tadka for a family pot.
- **Order in the tadka.** Ghee, cumin, then dried chilli and garlic, then hing right at the end for a few seconds so it doesn't burn.
- **A finishing touch.** Fresh coriander, a pinch of garam masala, or a second small tadka just before serving.

It might also be worth watching her make it once. Small details like heat level and timing are hard to describe.
watching her is a good idea actually. the kids find it a bit spicy with the chillies, but if I leave them out it's boring again

You can keep the flavor without the heat:

- **Use Kashmiri dried chillies.** They're mild with lots of colour and a fruity flavor. Or use fewer regular chillies and keep them whole: break them and they release much more heat.
- **Add the chillies for a few seconds only** in the tadka, then remove them before pouring.
- **Split the tadka.** Make the main tadka without chillies for everyone, then a small chilli-ghee tadka for the adults' bowls.
- **Add other flavor instead of heat:** a pinch of sugar or jaggery, more ginger, a bit of cumin powder, or a squeeze of lemon. These make dal taste fuller without spice.
- **Swap fresh green chilli for a tiny bit of black pepper** if you want warmth without a sharp burn.

A dab of ghee and a pinch of salt on the kids' portions also tends to make them happier with it.

I cook on Sundays for the whole week since I work full time and my two kids have activities most evenings. By Thursday the chicken I cooked always tastes dry and kind of off when I reheat it. Why does reheated chicken get like that, and is it actually safe?

Two things are happening. The dryness is because chicken breast is lean and already cooked until firm, so reheating pushes out more moisture. The 'off' taste is often called warmed-over flavor: once cooked meat sits, fats in it oxidize quickly, which gives that stale, cardboard-like taste. Poultry is especially prone to it.

Safety-wise, cooked chicken is generally good for 3 to 4 days in the fridge at or below 4C (40F). So Sunday's chicken is at the edge by Thursday. Reheat it to 74C (165F) throughout.
oh so thursday is too late? what should i do instead

It's borderline, so I'd treat Thursday as past the safe zone, especially if your fridge isn't super cold. A couple of options:

- Freeze half of the cooked chicken on Sunday and thaw portions overnight on Wednesday.
- Do a mini prep on Wednesday evening for the last days.
- Keep Thursday and Friday meals vegetarian or based on beans, eggs, or canned fish.

Also cool it quickly: portion into shallow containers and refrigerate within two hours, rather than letting a big pot sit out.
and why does freezing help? doesnt it also dry stuff out

Freezing doesn't stop bacterial growth permanently, but it pauses it, since bacteria become dormant below about -18C. So the clock basically stops while it's frozen, and starts again once thawed. That's why thawed leftovers should be eaten within a day or two.

It can dry things out slightly if air gets to the food, which is freezer burn, plus some moisture is lost as ice crystals form and thaw. The fix is to seal it airtight, press out the air, and, for chicken, freeze it with some sauce or broth. That keeps it moist.
ok so thigh meat instead of breast would be better right? and sauce

Yes. Thighs have more fat and connective tissue, so they stay tender and juicy through reheating, and the extra fat also makes them more forgiving. Cooking them in a sauce, like a braise, curry, or salsa chicken, helps even more because the liquid protects the meat as it warms again. If you still want breast, slice it and store it in the sauce, then reheat gently in a covered pan or at 50% power in the microwave instead of full blast.

turns: can my landlord raise rent during a fixed 12 month lease in toronto or do they have to wait til it ends

In Ontario, a landlord generally can't raise rent during a fixed-term lease unless the lease itself has a clause allowing it, and those clauses are uncommon. Once the lease rolls over into a period-to-period tenancy, the landlord can increase rent once every 12 months, with at least 90 days written notice. The amount is capped by the provincial rent increase guideline for most units, but that cap doesn't apply to every building, so check which rules cover your unit.
ok what about units built after 2018, is it different

Yes. For units first occupied after November 15, 2018, rent control under the Residential Tenancies Act doesn't apply, so the landlord can set the increase amount. The 12-month rule and the 90-day written notice still apply. Ask the landlord whether the unit is exempt, and you can check the rules on the Landlord and Tenant Board website if you want to confirm.
lol ok my place is 2020 so no rent control. what if the new rent is like 15% more, can i just say no

You can refuse an increase that isn't legally permitted, such as one with the wrong notice or one during a fixed term. For an exempt unit, a valid increase still applies even if it's large. If you just refuse to pay a valid increase, the landlord can file an L1 application with the Landlord and Tenant Board for non-payment, and that can end in an eviction order. Your realistic options are to negotiate, to offer a longer lease in exchange for a smaller increase, or to give notice and move.
ok fine. if i negotiate what do i actually say, is there a script

Something like this works: 'Hi [name], thanks for the notice on the increase. I'd like to stay long term. Would you consider [X]% if I sign a two-year lease?' Keep it calm and short, and bring a couple of comparable listings in your area with their rents. If they agree, get the new terms in writing, either as an amendment to your lease or a signed letter, so the number is enforceable.

ok got it. unrelated, my lower back has been killing me for like 3 weeks. im a PM so basically laptop all day + meetings, i dont have a proper desk setup, mostly couch or kitchen table lol. no injury or anything just started aching. i want a plan to fix it, ive got maybe 20 min a day

That pattern (gradual onset, no injury, lots of sitting in poor positions) is the most common type of lower back pain, and it usually responds well to changes in setup and movement. If you get numbness, pain down the leg, weakness, bladder/bowel changes, or it's getting worse quickly, see a doctor first.

A simple plan for 20 min a day:

**Week 1 to 2: reduce irritation + move more**
- Fix the worst of the setup (more on this below)
- Walk 10 min daily, ideally broken up
- 10 min gentle mobility: cat-cow, child's pose, knee-to-chest, pelvic tilts

**Week 3 to 4: start strengthening**
- 10 min walking
- 10 min core and glutes: glute bridges, bird dogs, dead bugs, side planks

**Daily throughout**
- Get up every 30 to 45 min, even for a minute

ya kitchen table is doable. chairs are those wooden ones tho, not great

1. **Laptop up to eye level.** Stack books or get a laptop stand (~$20 to 30), plus a separate keyboard and mouse. This stops you hunching forward, which is a big contributor.
2. **Lumbar support on the chair.** A rolled towel or small cushion at your lower back, at belt height.
3. **Feet flat on the floor.** If the chair is high, use a box or footrest.
4. **Sit back in the chair** so your back touches the backrest with the cushion, rather than perching on the edge.
5. **Switch positions.** Some calls standing at a kitchen counter, some walking with earbuds.

The wooden chair is fine with a cushion. Moving often matters more than having the perfect chair.

- **Walking meetings.** Take 1 or 2 calls a day on foot, especially 1:1s.
- **Afternoon reset at 3pm.** 5 min: cat-cow, child's pose, a few glute bridges on the floor.
- **Stand for the end of the day.** Last hour at the kitchen counter, laptop on books.

Give it a week. The 5pm ache should show up later or less intensely.
what exactly do i do for the 20 min, like the actual routine

**Walk (10 min)**, easy pace, outside if possible.

**Mobility (10 min)**
1. Cat-cow: 10 slow reps
2. Child's pose: hold 30 sec, breathe deeply
3. Knee-to-chest: 30 sec each leg, lying on your back
4. Pelvic tilts: 15 reps, lying on back, flatten and arch your lower back gently
5. Glute bridges: 2 x 10, squeeze at the top
6. Figure-4 stretch: 30 sec each side (ankle on opposite knee, pull toward chest)
7. Lying spinal twist: 30 sec each side

All movements should feel like gentle stretching or effort, not sharp pain. If something hurts more, skip it.
and then week 3+ the strength stuff?

Yes. From week 3, swap most of the mobility for strength, but keep a couple of stretches:

**Walk (8 to 10 min)**

**Strength (10 to 12 min)**
1. Glute bridges: 3 x 12 (progress to single-leg)
2. Bird dog: 3 x 8 each side, slow, hold 2 sec at the end
3. Dead bug: 3 x 8 each side, keep lower back pressed down
4. Side plank: 2 x 20 to 30 sec each side (on knees if needed)
5. Cat-cow: 10 reps to finish

Do this 4 to 5 days a week. On the other days, just walk and do the stretching routine.

Progress every week or so: more reps, longer holds, or harder versions. The goal is a stronger core and glutes so your back isn't doing all the work.
how long til it actually goes away. i have a team offsite in 5 weeks w a lot of sitting lol

Most non-specific lower back pain like yours improves significantly within 4 to 6 weeks, especially when the trigger (sitting badly) is fixed. Since you already felt better after one day of setup changes, you're likely on the faster side.

Realistic expectations:
- **Week 1 to 2:** less pain during the day, shorter and milder flare-ups.
- **Week 3 to 4:** mostly fine, maybe some stiffness after long sitting.
- **Week 5:** should be in decent shape, though long sitting days might still cause some aching.

is a standing desk worth it or overhyped

A bit of both. Standing all day isn't better than sitting all day: it causes its own aches in feet, knees and back. The real benefit is being able to **switch** positions easily.

- You work from home most days long term.
- You'd actually alternate, like 30 to 60 min standing a few times a day.
- You have the space and budget ($200 to 500 for a decent electric one).

Probably not needed yet if:
- The kitchen counter already lets you stand for some calls.
- You're not sure you'll keep working from home.

ok so my niece asked me for help with her physics hw and i realized i remember nothing lol. problem: 5 kg block on a ramp at 30 degrees, coefficient of friction 0.2, find acceleration down the ramp. how do i even start these

These all follow the same recipe. Step by step:

1. **Draw the block and the forces on it.** There are three: gravity (mg, straight down), the normal force (N, perpendicular to the ramp, pushing out), and friction (f, along the ramp, opposing motion, so pointing up the ramp here).
2. **Tilt your axes.** Use x along the ramp (positive pointing down the slope) and y perpendicular to it. This is the key trick for ramps.
3. **Split gravity into components:**
   - Along the ramp: mg sin(30°)
   - Into the ramp: mg cos(30°)
4. **Perpendicular direction (y):** the block isn't moving into or off the ramp, so forces balance: N = mg cos(30°).
5. **Friction:** f = μN = μ mg cos(30°).
6. **Along the ramp (x), Newton's second law:** ma = mg sin(30°) - μ mg cos(30°).

Try plugging in the numbers (g = 9.8 m/s²) and see what you get.

That's right: a = 4.9 - 1.70 = **3.2 m/s²** (about 3.20).

Notice the mass canceled out. Every term had an m in it, so you could divide it away. That's why the 5 kg didn't matter for the acceleration. It'd matter if the question asked for the friction force or the normal force, though:

- N = 5 × 9.8 × 0.866 ≈ 42.4 N
- f = 0.2 × 42.4 ≈ 8.5 N

Teachers love asking for those in part (b), so worth having your niece compute them too.
she has a part b actually. now its pushed UP the ramp with initial speed 6 m/s, how far does it go before stopping

Same setup, but friction flips direction. Step by step:

1. **Moving up the ramp:** gravity's component still pulls down the ramp, and friction now also points down the ramp (opposing motion). Both slow it down.
2. **Net deceleration:** a = g sin(30°) + μ g cos(30°) = 4.9 + 1.70 = **6.6 m/s²**, pointing down the ramp.
3. **Use a kinematics equation** without time, since you don't know it:
   v² = v₀² - 2 a d
4. **At the stopping point** v = 0, so:
   0 = 6² - 2 × 6.6 × d
   d = 36 / 13.2 ≈ **2.7 m**

The main thing to remember: friction always opposes the direction of motion, so its sign depends on which way the block is moving.
wait why can we use that equation, she says they learned like 4 of them and she never knows which

The trick is to pick the one that doesn't include the quantity you don't know and don't care about. The four constant-acceleration equations:

1. v = v₀ + at (no d)
2. d = v₀t + ½at² (no v)
3. v² = v₀² + 2ad (no t)
4. d = ½(v₀ + v)t (no a)

How to pick, step by step:
1. List what you know: here v₀ = 6, v = 0, a = -6.6.
2. List what you want: d.
3. Find what's missing and irrelevant: t.
4. Use the equation without t: number 3.

In my last message I wrote it as v² = v₀² - 2ad because I made a positive and put the minus sign in. Same equation, just a sign convention. Tell her to pick a positive direction at the start and stick with it.
ok she gets it now. part c is 'will the block slide back down after stopping'. no idea how to approach that one

Compare the force pulling it down with the maximum friction that could hold it in place.

1. **Force pulling it down the ramp:** mg sin(30°) = 5 × 9.8 × 0.5 = 24.5 N
2. **Maximum static friction:** f_max = μ_s × N. The problem only gives one coefficient (0.2), so use that: 0.2 × 42.4 ≈ 8.5 N
3. **Compare:** 24.5 N > 8.5 N, so friction can't hold it. **Yes, it slides back down**, with the acceleration from part (a), 3.2 m/s².

A shortcut: a block on a ramp stays put only if tan(θ) ≤ μ_s. Here tan(30°) ≈ 0.577, which is way more than 0.2, so it slides.

If the problem gave a separate static coefficient (μ_s), you'd use that one for this step instead.
the tan thing is neat where does that come from

It comes from setting the two forces equal at the point where the block is just about to slip:

1. Down-ramp pull: mg sin(θ)
2. Max friction: μ_s mg cos(θ)
3. Just about to slip, they're equal: mg sin(θ) = μ_s mg cos(θ)
4. Cancel mg on both sides: sin(θ) = μ_s cos(θ)
5. Divide by cos(θ): tan(θ) = μ_s

So if tan(θ) is bigger than μ_s, gravity wins and it slides. If smaller, friction can hold it. The mass cancels again, which is why a heavy and a light block made of the same material start slipping at the same angle.

It's also a real experiment: tilt a board slowly until a block just starts to slide, measure the angle, and tan of that angle is the static friction coefficient.
ok last q, does she lose marks if she uses 10 for g instead of 9.8

Depends on the teacher and the course. Many high school classes allow g = 10 m/s² if the problem or teacher says so, or if it's an exam that states it. Otherwise 9.8 (or 9.81) is the standard.

What to tell her:
- Check the problem statement, her textbook, or past graded work to see what's been used.
- If unsure, use 9.8. It's never wrong.
- Write the formula with g first, then plug in. If the teacher wanted 10, she'll usually still get full or near-full credit for showing the method.

With g = 10, part (a) would give 5 - 1.73 = 3.27 m/s² instead of 3.20, so the answers are close but not identical. If it's auto-graded online, that difference can matter.

quick one. TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable what does that mean in plain english

It means you tried to use square brackets on something that is `None`.

For example:

```python
result = None
result[0]  # TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable
```

"Subscriptable" just means "can use `[ ]` on it," like lists, dicts, and strings. `None` isn't one of those.

Usually a variable you expected to hold a list or dict is actually `None`, often because a function returned nothing.
the line is data = resp.json()['items']

Then `resp.json()` returned `None`. The API response body was literally `null` (valid JSON, which parses to `None` in Python).

That often happens when the API returns an empty or error response with a 200 status. Print it to check:

```python
print(resp.status_code, resp.text)
```
status 200, text is 'null'. weird. why would an api do that

Common reasons:

- **No results.** Some APIs return `null` instead of an empty list when nothing matches.
- **Wrong endpoint or parameter**, like a missing ID, and the API fails quietly.
- **Auth issue** that some APIs report as an empty body instead of a 401.

Check the API docs for that endpoint, and try the same request in a browser or Postman with the same parameters.
ok yea it was a wrong id param. but how do i stop this crashing the script next time

Handle the `None` case before indexing:

```python
body = resp.json()
items = body.get("items", []) if body else []
```

If `body` is `None` or missing `items`, you get an empty list instead of a crash.

Also add `resp.raise_for_status()` right after the request so real HTTP errors (4xx/5xx) raise a clear error early.
whats the diff between that and a try except

- **The `if`/`.get()` approach** handles a case you expect (empty result) as normal flow. The script keeps going with an empty list.
- **`try/except`** catches errors after they happen. Useful for things you can't easily check in advance, like network failures.

```python
try:
    items = resp.json()["items"]
except (TypeError, KeyError):
    items = []
```

That works, but it can hide other bugs, since any TypeError in that line gets swallowed. For a known "might be None" case, the explicit check is cleaner.
makes sense. is KeyError the one when the dict doesnt have the key?

Yes. `KeyError` is raised when you do `d["something"]` and the dict has no key `"something"`.

Using `d.get("something")` instead returns `None` (or a default you pass) rather than raising.
and IndexError is the list version right

Right. `IndexError` happens when you access a list (or tuple, or string) position that doesn't exist, like `items[5]` on a list with 3 elements.

Lists don't have `.get()`, so the usual guard is checking length first: `items[0] if items else None`.

random q. got an intimation from income tax dept u/s 143(1) for AY 2026-27 saying i owe ₹41,200 more. i filed ITR-2 in old regime, claimed 80C 1.5L, HRA, 80D. but the intimation shows tax computed under new regime and all my deductions are gone?? what happened

That pattern, where the CPC (Centralized Processing Centre) recomputes your tax under the new regime and drops all deductions, usually has one of these causes:

1. **The return was filed after the due date (belated return u/s 139(4)).** For individuals without business income, you can choose the old regime only in a return filed **on or before the due date u/s 139(1)**. If it was filed late, the law forces the new regime, and the CPC applies it automatically.
2. **The old regime option wasn't selected correctly** in the ITR form, e.g., the "opting out of new tax regime" question answered "No."
3. **A mismatch in schedules** caused the system to default, less common.

Can you check two things: the filing date on your ITR-V acknowledgement, and whether it says "139(1)" or "139(4)" as the section under which it was filed?
ugh. filed on 3rd oct and yea it says 139(4). i thought there was a late fee but thats it

That's the cause. The late fee u/s 234F (₹5,000 if income is above ₹5 lakh) is the well-known penalty, but losing the old regime option is a less obvious consequence of filing late.

Under section 115BAC, the new regime is the default. Salaried individuals can opt out each year, but only in a return filed by the original due date. A belated return can't opt out, so your deductions (80C, HRA, 80D) are disallowed and tax is recomputed with new regime slabs.

So the intimation is correct according to the law, unfortunately.

Before paying, double-check the computation in the intimation: compare the income figures with your Form 16 and AIS, and check that all TDS credits are counted. Sometimes the demand also includes interest u/s 234A/B/C.
can i file a revised return and fix the regime?

Unfortunately, no. A revised return u/s 139(5) replaces your belated return, but it doesn't change the fact that the original was filed after the due date. The regime choice is still blocked.

Revising makes sense only if there's another error to fix, like a missed income source or wrong TDS details.

Options left:
- **Accept and pay the demand.**
- **Disagree with the computation** (not the regime) if the figures don't match your documents. Respond on the e-filing portal under "Pending Actions > Response to Outstanding Demand" and select "Disagree" with reasons.
- **Rectification u/s 154** is for mistakes apparent from record, like TDS not credited. It won't restore the old regime.

If the amount seems big for the difference in regimes, it's worth checking whether TDS was missed.
TDS matches my form 16. but my employer deducted TDS assuming old regime, thats why its short right?

Yes, exactly. You declared old regime to your employer at the start of the year, so they deducted TDS based on old regime tax (after 80C, HRA, 80D). That tax was lower than what's now owed under the new regime with no deductions, so there's a shortfall.

The ₹41,200 is likely made up of:
- Difference between new regime tax and the TDS already paid
- Interest u/s 234B (shortfall in advance tax) and 234C
- Interest u/s 234A (late filing) on the unpaid amount

One thing worth checking: for some income levels, the new regime with its lower slabs and higher standard deduction (₹75,000) isn't much worse than old regime with deductions. If the difference seems too high relative to your income, look closely at how the CPC computed it, especially HRA and 80C being removed from the salary schedule.
ok numbers look right honestly. how do i pay it, and is there a deadline

1. Log in to the e-filing portal (incometax.gov.in).
2. Go to **Pending Actions > Response to Outstanding Demand**. Select "Demand is correct" for this AY.
3. Click **Pay Now**, which takes you to the e-Pay Tax page with the demand details filled in, or go to **e-File > e-Pay Tax**, choose **Regular Assessment Tax (400)** for AY 2026-27.
4. Pay by net banking, UPI, or card. You'll get a challan (CRN) with BSR code and serial number.

The deadline is usually **30 days from receiving the intimation**, as stated in the notice. After that, interest u/s 220(2) at 1% per month applies, and the department can adjust it against future refunds.

Keep the challan receipt. After payment, the demand status on the portal can take a few days to a couple of weeks to update.

A few things:

- **Calendar reminder** for mid-July. The usual due date for non-audit individuals is July 31, sometimes extended, but don't count on extensions.
- **Collect documents early.** Form 16 usually comes by mid-June. Download AIS and 26AS at the same time.
- **Decide your regime early in the year.** Compare old vs new using the tax calculator on the e-filing portal when you submit investment declarations to your employer in April.
- **If you pick old regime, file before the due date.** That's the non-negotiable part.
- **Check that your employer's regime matches what you'll file**, so TDS isn't short.
- **If you'll miss the due date anyway,** know that you'll be on the new regime and plan TDS accordingly.

Also consider whether the new regime might just be better for you anyway. With higher slabs and the ₹75k standard deduction, many salaried people with modest deductions now pay less under it.

Small caps going down 8% in a year isn't unusual. They're the most volatile category. But putting your only SIP there is a lot of risk for a first fund. Some ideas for structuring 30k/month:

**Option 1: Simple core**
- 20k in a Nifty 50 index fund
- 10k in a flexi cap fund

**Option 2: Core + satellite**
- 15k Nifty 50 index fund
- 7k flexi cap
- 5k midcap or small cap (keep your existing one if you like it)
- 3k in a different style, e.g., value or international

**Option 3: Index only**

Good, the emergency fund is the right first step.

A house in 5 to 6 years changes things a bit, because equity can easily be down at the time you need the money. Ideas:

- **Two buckets.** Long-term SIPs (retirement, wealth) stay in equity. For the house, use a separate SIP in something calmer.
- **For the house bucket:** balanced advantage fund, aggressive hybrid fund, or equity savings fund. Less drop in bad years.
- **Or a glide path.** Put the house money in equity now, then shift gradually to debt/liquid funds in the last 2 years before buying.
- **Short-duration debt funds or FDs** for the portion you'll definitely need, like stamp duty and registration.

Split example: 20k long-term equity, 10k toward the house in a hybrid fund.
what about the small cap fund i have. sell it or keep it

Some ways to think about it:

- **Keep it but stop adding.** Pause or stop the SIP, leave the existing money in. Small caps can recover strongly over 5 to 7+ years.
- **Keep it as your satellite.** Reduce the SIP to 3 to 5k as part of the core-satellite approach.
- **Switch out.** If you don't actually want small cap exposure, redeem and move to a flexi cap or index fund. Within one year of purchase, gains would be short-term, but since it's down, there's no tax and no gain to worry about. Check the exit load (usually 1% within a year).
- **Check the fund quality.** If it has done worse than its peers and its benchmark (Nifty Smallcap 250) consistently, it's a better reason to switch than the 8% drop itself.

how do i pick which index fund, theres like 30 nifty 50 ones

They all track the same index, so you're mostly comparing cost and how closely they track. Things to look at:

1. **Expense ratio (direct plan).** Lower is better. Good ones are around 0.1 to 0.2%.
2. **Tracking error.** How closely the fund follows the index. Lower is better. Look for under 0.1%.
3. **AUM.** Bigger funds tend to have lower tracking error and better liquidity. A few thousand crore is plenty.
4. **Fund house.** Pick a large, established AMC: UTI, HDFC, ICICI Prudential, Nippon, SBI, Navi, etc.
5. **Direct plan, not regular.** Regular plans pay a commission to a distributor, which adds ~0.5 to 1% a year.

Value Research and the AMFI site let you compare these side by side. Honestly, any large, cheap one is fine. Don't spend weeks on it.
direct vs regular, my friend's bank RM set his up. probably regular right

Most likely, yes. Bank RMs usually sell regular plans because they earn commission from them.

Ideas to check and fix:

- **Look at the fund name** in his statement. If it doesn't say "Direct," it's regular.
- **Compare expense ratios.** Regular is often 0.5 to 1% higher per year. Over 20 years, that can reduce the final amount by 10 to 20%.
- **To switch:** start new SIPs in the direct plan, and either keep the old units or redeem and reinvest them. Redeeming may trigger capital gains tax and exit load, so check before doing it.
- **For yourself:** set up through a direct platform like Kuvera, Zerodha Coin, Groww, Paytm Money, or directly with the AMC or via MF Central.

If someone genuinely gives valuable advice, paying for it is fine, but then a fee-only SEBI-registered investment advisor is usually a better deal than commission.

- **If they come along,** just tell your 8-year-old someone might ask their name or school, and it's fine to answer quietly.
- **Bring their documents:** passports, birth certificates, and school letters or bonafide certificates showing they're enrolled.

- Employment letters for you and your husband (role, years, approved leave dates)

One folder, with tabs or clear sections. Most applicants are never asked for documents, but being organized helps you feel calm, and that comes across in the interview.

thanks!! another thing, so im learning python in the evenings after the kids go to bed, made a script to rename our family photos by date taken. it crashes halfway thru with KeyError: 36867. heres the code can u look at it

Nice script. It's a solid start, and the crash is a common one.

**What KeyError: 36867 means:** 36867 is the EXIF tag for "DateTimeOriginal" (when the photo was taken). Some photos don't have it, like screenshots, edited images, or photos from WhatsApp, which strips metadata. When you hit one of those, `exif[36867]` fails.

There's a second problem waiting: if a file has no EXIF at all, `img._getexif()` returns `None`, and you'd get a `TypeError` instead.

Fix both by checking first:

```python
exif = img._getexif() or {}
date = exif.get(36867)
if not date:
    print("no date, skipping:", f)
    continue
```

A couple of other things worth fixing before you run it on your whole photo collection, but this one will stop the crash.
ok that fixed the crash. what are the other things

Three more:

1. **Two photos taken in the same second** get the same name, and `os.rename` will fail (on Windows) or overwrite (on Mac/Linux). Burst shots do this a lot. Add a counter if the name exists:
```python
base = date.replace(':', '-').replace(' ', '_')
new = base + '.jpg'
i = 1
while os.path.exists(os.path.join(folder, new)):
    new = f"{base}_{i}.jpg"
    i += 1
```

2. **Non-image files.** If there's a `.mp4`, `.txt` or `desktop.ini` in the folder, `Image.open` will crash. Skip anything that isn't a photo:
```python
if not f.lower().endswith(('.jpg', '.jpeg')):
    continue
```

3. **The file is still open when you rename it.** On Windows that can cause a "file in use" error. Use `with Image.open(...) as img:` so it closes before renaming.

Also: test on a copy of the folder first. Renaming is hard to undo.
the with thing, where does the rename go then, inside or outside

Outside, after the `with` block ends. That's the point: the file closes when the block finishes, then you rename it.

```python
with Image.open(path) as img:
    exif = img._getexif() or {}

date = exif.get(36867)
# ...build new name...
os.rename(path, new_path)
```

Read what you need (the EXIF) inside the block, and do everything else after. The `exif` variable is still available outside because it's just a normal dictionary you saved.

WhatsApp strips EXIF, but its filenames usually contain the date, like `IMG-20240603-WA0012.jpg`. You can pull the date from the name as a fallback:

```python
import re

m = re.search(r'(\d{4})(\d{2})(\d{2})', f)
if not date and m:
    y, mo, d = m.groups()
    date = f'{y}:{mo}:{d} 00:00:00'
```

title: I'm working on a group project…

question_types: brainstorming: wants ideas or options to choose from
how-to: wants step-by-step instructions to do something
how-to: wants step-by-step instructions to do something

turns: I'm working on a group project with three other people, and our git history is a mess because everyone pushes straight to main. Could you give me some ideas for a simple workflow we could adopt that won't be too heavy for a student project?

A few options, from lightest to heaviest:

1. **Feature branches + pull requests**: everyone works on a branch named for what they're doing, then opens a PR into main. One teammate reviews it before merging. This is the best fit for a team of four.
2. **Feature branches, no required review**: same thing, but you merge your own PR once tests pass. Less friction, but fewer chances to catch mistakes.
3. **A shared 'dev' branch** that everyone merges into, with main only updated for milestones or submission. Useful if you have a deadline-based demo.
4. **Trunk-based with short-lived branches**: small branches that live a day or less.

I'd pick option 1, and turn on branch protection so main can't be pushed to directly.
Option 1 sounds good. What should we do about merge conflicts? Two of us always edit the same file.

Some ideas to reduce them:

- Pull from main (or rebase onto it) often, at least before starting work each day, so conflicts are small.
- Keep branches short-lived and PRs small.
- Split files up so that each person tends to own certain parts of the code.
- Agree who's editing the shared file and when, over chat.
- When a conflict does happen, resolve it in your own branch before the PR, not in main.

It also helps to use a code formatter so that style differences don't create fake conflicts.
Should we squash commits when merging or keep everything? Some of our commits are just 'fix' or 'wip'.

For a student project, squash merge is a good default. Each PR becomes one clean commit on main, so the history is readable and the 'wip' commits disappear. The downside is losing the detailed history within a PR, which rarely matters here.

Alternatively, you can each tidy your own branch before merging with an interactive rebase, but that's more work and easier to get wrong. GitHub has a setting to allow only squash merges, which keeps things consistent.
That makes sense. Is there anything we can do to make the commit messages better without being annoying about it?

A few light-touch ideas:

- Agree on a simple format, like a short imperative sentence ('Add login form', not 'stuff'), and nothing more.
- Since you're squashing, the PR title becomes the commit message, so only the PR title needs to be good.
- Add a PR template with a couple of prompts, such as 'What does this change?' and 'How did you test it?'.
- Optionally use a commit-msg hook later if it keeps being a problem.

Focusing on PR titles is the lowest-effort approach.
Great. One more: someone already pushed a broken commit to main. What are our options to fix it?

Depends on whether others have pulled it yet:

- **git revert <commit>**: creates a new commit that undoes the bad one. Safe for a shared branch and the usual choice. Everyone just pulls.
- **Fix forward**: push a new commit that corrects the problem, if the fix is small and obvious.
- **Reset and force-push** (git reset --hard <good commit>, git push --force): rewrites history. Only do this if nobody else has pulled yet and you've told the team, otherwise it will cause confusing problems for them.

I'd go with revert. Then turn on branch protection so it can't happen again.

Thanks. On a completely different subject, I'd like to run my first 5K in about 8 weeks. I can currently jog maybe 5 minutes without stopping. Could you walk me through how to build up to it, step by step?

Sure. A run/walk approach works well. Train three days a week with rest days in between, for example Monday, Wednesday and Saturday.

Weeks 1-2: alternate 1 minute jogging and 2 minutes walking, 8 rounds (24 minutes).
Weeks 3-4: jog 3 minutes, walk 1 minute, 6 rounds.
Weeks 5-6: jog 5 minutes, walk 1 minute, 4 rounds, then try 8 minutes jogging with 1 minute walking.
Week 7: jog 15 to 20 minutes continuously.
Week 8: one easy run of 25 to 30 minutes early in the week, then rest, then race.

Go slow enough that you could hold a conversation.
Thank you. Do I need to do anything besides running, like stretching or strength work?

It helps, but keep it short. Before each run, do a 5-minute brisk walk and some dynamic moves such as leg swings and walking lunges. Save static stretching for after your run.

On one of your off days, do 15 to 20 minutes of basic strength work: squats, glute bridges, calf raises, planks, and single-leg balance. Strong hips, calves and core help prevent common beginner problems like shin splints and knee pain.
What should I do if I get shin pain? That happened last time I tried running.

Shin pain is common for beginners. Here's what to do:

1. Stop running if the pain is sharp or gets worse as you run. Mild soreness that goes away after warming up is less worrying.
2. Rest for several days and ice it 10 to 15 minutes.
3. Replace a run with walking, cycling or swimming for a week.
4. Come back with shorter run intervals, and increase gradually.
5. Check your shoes. Worn-out or unsuitable shoes are a frequent cause, and shoes generally last 500 to 800 km.

Also, run on softer surfaces when you can. If the pain is pinpoint, persistent, or hurts at rest, see a doctor to rule out a stress fracture.
Okay. And how should I pace the actual race day?

Start slower than you feel like you should. Race day adrenaline and the crowd will make the first kilometer feel easy and tempt you to go out too fast.

- Go at your usual training pace for the first km, maybe even a bit slower.
- Settle in for km 2 to 4. You should be able to speak in short sentences.
- In the final km, if you have energy left, speed up gradually.
- It's totally fine to use your walk breaks if you need them.

Eat something light 2 to 3 hours before, and don't try anything new that morning, such as new shoes or foods.
That's helpful. Should I run the full 5K distance before the race?

It's not necessary, and for a beginner it's often better not to. If you can run 20 to 25 minutes continuously in week 7, you can finish a 5K in the race, because the crowd and the atmosphere give you a boost. If you'd like the reassurance, you can do one 4 km run about 10 days before the race, easy pace. After that, keep the last week light so you arrive fresh.

Hi, I'm a third-year computer science student applying for summer 2027 software engineering internships. Sure. "Too thin" usually means it doesn't show what you can build. Here's a step-by-step way to rebuild it:

1. **Choose a clean one-page template.** Single column, standard fonts. Jake's Resume template (LaTeX or Word versions) is popular for CS students.
2. **Order the sections:** Education, Skills, Projects, Experience, and optionally Leadership/Activities.
3. **Shrink the coursework.** One line with 4 to 6 relevant courses, inside the Education section.
4. **Add a Projects section.** This is the big one for internships. 2 to 3 projects with bullets about what you built and how.
5. **Rewrite the library job** to highlight transferable skills.
6. **Add a Skills section** with languages, frameworks, and tools you've actually used.
7. **Tailor and proofread** for each application.

Do you have any projects, even class projects or something small you built on your own?

They definitely count. The study room app especially: it's a real web app, built in a team, which is exactly what internship recruiters want to see.

How to write each project:

1. **Title line:** project name, tech stack, and date. For example: *StudyRoom Booker | React, Node.js, PostgreSQL | Spring 2026*
2. **2 to 4 bullets**, each starting with an action verb and saying what **you** did specifically, not the whole team.
3. **Include numbers** where you can: users, features, test coverage, performance.

Example bullets:
- Built the booking API in Node.js with endpoints for availability, reservations, and cancellations
- Designed the PostgreSQL schema to prevent double-booking using unique constraints
- Collaborated in a team of 4 using Git and weekly sprints; reviewed teammates' pull requests

What parts of the app did you personally work on?
I mostly did the backend: the API and the database. I also wrote some tests with Jest. For the budget script, it reads my bank's CSV exports and categorizes spending.

That's a strong combination. Here's a draft for both:

**StudyRoom Booker** | Node.js, Express, PostgreSQL, Jest | Spring 2026
- Developed REST API for room availability, reservations, and cancellations used by a 4-person team's React frontend
- Designed PostgreSQL schema with constraints to prevent double-booking
- Wrote Jest unit and integration tests covering core booking logic

**Budget Tracker** | Python, pandas | 2025
- Built a Python script that parses bank CSV exports and auto-categorizes transactions using keyword rules
- Generates monthly spending summaries by category

Next steps for making these stronger:
1. Put both projects on GitHub with a short README, and link them on the resume.
2. Add a number if you have one: number of endpoints, test count, coverage percentage, or how many months of transactions the script handles.
3. If you used pandas or any other library, list it. If not, adjust the tech stack.

Did you use pandas, or plain Python with the csv module?
Plain Python with the csv module. And I'm not sure how to make the library job sound relevant at all.

Then change the stack line to just **Python** (you could add "csv, matplotlib" if you plotted anything).

For the library job, focus on reliability, communication, and anything technical, even small:

1. **List what you actually do:** help patrons, check out books, reshelve, maybe troubleshoot printers or computers.
2. **Pick 2 or 3 tasks** that show responsibility, problem-solving, or tech skills.
3. **Write them as accomplishments.**

Example:

**Library Assistant**, [University] Library | Sep 2024 to present
- Assist 50+ students and faculty per shift with research resources, printing and account issues
- Troubleshoot public computer and printer problems, escalating hardware issues to IT
- Trusted with opening and closing procedures for the circulation desk

It doesn't need to be impressive, just show you're dependable and can work with people. Two or three bullets is enough; projects should take up more space than this.
That's much better. What should go in the skills section? I've touched a lot of languages in classes but I'm only really comfortable in a few.

List only what you could talk about confidently in an interview. Anything on your resume is fair game for questions.

Steps:

1. **Write down everything** you've used.
2. **Remove anything** you couldn't write a small program in without heavy googling, or explain basic concepts of.
3. **Group the rest** into categories:

**Languages:** Python, JavaScript, Java, SQL
**Frameworks/Libraries:** Node.js, Express, Jest
**Tools:** Git, PostgreSQL, VS Code, Linux command line

4. **Order by strength** within each line, strongest first.

You can skip proficiency labels like "Advanced" or "Intermediate," since they're subjective and take space. Avoid listing soft skills like "teamwork" here; show those in bullets instead.

If you have a language you used in one class two years ago, leave it off.
Okay. For the education section, should I include my GPA? It's a 3.3.

A common guideline is to include GPA if it's 3.0 or higher, so 3.3 is fine to include. Some companies, especially larger tech firms, filter by GPA, and leaving it off can make recruiters assume it's lower than it is.

How to format the Education section:

**[University Name]** | City, State
B.S. in Computer Science | Expected May 2028
GPA: 3.3/4.0
Relevant Coursework: Data Structures, Algorithms, Databases, Software Engineering, Operating Systems

If your major GPA (CS courses only) is noticeably higher, say 3.6, you can list that instead as "Major GPA: 3.6/4.0." Just make sure it's clearly labeled.

Also include any honors, dean's list, or scholarships on one more line if you have them.
Thank you, this is really helpful. Is there anything I should do before I start sending it out?

Yes, a short final checklist:

1. **One page.** For a student, always.
2. **Proofread** carefully, then read it out loud. Ask a friend to check it too.
3. **Check links.** GitHub and LinkedIn URLs should work and be clickable in the PDF.
4. **Make sure GitHub is presentable.** READMEs on both projects with a short description and how to run them.
5. **Save as PDF** with a clear filename like `FirstName_LastName_Resume.pdf`.
6. **Test ATS readability.** Copy-paste all the text from the PDF into a plain text file. If it comes out in a sensible order, you're fine.
7. **Take it back to career services.** Now that it has content, they can give more specific feedback.
8. **Tailor a little for each application.** Reorder skills or tweak a bullet to match the job description's keywords.

Many summer 2027 internship applications open in August to October, so starting now is good timing.

turns: I'm trying to train a small image classifier to sort my design assets (icons vs illustrations vs photos), like 600 images total. Training accuracy goes to 99% but when I test on new stuff it's like 55%. I watched two YouTube tutorials and did exactly what they did. Why does it look perfect in training and then fall apart?

That's **overfitting**. The model has memorized your 600 training images instead of learning the general differences between icons, illustrations, and photos.

Why it happens: a neural network has a huge number of adjustable parameters, often millions. With only 600 examples, it has enough capacity to learn tiny details specific to each image, like a particular color in one corner or a watermark, rather than the broader patterns. On training data that looks perfect. On new data those memorized details don't exist, so it guesses.

The tutorials probably used datasets with tens of thousands of images, where memorizing is much harder, so the same setup works for them.

The usual fixes:
- **Transfer learning:** start from a model pretrained on millions of images (like ResNet or EfficientNet) and only train the last layer or two.
- **Data augmentation:** random flips, crops, color shifts to effectively create more varied examples.
- **A validation set:** hold out 15 to 20% to see overfitting as it happens.
I did hold out a test set, that's how I got 55%. but why would the model learn some random corner color instead of the obvious stuff, like photos look like photos??

Because the model has no idea what "obvious" means. It doesn't know what a photo is. It just adjusts numbers to reduce errors on the training set, and it uses whatever pattern does that fastest.

If, in your 600 images, most icons happen to be PNGs with transparent (black after loading) backgrounds, and photos happen to be larger with certain dimensions, the model can hit near 100% by learning those shortcuts. They're easier to pick up than abstract concepts like "realistic lighting" or "flat shapes." This is sometimes called **shortcut learning**.

On your test set, if the shortcuts don't hold as well, accuracy drops.

Things to check:
- Are classes different in size, format, or background in ways that aren't the real distinction?
- Is the test set from a different source than training, like newer projects or a different style?

A pretrained model helps here a lot. It already knows general visual features like edges, textures and shading, so the "real" differences are much easier for it to use than a random shortcut.
ok the transparent background thing is probably it, all my icons are PNGs. if I use the pretrained thing does that just fix it or do I still need to deal with that

Transfer learning will help a lot, but it won't fully fix a shortcut that strong. If transparent background equals icon in 100% of your training data, even a pretrained model can still lean on it, because it's the easiest signal.

Things to deal with it directly:
