It depends on the firmness. Extra firm tofu has roughly 15 to 17 grams of protein per 100 grams, while soft or silken tofu has less, often around 5 to 8 grams. Firm or extra firm is the best choice if you want protein density. Check the label, since brands vary.
is that enough for a day or do i need more than that

Many adults need around 50 to 60 grams a day, so you can get a lot of protein from plants if you combine sources. For example, a cup of lentils, 100g of extra firm tofu, and a cup of oats or some soy milk would cover a good chunk of that. Spread it across meals rather than putting all of it in one. If you're active or trying to build muscle, aim higher, closer to 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight.
what about tempeh

Tempeh is one of the best options, with around 19 to 20 grams of protein per 100 grams. It's made from fermented soybeans, so it's whole food protein, and it has a firm texture that holds up well in stir fries, sandwiches or grain bowls. Like tofu, it's easy to add to other dishes, so you can build a day around it.

title: need ideas for what to bake…

question_types: brainstorming: wants ideas or options to choose from
sanity check: already has an answer in mind and wants it confirmed
sanity check: already has an answer in mind and wants it confirmed

turns: need ideas for what to bake this weekend that isnt the same sourdough loaf for the 10th time. something with a starter maybe or whatever

Here are some options that use a sourdough starter but aren't a standard loaf:

- Sourdough focaccia: a wet dough with olive oil, very forgiving and great for a crowd.
- Sourdough discard crackers: thin, crisp and flavored with herbs or cheese.
- Sourdough pancakes or waffles: a good way to use discard, with a slight tang.
- Sourdough cinnamon rolls: enriched dough, so it takes longer but is worth it.
- Sourdough pizza: a quick dough in a hot oven, good for a Friday night bake.

Focaccia or cinnamon rolls are the most impressive if you have a long weekend. Crackers or pancakes are the easiest if you want something quick.
the focaccia sounds good but i dont have a 9x13 pan

You can use what you have. A 10 inch cast iron skillet works well and gives you a crisp bottom, or use a round cake pan or a rimmed baking sheet. The dough spreads more in a larger pan, so a baking sheet makes a thinner focaccia. If you use a smaller pan, the dough will be thicker and taller, which is fine. Oil the pan generously and let the dough rest in it for a bit so it stretches to the edges before baking.
btw my dog is 8 months and hasnt chewed anything in like 6 weeks so i think its fine to stop crating him at night and just let him sleep in the bedroom. sanity check?

That sounds reasonable, with a couple of conditions. Six weeks without chewing or accidents is a good sign, and many dogs can move to free roaming at night around this age. Before you fully stop the crate, try a few nights with the bedroom door closed and the crate door open, so he has the option of his own space. Keep a potty break right before bed and first thing in the morning, since his bladder may not hold overnight yet. If he wakes you up with whining or accidents, go back to the crate for a while.
making my first no knead bread tmrw. recipe says 3 cups flour, 1.5 cups water, 1/4 tsp yeast, 1.5 tsp salt, mix and leave on counter 12-18 hrs. i think thats right? seems like not much yeast lol

Yes, that matches the classic no-knead recipe. The tiny amount of yeast is on purpose. With 12 to 18 hours, even 1/4 tsp multiplies a lot, and the long slow rise builds flavor and gluten structure for you without kneading.

The dough will look shaggy and sticky when you mix it, which is normal. When it's ready, it should be bubbly on top and more than doubled.
ok and then i bake it in my dutch oven at 450 for 30 w lid and 15 w/o?

That's the standard method. Preheat the Dutch oven in the oven at 450 F for 30 minutes before you put the dough in. Then bake 30 minutes with the lid on, and 15 minutes with the lid off until the crust is deep brown.

If you're worried about it sticking, lift the dough in on a piece of parchment paper. Just be careful, because the pot will be extremely hot. Also check that your Dutch oven's knob is oven-safe to 450 F. Some plastic knobs aren't.
its a 5 qt, is that too big

No, 5 quarts is fine. Most recipes call for 4 to 6 quarts. A bigger pot just means the loaf spreads a bit wider and may end up slightly flatter, but it will still turn out well.

If you want a taller loaf, shape the dough into a tight ball during the folding step, and use a bit less water (maybe 1 1/3 cups) if the dough seems too slack. For a first try, follow the recipe as written.
cool. should i wait for it to cool before cutting? the smell is gonna kill me

Yes, wait at least 30 to 60 minutes if you can. The crumb is still setting as it cools, and steam is still escaping. If you cut it right out of the oven, it can seem gummy and doughy inside even though it's cooked.

A fully done loaf sounds hollow when you tap the bottom, and the inside reaches about 205 to 210 F. Put it on a wire rack, not a plate, so the bottom doesn't get soggy. You'll hear it crackle as it cools, which is a good sign.
what if it comes out flat tho

Common causes of a flat loaf:

- Dough proofed too long, so it collapsed. If it's very runny and the bubbles have flattened, it over-fermented.
- Too cold a kitchen or old yeast, so it didn't rise much.
- Too much water or no shaping, so the dough spread out.
- A Dutch oven that wasn't preheated enough.

It will still taste good and make great toast. Next time, adjust: fold the dough and shape it tightly before the second rise, and shorten the first rise by a couple of hours if your kitchen is warm.

title: trying to get from Austin to…

question_types: brainstorming: wants ideas or options to choose from
recommendation: asks what they should pick or do in their situation
sanity check: already has an answer in mind and wants it confirmed

turns: trying to get from Austin to Tokyo for Dec 20 - Jan 3 and everything is $1,700+ round trip. set a google flights alert two weeks ago thinking it'd drop, it went UP $200. what are my actual options here, I'm flexible-ish on dates and airports but not on being in Tokyo for new years

Holiday flights to Tokyo are some of the hardest to get cheap, so the alert going up isn't surprising. Some ideas to try:

1. **Fly from a bigger hub.** Dallas (DFW) and Houston (IAH) have nonstops to Tokyo and more competition. A cheap positioning flight or a 3-hour drive to Houston can save several hundred.
2. **West coast connection on separate tickets.** Austin to LAX/SFO/SEA on a cheap domestic fare, then a separate ticket to Tokyo. Riskier (no protection if you miss the connection), so leave a big buffer.
3. **Shift the dates.** Leaving Dec 17-18 or returning Jan 5-6 is often much cheaper than the peak days around Dec 20-21 and Jan 2-3.
4. **Try Osaka (KIX).** Fly into Osaka, shinkansen to Tokyo is ~2.5 hours, ~$100.
5. **Asian carriers with a stop.** Korean Air via Seoul, EVA or China Airlines via Taipei sometimes undercut US and Japanese airlines.
6. **Use points** if you have any credit card points. Award seats on ANA or JAL via partner programs can be great value even at peak dates.

What's your budget?
budget is like $1,300. I checked DFW and IAH and they're barely cheaper, like $1,600. points I have ~80k chase

Chase points are your best bet then. Ideas:

- **Transfer to United** and book ANA or United flights. Economy to Japan is often around 35-40k miles one way, so 80k could cover most of a round trip if award space exists.
- **Transfer to Virgin Atlantic** to book ANA. Virgin's prices for ANA are very low (round trip economy has been in the 60k range), but finding ANA availability on peak dates is hard. Search ANA's site for 'partner' seats first.
- **Transfer to British Airways Avios** for JAL flights from Dallas. Distance-based pricing, usually reasonable.
- **Mix cash and points:** book the expensive direction (outbound around Dec 20) with points and the return with cash, or vice versa.

Important: never transfer points until you've found an actual seat. Transfers are one-way.

If no award seats, consider Chase travel portal: with some cards your points are worth 1.25-1.5 cents each, so 80k = $1,000-1,200 toward a cash fare.
found united award seats via SFO outbound dec 19 for 40k. return is crazy expensive in miles though. what about the return

Good find. For the return, a few options:

- **Cash one-way.** One-way fares from Tokyo to the US can be reasonable, especially on ZIPAIR (Japan Airlines' low-cost carrier) from Narita to LAX, SFO or San Jose, sometimes $300-500 one-way. Then a cheap domestic flight to Austin.
- **Search different dates.** Returning Jan 4-6 instead of Jan 3 might open lower award prices.
- **Other partners for the return:** Check Air Canada Aeroplan (Chase doesn't transfer there, but if you have Amex/Capital One...) or remaining Chase points with Virgin Atlantic for ANA.
- **Use the remaining 40k in the Chase portal** toward a cash return fare. Worth around $400-600.

ZIPAIR + domestic flight + 40k miles outbound could get you well under $1,300 total. Just watch ZIPAIR's bag fees, and book the domestic connection with a generous buffer.

ok thanks. switching topics, i have 4200 on a card at 26% and 1800 on a store card at 29%. i can put 350 a month extra on top of minimums. avalanche or pay off the small one first? i'm kinda tired of this

Go with the store card first, at 29%. That's the higher rate, so it's costing you more each month, and paying it down first saves the most interest overall. At 350 extra a month, the 1800 balance will be cleared in roughly 4 to 6 months, depending on how the minimums split, and then all of the 350 plus the freed-up minimum goes to the 26% card. If you need quick wins to stay motivated, the store card is also the smaller balance, so it's both the cheapest to finish and the one you'll see drop fastest. Once it's gone, put everything you were paying on it toward the main card.

tried to book sfo to lisbon last night and the payment failed twice, and now the fare is up. the one im looking at is 640 round trip nonstop on tap, leaving thursday, back the following thursday. is 640 still reasonable or should i wait

640 round trip is a reasonable price for SFO to Lisbon in most seasons, and nonstop routes from the West Coast to Lisbon aren't always available, so the nonstop is worth something. Before you book, check that the payment didn't go through twice, since failed attempts can sometimes show as pending charges. If you see pending charges, don't rebook yet, and check your bank. As for waiting, fares are rising as the departure gets closer, so waiting is a gamble. If your dates are fixed and the trip is worth it, book it now. If the dates are flexible, check a day either side on the calendar view.

title: I'm in Tokyo for a two-week…

question_types: troubleshooting: something is broken or not working and they describe what they see

troubleshooting: something is broken or not working and they describe what they see
quick fact: a short factual question, then a follow-up or two

turns: I'm in Tokyo for a two-week study abroad trip and I'm having a problem with my JR Pass. I bought the 7-day pass online before coming and exchanged it at Narita, but when I tried to use it to go to Kyoto today the gate at Tokyo Station wouldn't let me through, and the staff said I need a seat reservation for the Nozomi. I thought the pass covered all shinkansen? I'm a bit confused.

The JR Pass covers most shinkansen, but historically not the fastest ones on the Tokaido line: the **Nozomi** and **Mizuho**. Since October 2023, you can ride them, but only by buying an extra 'special ticket' on top of the pass (around ¥4,960 one way Tokyo-Kyoto).

So you have two options:

1. **Take the Hikari instead.** It's fully covered by your pass, and only about 30 minutes slower than the Nozomi (around 2h40 to Kyoto). Hikari trains run roughly twice an hour.
2. **Pay the Nozomi supplement**, if you want the faster train.

At the JR ticket office or a reservation machine, ask for a seat reservation on a Hikari to Kyoto. Reservations are free with the pass.
Thank you, that helps. I went to the ticket machine, but it asked me to scan a QR code and I don't have one. My pass is a paper ticket.

The QR code step is for passes bought through the JR online reservation system. With a paper (magnetic) pass, many machines let you insert the pass ticket directly instead.

Try this:
- Look for a machine with a **'JR Pass'** or **'Japan Rail Pass'** option on the screen (some have an English button first).
- Choose the option to **insert your pass ticket** instead of scanning a QR code.

If the machine still doesn't cooperate, go to the **JR ticket office (Midori-no-madoguchi)** or the JR East Travel Service Center at Tokyo Station. Show your pass and passport and say 'Hikari to Kyoto, reserved seat please.' They'll print a seat ticket. It sometimes takes a while in line, but it always works.

I got the seat reservation at the ticket office. But when I put my pass and the seat ticket through the gate, the gate kept the seat ticket and gave my pass back. Is that a problem? Will I need it on the train?

Hmm, normally the gate should return both tickets. If it kept the seat reservation, a few possibilities:

- You may have put both tickets through in a way where the gate read them as finished. Sometimes the gate returns them a second later on the far side, so check the slot after you walk through.
- If you went through the shinkansen transfer gate, it sometimes keeps the regular ticket and returns the express one, but with a JR Pass it should return everything.

If it's truly gone, it's not a big problem. Go to the staffed window at the gate (there's always one next to the automatic gates) and explain. They can confirm your reservation, or reissue it. On the train, conductors do check, and your pass plus the seat number is usually enough if you explain.

If you still have a photo or your receipt with the car and seat number, that helps.
It came out on the other side, I just didn't see it at first. Sorry! Last question, for my return in a few days, can I just reserve at a machine now that I know how?

No need to apologize, that happens a lot. The slot on the other side is easy to miss.

Yes, you can reserve your return at a machine now. A few tips:

- **Reserve early** if you're travelling on a weekend, holiday or Friday evening; Hikari reserved seats can fill up.
- **Check that it says Hikari or Kodama**, not Nozomi, so you don't get charged extra or end up with a seat you can't use.
- **Pass expiry:** make sure your return date is within the 7 days of your pass. If not, you'll need to buy a regular ticket for that trip.
- If anything is confusing, the ticket office at Kyoto Station works the same way.

If you can't get a reserved seat, the non-reserved cars (usually cars 1-3) are covered by the pass too. You just need to queue on the platform a bit early.

Okay, different question. I'm a second-year student and I want to start meal prepping on Sundays so I stop spending so much on takeout (probably $80 a week right now). I have a small kitchen in my apartment with two burners and an oven. Here's my plan, could you tell me if it makes sense?

- Lunch: chicken and rice with broccoli, 5 containers
- Dinner: pasta with meat sauce, 5 containers
- Breakfast: overnight oats, 5 jars

Budget around $40 for the week.

It's a solid, realistic plan for a first try, and it should fit $40 if you buy chicken thighs, rice and oats in bulk. A few thoughts:

- **Boredom is the main risk.** Eating the exact same lunch and dinner for 5 days is where most people give up by Wednesday. Varying sauces or seasonings helps a lot (e.g. half the chicken with teriyaki, half with lemon-garlic).
- **Food safety:** cooked chicken and rice are best eaten within 3-4 days in the fridge. Consider freezing the last two days' portions and moving them to the fridge the night before.
- **Two burners:** the timing works if you cook chicken and broccoli in the oven while rice and pasta use the burners.
- **Overnight oats:** these keep fine for 4-5 days, so that's good.

Roughly how much time do you have on Sunday?

I have about 3 hours. And I'm fine eating the same thing honestly, I just want it to be cheap. Here's my shopping list with prices from my local store, can you check it:

- chicken thighs 3 lb: $9
- rice 2 lb: $2.50
- frozen broccoli 2 bags: $4
- pasta 2 lb: $3
- ground beef 1 lb: $6
- jar of pasta sauce: $3
- oats: $4
- milk: $3.50
- bananas: $2
- peanut butter: $3

Total is $40.

Nice work, that's realistic and right at $40. A few checks:

- **Chicken:** 3 lb of thighs is about 2.2 lb after cooking and trimming, so about 7 oz per lunch. That's a solid portion.
- **Pasta and beef:** 2 lb of pasta is a lot for 5 dinners (about 6.4 oz dry per serving, which is big). 1 lb of beef spread over 5 servings is only about 3 oz each, which is a bit light on protein. You could cut to 1.5 lb pasta and add a can of lentils or beans to the sauce (~$1) to bulk it out.
- **Vegetables:** dinner has no vegetables at all. A bag of frozen spinach or mixed vegetables in the sauce (~$2) fixes that.
- **Oats:** that container probably lasts several weeks, so your weekly cost drops after the first week. Same with peanut butter and rice.

So week one is about $40, but later weeks will be cheaper.
Good point about vegetables. I'll add frozen spinach to the sauce. How should I order things on Sunday so it fits in 3 hours?

Here's an order that uses the oven and both burners in parallel:

**0:00** Preheat oven to 425°F. Season chicken thighs, put on a sheet pan.
**0:10** Chicken in the oven (about 30-35 min). Start rice on burner 1.
**0:15** Burner 2: brown the ground beef with some onion if you have it.
**0:30** Add sauce, frozen spinach (and lentils if using) to the beef. Simmer on low.
**0:35** Rice done, set aside. Put a large pot of water on burner 1 for pasta.
**0:45** Take chicken out. Put frozen broccoli on the same sheet pan, roast ~15-20 min.
**0:50** Cook pasta.
**1:05** Drain pasta, mix with sauce.
**1:10** Make overnight oats in jars (oats, milk, banana, peanut butter).
**1:20** Let everything cool a bit, then portion into containers.
**1:40** Clean up.

It should take about 2 hours, so you have extra time.
That looks very doable. Do I need to let the food cool before putting it in the fridge? I've heard different things.

The general food safety advice is to get cooked food into the fridge within 2 hours. You don't need to wait until it's completely cold.

What works best:
- Let it sit for 15-30 minutes to stop steaming, especially if your containers are plastic.
- Portion into the individual containers first. Small, shallow portions cool much faster than one big pot.
- Leave the lids slightly open in the fridge for the first 30 minutes or so, then close them.

The main thing to avoid is putting a large, hot pot of pasta sauce straight in the fridge, since the middle can stay warm for hours. Portioning first solves that.
I'm going to freeze the Thursday and Friday portions like you said. Will the pasta be okay frozen and reheated?

Yes, pasta with meat sauce freezes and reheats quite well. A few tips:

- **Cook the pasta slightly al dente** (a minute less than the package says). It softens more when reheated, so this keeps it from getting mushy.
- **Make sure the pasta is well coated in sauce**, which protects it from drying out.
- **Thaw in the fridge overnight**, then microwave with a splash of water and the lid loosely on. Stir halfway.

The chicken and rice freeze fine too. The broccoli may be a bit softer after freezing, but it's still good.

Frozen meals keep for 2-3 months, so you could even make extra portions for weeks when you're busy.
Thank you! Last thing, does it make sense to double everything and do it every two weeks instead?

It can, but there are tradeoffs:

**Pros**
- Saves a Sunday every other week.
- Buying bigger packs is often cheaper per pound.

**Cons**
- About half the meals would need to be frozen, and you'd need room in your freezer for maybe 15 containers. Small apartment freezers fill quickly.
- More containers to buy.
- The schedule gets longer, maybe 3-3.5 hours, because pots and pans limit how much you can cook at once.
- Eating the same meals for two weeks is a lot, even if you don't mind repetition now.

I'd suggest doing the weekly version for a few weeks first. Once it feels routine, try a doubled batch of just one dish (like the pasta, which freezes best) to see how it fits.

I'm working on a physics problem set and I keep getting a different answer than the textbook. The problem is: a 5 kg block is on a 30° frictionless incline, and it's connected by a string over a pulley to a hanging 3 kg mass. Find the acceleration. I got 0.98 m/s², but the book says 0.61 m/s². I'm not sure what I'm doing wrong.

Let's go through it. Taking g = 9.8 m/s²:

- Force pulling the hanging mass down: m2·g = 3 × 9.8 = 29.4 N
- Component of gravity pulling the block down the incline: m1·g·sin30° = 5 × 9.8 × 0.5 = 24.5 N

Since 29.4 > 24.5, the hanging mass goes down and the block goes up the slope.

Net force = 29.4 − 24.5 = 4.9 N
Total mass = 5 + 3 = 8 kg
a = 4.9 / 8 = **0.61 m/s²**

So the book is right. My guess is that you divided by 5 kg instead of 8 kg (4.9/5 = 0.98). Both masses accelerate together, so you need the total mass. Does that match what you did?
Yes, that's exactly what I did. I divided by just the block mass. Why is it the total mass though? The string is only pulling the block.

The string pulls on the block, but it also pulls up on the hanging mass, and both are accelerating. If you only look at the block, you'd need the tension, which you don't know yet.

There are two ways to think about it:

**1. System approach:** treat both masses as one object connected by the string. The tension is an internal force: it pulls the block up the slope and pulls the hanging mass up by the same amount, so it cancels. The only external forces along the motion are the hanging weight and the incline component. So F_net / (m1 + m2).

**2. Separate equations:**
- Block: T − m1·g·sin30° = m1·a
- Hanging mass: m2·g − T = m2·a

Add them and T cancels: m2·g − m1·g·sin30° = (m1 + m2)·a. Same result.

Your mistake was using the system's net force but only one object's mass.
That makes sense. The next part asks for the tension in the string. I used T = m2·g = 29.4 N but the book says 27.6 N.

That's another common one. T = m2·g would only be true if the hanging mass were at rest or moving at constant speed. Here it's accelerating downward, so the string pulls up with less than its weight.

Use the hanging mass equation:

m2·g − T = m2·a
T = m2·g − m2·a = m2(g − a)
T = 3 × (9.8 − 0.61) = 3 × 9.19 = **27.6 N**

You can check with the block's equation too:
T = m1·a + m1·g·sin30° = 5 × 0.61 + 24.5 = 3.05 + 24.5 = 27.55 ≈ 27.6 N ✓

If both equations give the same tension, your answer is almost certainly right.
Okay, I understand that now. There's a part (c) that adds friction with μk = 0.2 on the incline. I tried it and got a negative acceleration, which seems wrong.

A negative value doesn't necessarily mean the method is wrong, but here it suggests a sign issue. Let's check.

Kinetic friction on the block: f = μk·N, and on an incline N = m1·g·cos30°.
N = 5 × 9.8 × 0.866 = 42.4 N
f = 0.2 × 42.4 = 8.49 N

The block is moving up the slope (hanging mass goes down), so friction acts down the slope, opposing the motion. It adds to the gravity component:

Net force = m2·g − m1·g·sin30° − f = 29.4 − 24.5 − 8.49 = −3.59 N

So it is negative! That means friction is strong enough that the system can't move in that direction at all. Did the problem say the system starts at rest?
Yes, it says it's released from rest. So does that mean the answer is just zero?

Yes, most likely the answer is a = 0, but technically you should check static friction, not kinetic, because the block isn't moving yet.

The idea:
- Without friction, the net force tries to move the system with 4.9 N (hanging mass pulling down).
- Friction can resist with up to μs·N. If μs is at least as big as μk (which it always is), the maximum static friction is at least 8.49 N.
- 4.9 N < 8.49 N, so static friction holds it and the system stays at rest.

Also check the other direction: could the block slide down the slope? That would need m1·g·sin30° > m2·g, but 24.5 < 29.4, so no.

So: the system stays at rest, a = 0. The negative number you got was the kinetic friction formula being applied to a situation where nothing is moving.
What if the problem only gives μk and not μs? Can I still say it doesn't move?

Yes. Since μs ≥ μk for basically all real surfaces, if kinetic friction alone would already be enough to stop the motion, static friction is definitely enough to prevent it from starting.

So the reasoning is:
1. Compute the driving force without friction: 4.9 N.
2. Compute kinetic friction: 8.49 N.
3. Since 8.49 > 4.9, and static friction is at least as large, the system remains at rest.

In your written answer, state that assumption explicitly ('assuming μs ≥ μk, static friction can hold the system'). Most graders expect that, and it shows you understand why the negative value happened instead of just writing 0.
That's really helpful. Is there a general way to avoid these sign mistakes on future problems?

Yes, a consistent routine helps a lot:

1. **Draw a free-body diagram for each object.** Every force with its direction.
2. **Pick the direction of motion first**, and define positive along that direction for each object (up the incline for the block, down for the hanging mass).
3. **Check which way it moves without friction.** Compare driving forces first. This tells you which way friction will point.
4. **Then add friction** opposite to the motion, and check if it's large enough to stop motion altogether.
5. **Sanity-check the answer.** Acceleration should be less than g; tension in a hanging string should be less than its weight if the mass accelerates down and more if it accelerates up.

Most errors in pulley/incline problems come from skipping step 3. If you do that one every time, sign problems become rare.
Thanks, that helps. Quick question about my Japan trip: is it true that you can't tip in restaurants in Japan?

Mostly, yes. Tipping isn't part of Japanese culture, and in most restaurants, cafes and taxis it isn't expected. Trying to leave money on the table often leads to staff running after you to return it. Good service is considered part of the job and already included in the price. Some higher-end restaurants and hotels add a service charge (around 10%) to the bill, which replaces the idea of a tip.
What about at a ryokan? We're staying one night in Hakone.

At a ryokan it's also not expected. Some guests give a small 'kokorozuke' (a thank-you gift of money) to the attendant who serves dinner in your room, usually ¥1,000-3,000 placed in an envelope and handed over at the start of the stay. But it's optional, increasingly rare, and you won't offend anyone by skipping it, especially as a foreign visitor.
Thank you. How much cash should we bring? We're two students on a budget for 10 days.

Japan is more card-friendly than it used to be, but cash is still needed for small restaurants, shrines, temples, some ryokan and local shops. For two people on a budget for 10 days, around ¥30,000-50,000 in cash (about $200-330 USD) is a reasonable starting point, plus a card for bigger costs.

You can withdraw more anytime from ATMs at 7-Eleven, Lawson, FamilyMart or post offices, which accept most foreign cards. 7-Eleven ATMs are the most reliable.
Do ATMs charge fees?

Usually yes, a small one. 7-Eleven ATMs typically charge around ¥110-220 per withdrawal on their end. Your home bank may also charge a foreign transaction fee and an ATM fee.

To keep fees down:
- Withdraw larger amounts less often.
- Use a card with no foreign fees if you have one (e.g. Charles Schwab, some student accounts, or Wise).
- When the ATM asks whether to convert to your home currency, decline and choose yen. Their conversion rate is usually worse.
Is a Suica card still the best option for trains, or should we get something else?

A Suica (or PASMO, which works the same way) is still the easiest option for local trains, subways and buses in most cities, and you can use it at convenience stores and vending machines too.

A few updates:
- Physical Suica cards had sales restrictions for a while because of a chip shortage, though they've largely returned. The **Welcome Suica** is aimed at tourists and sold at airports.
- If you have an iPhone, you can add **Suica to Apple Wallet** and top it up with a card. Many visitors do this now. Some Android phones support it too, but not all.

For long trips like Tokyo-Kyoto, you'd buy shinkansen tickets separately.
Our trip is Tokyo 4 days, Hakone 1 night, Kyoto 4 days, then back to Tokyo for the flight. Is a JR Pass worth it?

Probably not, after the October 2023 price increase. A 7-day JR Pass now costs ¥50,000 per person.

Rough cost of individual tickets for your route:
- Tokyo to Odawara (for Hakone): about ¥3,500-4,000 by shinkansen, or cheaper by Odakyu Romancecar (not covered by JR Pass)
- Odawara to Kyoto: about ¥12,000
- Kyoto to Tokyo: about ¥14,000

That's around ¥30,000 total, well under ¥50,000. Your trip is also 10 days, so a 7-day pass wouldn't cover it all anyway.

Buying individual tickets is the better deal for this itinerary.
For Hakone, is the Hakone Free Pass worth it?

Usually yes, if you plan to do the standard loop. The Hakone Free Pass from Odakyu covers the round trip from Shinjuku (or from Odawara, depending on the version), plus the Hakone Tozan train, cable car, ropeway, Lake Ashi sightseeing cruise and most local buses.

The 2-day pass from Shinjuku is about ¥6,100 per adult (Romancecar seat is extra). Doing the loop individually plus the train from Tokyo usually costs more than that. It also gives small discounts at some museums and onsen. Check the current price on Odakyu's site before buying, as prices change.
Last one: can we use the Hakone pass to get to Kyoto after, or do we need to go back to Tokyo first?

You don't need to go back to Tokyo. Buy the Hakone Free Pass version starting from Odawara, not Shinjuku, and get yourself to Odawara from Tokyo separately (shinkansen or a JR local train).

Then on the day you leave Hakone:
1. Use the free pass to get back down to Odawara (Hakone-Yumoto to Odawara is covered).
2. At Odawara, buy a shinkansen ticket to Kyoto. Note that most fast Nozomi trains don't stop at Odawara, so you'll likely take a Hikari, possibly changing at Nagoya or Shin-Yokohama depending on the timetable.

The ride is about 2-2.5 hours. Check times on a site like Jorudan or Google Maps the day before.

title: so if a block slides down…

turns: so if a block slides down a frictionless incline from rest, its speed at the bottom only depends on the height it drops, not its mass or the angle of the incline, right? i wrote that in my notes and want to make sure

Yes, that's right. With no friction, mechanical energy is conserved, so the gravitational potential energy lost, mgh, becomes kinetic energy, 1/2 mv squared. Set them equal and the mass cancels, leaving v = sqrt(2gh). The angle also drops out, since it only changes the path length and not the vertical height the block falls. So a block at the same height reaches the same speed at the bottom whether the incline is steep or gentle, and whatever its mass.
and with friction, the energy lost is mu times normal force times distance, so the speed is lower. check?

Check, with one refinement. Friction does work on the block, and the work done against friction is mu times the normal force times the distance along the incline. On an incline, the normal force is mg cos theta, so the energy lost is mu mg cos theta times the distance d. The speed at the bottom is lower because that energy is lost as heat. The angle now matters, since it changes both the normal force and the distance traveled. Your reasoning is right, but include the cos theta term in your notes.

Hello, my husband and I are trying to decide between the old and new tax regime for this year. I earn about 14 lakh as a teacher, he is a contractor with roughly 9 lakh income. We have a home loan, with about 1.6 lakh interest a year on it, and we pay 1.5 lakh into PPF between us. Which regime is better for each of us?

You'd compare each of you separately, since regimes are chosen individually.

For you (₹14 lakh, salaried): in the old regime you can claim the standard deduction, 80C (₹1.5 lakh if you use all of it), and home loan interest up to ₹2 lakh if the property is in your name or shared, plus 80D. If your total deductions are above ₹4 to 5 lakh, the old regime tends to win. Otherwise the new regime is often better.

For your husband (₹9 lakh, contractor): the new regime may be better if he has few deductions. The home loan interest can only be claimed in the old regime. Who is the loan holder? Is the loan jointly held?
jointly held, we each pay half. and he doesn't have much else, maybe 50k in health insurance

With a joint loan and both of you paying, each can claim a share of the interest. Your ₹1.6 lakh interest splits into ₹80,000 each, assuming you're co-owners and you both pay the EMI.

For your husband under the old regime: ₹80,000 interest + ₹50,000 health insurance (80D, within limit) + part of the ₹1.5 lakh PPF if he contributes, maybe ₹75,000. That's about ₹2 lakh in deductions, probably not enough to beat the new regime at ₹9 lakh. He'll likely be better under the new regime.

For you: ₹80,000 interest + ₹75,000 80C + standard deduction ₹50,000 comes to about ₹2 lakh as well, so the new regime might win for you too. Let's check the numbers.
ok let's do the numbers, for me. 14 lakh salary

Using FY 2024-25 rules:

**New regime:** 14,00,000 minus ₹75,000 standard deduction = ₹13,25,000. Tax: 0 to 3L nil, 3-7L at 5% = ₹20,000, 7-10L at 10% = ₹30,000, 10-12L at 15% = ₹30,000, 12-13.25L at 20% = ₹25,000. Total ₹1,05,000 + 4% cess = about ₹1,09,200.

**Old regime:** 14,00,000 minus 50,000 minus 80,000 interest minus 75,000 (80C) = ₹11,95,000. Tax: 2.5-5L at 5% = ₹12,500, 5-10L at 20% = ₹1,00,000, 10-11.95L at 30% = ₹58,500. Total ₹1,71,000 + cess = about ₹1,77,800.

So the new regime saves you roughly ₹68,000 under these assumptions.
wow that's a big gap. even if we put the full 1.5 lakh in 80C?

Yes. With full 80C of ₹1.5 lakh, your old regime taxable income falls by another ₹75,000 to ₹11,20,000, and tax drops by 30% of that, about ₹22,500 plus cess, so around ₹1,54,400. The new regime is still lower at about ₹1,09,200, a gap of roughly ₹45,000.

The old regime would only start to win if your deductions were higher, e.g. additional ₹50,000 via NPS 80CCD(1B), full ₹2 lakh home loan interest on your name alone, and HRA if you pay rent. Without these, it's the new regime.
what about for my husband then, 9 lakh?

For ₹9 lakh:

**New regime:** 9,00,000 minus ₹75,000 = ₹8,25,000. Tax: 3-7L at 5% = ₹20,000, 7-8.25L at 10% = ₹12,500. Total ₹32,500 + cess = about ₹33,800. (If the rebate limit applies after the latest budget changes, it may be lower, so check the slab for your year.)

**Old regime:** 9,00,000 minus 50,000 (if salaried; contractors under presumptive taxation work differently) minus 80,000 interest minus 50,000 health minus 75,000 (80C) = ₹6,45,000. Tax: ₹12,500 + 20% of 1,45,000 = ₹29,000, so ₹41,500 + cess = ₹43,200.

The new regime is better for him, too, by around ₹9,000.
thank you. since he's a contractor, does the standard deduction even apply to him?

Good catch, it doesn't. The standard deduction is only for salary and pension income. If he's a contractor with business or professional income, he can't claim it, but he can deduct genuine business expenses (internet, equipment, travel, etc.), or opt for presumptive taxation under 44ADA (for professionals, 50% of receipts treated as income) or 44AD, depending on his work and turnover.

So his taxable income could actually be lower than I estimated, especially under 44ADA. Note that business-income taxpayers can switch from new to old regime only once in their life. It's worth having a CA look at his return.

Okay, thank you. Another thing, I'm trying to improve my dal and can't decide which lentil to buy for everyday cooking: toor dal, masoor dal or moong dal. I cook for two kids and a husband who prefers things soft and mild. What would you recommend?

All three are good, but they suit different things:

- **Masoor (red lentils)**: cooks in 15 to 20 minutes with no soaking, breaks down into a creamy soup. Mild flavor, great for kids and weeknights.
- **Moong (split yellow)**: also quick, around 20 minutes, light and easy to digest. Gentle taste.
- **Toor (arhar)**: the classic everyday dal in many homes, with a deeper flavor and a slightly longer cooking time, about 30 minutes in a pressure cooker or longer if you're not using one.

For soft and mild on busy days, I'd keep moong and masoor in the pantry.
Which one is best for dal tadka specifically?

Toor dal is the most traditional choice for dal tadka, since it holds some texture and absorbs the tempering well. Many restaurant-style tadka dals use a mix of toor and a little moong or masoor so that the dal has body and creaminess.

If you want something mild, try half toor and half moong. Pressure cook with turmeric and salt, then finish with a tadka of ghee, cumin, garlic, dried red chili and asafoetida poured over the top. Masoor alone makes a good tadka, too, but it can go mushy.
Is it worth using a pressure cooker or can I just boil on the stove?

For masoor and moong, a pot on the stove is fine, as they soften in 20 to 25 minutes without soaking. For toor dal, a pressure cooker is worth it, since it brings cooking time to about 15 minutes (3 to 4 whistles) from 45 to 60 minutes on the stove, and the result is softer and more even.

If you cook dal several times a week, a basic pressure cooker pays for itself. An Instant Pot works equally well. If you don't have one, soak toor dal for 30 minutes before cooking to speed it up.
The kids don't like visible spices. Would you suggest ground spices or whole ones in the tadka?

For kids who dislike spots and bits, ground spices work better. Use ground cumin, turmeric and a pinch of mild Kashmiri chili powder, which gives colour without much heat. Add them to hot ghee and stir for just 10 seconds so they don't burn.

If you like the flavour of whole spices, you can fry whole cumin seeds and garlic in the ghee, then strain them out before pouring it into the dal, or blend the dal quickly with a hand blender after adding the tadka. That keeps the taste and hides the pieces.

I'm trying to set up Nextcloud on an old Dell desktop at home using Docker Compose so the family can share photos instead of paying for Google storage. I followed a guide and ran docker compose up -d, and both containers say they're running, but when I go to http://192.168.1.50:8080 in the browser I just get 'This site can't be reached'. Any idea what I should check?

Since the containers are running, the issue is likely the port mapping, a firewall, or the address. Let's check a few things:

1. **Port mapping.** In your docker-compose.yml, the Nextcloud service should have something like:
```yaml
ports:
  - "8080:80"
```
The left number is the port you use in the browser.

2. **Check from the Dell itself.** On the Dell, run:
```bash
curl -I http://localhost:8080
```
If that returns something like `HTTP/1.1 200` or `302`, Nextcloud is working and the problem is network/firewall.

3. **Confirm the IP.** Run `ip a` on the Dell and make sure 192.168.1.50 is really its address.

Could you share the ports section and what curl says?
The ports section is exactly like yours. curl -I on the Dell says 'curl: (7) Failed to connect to localhost port 8080: Connection refused'.

OK, so it's not reachable even locally. That usually means Nextcloud isn't actually listening, even though the container is 'running'. Let's look closer:

```bash
docker compose ps
```
Check the STATUS column (is it 'Up' or 'Restarting'?) and the PORTS column (does it show `0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp`?).

Then look at the logs:
```bash
docker compose logs nextcloud --tail 50
```

If the status flips between 'Up' and 'Restarting', the container is crashing on start and Docker keeps relaunching it. The logs will usually say why.
The status says 'Restarting (1) 4 seconds ago' for the nextcloud one. The logs end with: 'Error: Database connection failed. SQLSTATE[HY000] [2002] Connection refused'

That's the actual problem. Nextcloud can't reach its database, so it exits, and Docker keeps restarting it.

The most common causes:

1. **The database hostname is wrong.** In Compose, containers find each other by service name. If your database service is called `db`, Nextcloud's `MYSQL_HOST` must be `db`, not `localhost`.

2. **The database isn't ready yet.** MariaDB can take 20-30 seconds to start the first time. Nextcloud sometimes gives up before then.

3. **Mismatched credentials** between the two services.

Could you paste the environment section of both services (you can replace the passwords with xxx)?

Here it is:

db:
  image: mariadb:10.6
  environment:
    - MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=xxx
    - MYSQL_DATABASE=nextcloud
    - MYSQL_USER=nextcloud
    - MYSQL_PASSWORD=xxx

nextcloud:
  image: nextcloud
  environment:
    - MYSQL_HOST=localhost
    - MYSQL_DATABASE=nextcloud
    - MYSQL_USER=nextcloud
    - MYSQL_PASSWORD=xxx

Found it: `MYSQL_HOST=localhost`. Inside the Nextcloud container, `localhost` means the Nextcloud container itself, which has no database. It needs to point at the `db` service.

Change it to:
```yaml
    - MYSQL_HOST=db
```

Then recreate the containers:
```bash
docker compose down
docker compose up -d
```

Wait about a minute, then check `docker compose ps` again. The Nextcloud status should stay 'Up'.

Also double-check that `MYSQL_PASSWORD` is identical in both services.
It's 'Up' now and the setup page loads! But it's showing a warning: 'Access through untrusted domain'. I can only get past it on the Dell itself.

Good progress. That warning is a Nextcloud security feature: it only accepts requests for domains or IPs listed in its `trusted_domains` setting. The installer recorded `localhost` because that's what you used first.

To add your LAN IP, run this on the Dell:

```bash
docker compose exec -u www-data nextcloud php occ config:system:set trusted_domains 1 --value=192.168.1.50:8080
```

Then reload the page from another computer.

Alternatively, you can add an environment variable to the nextcloud service for future setups:
```yaml
    - NEXTCLOUD_TRUSTED_DOMAINS=192.168.1.50:8080 localhost
```
but that only applies on the very first install, so for your current setup, the occ command is the way.
That worked, I can log in from my laptop. My wife tried uploading photos from her phone, but it fails on anything over about 2 MB.

That's a PHP upload size limit. The Nextcloud Docker image has a default that can be low depending on the version.

Add these to the nextcloud service environment:

```yaml
    - PHP_UPLOAD_LIMIT=10G
    - PHP_MEMORY_LIMIT=512M
```

Then recreate it:
```bash
docker compose up -d
```

(This time you don't need `down`; Compose will recreate the Nextcloud container with the new settings. Your files and database are kept in volumes, so nothing is lost.)

If you later put a reverse proxy like nginx in front, it has its own upload limit (`client_max_body_size`) that you'd also need to raise. For now, without a proxy, the PHP setting should be enough.
Uploads work now, thank you. Is there anything important I should do before we move all our photos onto this?

Yes, a few important things before you trust it with family photos:

- **Backups.** This is the big one. If the Dell's drive fails, everything is gone. At minimum, regularly copy the Nextcloud data volume and a database dump to an external USB drive, and ideally also somewhere offsite (e.g. a cheap cloud backup like Backblaze B2).
- **Pin the image version.** Change `image: nextcloud` to a specific version like `nextcloud:29`. Otherwise a `docker compose pull` might jump a major version, and Nextcloud only supports upgrading one major version at a time.
- **Keep it on your home network** for now. Don't open ports on your router until you've set up HTTPS (e.g. through Tailscale, which is simple and avoids exposing anything publicly).
- **Turn on automatic phone upload** in the Nextcloud app, and check after a few days that it's actually syncing.
- **Keep the Google copy** until you've tested a restore from your backup at least once.

title: whats the actual difference between a…

question_types: explanation: wants to understand why or how something works
recommendation: asks what they should pick or do in their situation
quick fact: a short factual question, then a follow-up or two
brainstorming: wants ideas or options to choose from
how-to: wants step-by-step instructions to do something

turns: whats the actual difference between a docker image and a container. i keep seeing both used like they're the same

An image is a read-only template: the filesystem layers and metadata (the app, its dependencies, the default command). A container is a running instance of that image, with a thin writable layer on top and its own isolated processes and network.

A common analogy is a class and an object. You can start many containers from one image. Delete the container and the image is untouched. In the CLI, `docker images` lists images and `docker ps` lists running containers.
why are images in layers

Each instruction in the Dockerfile (FROM, RUN, COPY...) that changes the filesystem creates a layer. Layers are cached and shared, so:

- Rebuilds are fast: if nothing changed in a layer or those above it, Docker reuses the cached one.
- Images that share a base (say ubuntu or python:3.12-slim) store that base only once on disk.
- Pulls are quicker, since only missing layers are downloaded.

That's also why order matters in a Dockerfile: put things that rarely change (installing dependencies) before things that change often (copying your source code).
so if i delete a file in a later layer is the image smaller?

No. Layers are additive, so deleting a file in a later layer only hides it. The original bytes still exist in the earlier layer and count toward the image size. A common mistake is downloading a big archive in one RUN and removing it in the next.

Fix: do it all in a single RUN (`curl ... && tar ... && rm archive`), so the file is never stored in a layer, or use a multi-stage build where you only copy the final artifacts into a clean last stage.
how does a container isolate stuff if its not a vm

Containers are normal processes on the host's kernel, isolated with Linux features:

- **Namespaces**: give the process its own view of things, like process IDs, network interfaces, mount points, hostnames and users. Inside, it thinks it's PID 1 and the only thing running.
- **cgroups**: limit and account for resources like CPU, memory and I/O.
- **Capabilities and seccomp**: restrict which system calls and privileges the process has.

Because there's no separate guest OS, containers start in milliseconds and are light. The tradeoff is that they share the host kernel, so the isolation is weaker than a VM.
so can i run a windows container on my linux box

No. Containers share the host kernel, so a Windows container needs a Windows kernel. On Linux you can only run Linux containers natively. The reverse works in a way: Docker Desktop on Windows or Mac runs Linux containers inside a small hidden Linux VM (WSL2 or similar).

If you need Windows software, you'd run a full Windows VM (KVM, VirtualBox) on the Linux box, or use Wine for some apps. Windows containers need a Windows host with matching OS versions for process isolation.
last one, where does data go when container dies

Anything written in the container's writable layer is deleted when you remove the container. Stopping it keeps the data, but removing it (docker rm or `--rm`) loses it.

To keep data, use:
- **Volumes** (`-v mydata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`): managed by Docker, the usual choice for databases.
- **Bind mounts** (`-v ./data:/data`): map a host folder, handy for development.

The data lives on the host and any new container can mount it. External stores like S3 or a managed database are the other common option for production.
unrelated but need to eat more protein, mostly plant based, 6'1 190lbs lifting 4x a week. which is better for me, tofu, tempeh or seitan

All three work, and per serving they differ a lot:

- **Seitan**: highest protein, around 25g per 100g, but it's wheat gluten, so it's low in lysine and not an option if you have celiac disease.
- **Tempeh**: about 19g per 100g, a whole food made from fermented soybeans with fiber and a nutty taste.
- **Tofu** (firm): about 8 to 12g per 100g, cheap and versatile, with a mild taste.

For lifting I'd rotate all three, with tempeh and seitan as the main protein and tofu for variety. A mix of soy and wheat protein covers amino acids well.
how much protein a day should i aim for

For lifting, aim for roughly 1.6 to 2.2 g per kg of body weight. At 190 lbs (86 kg), that's about 140 to 190 g a day. On plant protein, aim for the higher half of that, around 150 to 170 g, since plant proteins are a bit less digestible.

Spread it across 3 to 4 meals with about 30 to 40 g each. If that sounds like a lot, a scoop of pea or soy protein powder (20 to 25 g) helps fill the gap.
ok and is soy protein powder or pea better

Soy has a slightly better amino acid profile, with more of the essential amino acids like leucine, and studies show similar muscle gains to whey. Pea is lower in methionine, but good in lysine, and it's easier on some stomachs.

My pick would be a pea and rice blend, or a soy isolate if you tolerate soy fine. Both are good choices. Check that the one you buy is third-party tested (e.g. Informed Choice) and watch added sugar.
anything else i might be missing on a vegan diet while lifting

A few nutrients to watch:

- **B12**: you need a supplement or fortified foods, as there's essentially none in plants. 250 mcg a day, or 2,500 mcg weekly.
- **Creatine**: plant diets contain none, and vegans often benefit from 3 to 5 g daily.
- **Iron and zinc**: eat legumes, seeds and pumpkin seeds, and pair iron with vitamin C.
- **Omega-3 (EPA/DHA)**: an algae oil supplement.
- **Vitamin D and calcium**: especially if you're in a cloudy area. Choose fortified soy milk.
- **Iodine**: iodized salt or a supplement.

A blood test once a year for B12, iron and vitamin D is a good idea.
got an offer of 96k for a senior analyst role, they said 92 is the top of the band. is it normal to counter? im at 88 now

Yes, countering is normal and expected in most offers, even when the first number is already a step up from where you are. Your current 88 is useful context, since 96 is about a 9% increase. A good counter is specific and tied to your value, something like asking for 102 and explaining the scope and skills you bring. Going well above the band is risky if it's truly fixed, so you might ask for 98 instead, which leaves room to settle without seeming unreasonable. Whatever you ask, make sure it's based on your skills or the scope of the role, not just on what you want.
what do i say if they say the band is fixed and no

If they say the band is fixed, shift from base pay to other terms. You could say: I understand the band is set. Is there room for a signing bonus, a higher level title, an earlier salary review, or extra equity or vacation? Keep it short and collaborative, and make clear you're still excited about the role. Asking once is fine, and repeating the same argument usually won't change the outcome. If nothing moves, decide whether 96 is acceptable as is, since it's still a clear step up.
they said they can do 94 plus a signing bonus of 3k. is that good

That's a reasonable middle ground. 94 is above the 92 they first named, so you've moved them, and 3k is a meaningful one time amount. Compare the total first year pay, which is 94 plus 3k, against 96 on its own. The gap is about 1k in year one, and it's 2k a year less in base going forward, which compounds in future raises. If the bonus is paid in full and not clawed back, and the offer is otherwise good, 94 plus the bonus is a fair deal. Make sure the bonus has no repayment clause if you leave early.
should i ask for the bonus to be paid in year one or after 6 months

Ask for it to be paid in the first paycheck or within the first month, if they can. A signing bonus is meant to offset the cost of starting, and the earlier it arrives, the less risk there is of it being lost in a negotiation later. If they can't do it right away, ask for the first half at start and the second half at six months, but make sure both dates are in writing. Also ask whether the bonus is taxed as income and whether there's a clawback period, since those terms affect how much you actually receive.

cool thanks. different q, indian passport, applying for schengen tourist visa for 2 weeks in june. visa got rejected last year for 'insufficient proof of ties'. what can i do to make the application stronger. ideas pls

Proof of ties means showing the consulate that you have strong reasons to return to India. Ideas to strengthen that:

- Employment letter with your role, salary, joining date and approved leave dates
- 6 months of salary slips and bank statements showing regular income and savings
- Income tax returns for the last 2 to 3 years
- Property documents or rent agreement, family responsibilities (dependents, parents)
- A clear itinerary with refundable hotel and flight bookings
- A short cover letter explaining the purpose and your plans to return

Also attach the previous refusal letter and explain what you've changed.
i changed jobs 4 months ago tho, might look bad

It can look weaker, but you can address it. Options:

- Get an employer letter that says you're a permanent employee (confirmed or on probation with leave approved) and the length of your contract.
- Include your previous employer's relieving letter and experience letter, to show a continuous career.
- Show salary credit in your bank for all 4 months, and the offer letter with compensation.
- If you can, explain the change in the cover letter in one line, e.g. a move for a better role.

A stable, continuous work history matters more than staying at one company.
also my savings arent big, like 3 lakh

Consulates look for enough funds to cover the trip, usually a minimum around €50 to €100 per day plus accommodation. For 14 days, you'd need roughly €1,000 to €1,500 in total, which is about ₹1 to 1.5 lakh. ₹3 lakh is enough if the stay is planned well.

Ways to support it: 6 months of bank statements with steady balance (avoid big sudden deposits), a fixed deposit or mutual fund statement, a family sponsor letter with their bank statements if someone else is paying, and prebooked refundable accommodation. A modest, realistic itinerary looks more credible than an expensive one.
what if i choose a different country to apply thru

You can choose the country where you'll spend the most nights, which is the usual rule. If you spend the same time in two countries, apply to the one you enter first.

Some ideas: apply through a country with higher approval rates for Indian applicants, but only if it matches your real itinerary. Applying to a consulate that isn't your main destination can be flagged as visa shopping. If your trip is mostly in, say, Italy, you apply to Italy. Also note that a past refusal is visible to all Schengen countries, so mention it honestly.
should i apply early or later

Early, but within the allowed window. You can apply up to 6 months before your trip, and I'd apply 6 to 8 weeks before, i.e. mid-April for a June trip. Appointment slots for Indian applicants fill fast in spring, and processing can take 15 days or longer.

Applying too early can mean your bank statements and leave approval are out of date. Applying too late risks a delay. Book the appointment now, collect documents in the meantime, and make sure your passport has 3 months validity beyond your return date.
how do i write a good thesis statement. im writing a 5 paragraph essay on whether social media is bad for teens

A good thesis makes a specific, arguable claim and hints at your reasons. Steps:

1. Decide your position. Is social media bad, good, or depends?
2. Narrow it down. 'Social media is bad' is too broad. Which harm, and under what conditions?
3. Add your 2 or 3 reasons.
4. Write it in one sentence.

Example: 'Social media harms teen mental health mainly through constant comparison and disrupted sleep, so schools and parents should limit late-night use.' Which side are you on?
i think its bad but not entirely, like its fine in moderation

Then your thesis can acknowledge both sides without being wishy-washy. Pattern: 'Although [good side], [your main claim] because [reasons].'

Example: 'Although social media helps teens stay connected, heavy use harms sleep and self-esteem, so moderation matters more than a total ban.'

This works because it's still arguable, shows you've considered the other view, and sets up your body paragraphs: one on benefits, one on sleep, one on self-esteem.
ok how do i structure the paragraphs after the intro

For five paragraphs:

1. **Intro**: hook, short context, thesis.
2. **Body 1**: your first reason, e.g. sleep. Topic sentence, evidence (a study or stat), explanation of how it supports your thesis.
3. **Body 2**: second reason, self-esteem, same pattern.
4. **Body 3**: the counterargument (the benefits of staying connected) and why moderation still matters.
5. **Conclusion**: restate the thesis in new words, summarize your points, end with a final thought.

Each body paragraph should be 5 to 7 sentences.
what goes in a topic sentence

A topic sentence states the single point of that paragraph, tied to your thesis. It should be a claim, not a fact. Compare:

- Weak: 'Teens use phones at night.' (a fact)
- Better: 'Late-night scrolling is one of the main ways social media damages teens' sleep.' (a claim you'll prove)

A good test is whether someone could disagree or ask 'why?'. If so, the rest of the paragraph answers it. Keep it to one sentence, usually the first in the paragraph.
how to find evidence tho

Steps:

1. Use Google Scholar or your school's library database, and search terms like 'social media adolescent sleep study'.
2. Check reputable sources: Pew Research Center, the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics, and peer-reviewed journals. Avoid random blogs.
3. Pick 1 or 2 concrete findings per paragraph, like a percentage or a study conclusion.
4. Write down the author, year and link as you go, for citations.
5. Quote or paraphrase it in your sentence, then explain why it matters.

Aim for a recent source, ideally from the past 5 years.
and the conclusion, how do I not just repeat everything

Don't copy your thesis and bullet points again. Instead:

1. Restate your thesis in fresh words, a little more confidently now that you've made your case.
2. Pull your points together into one idea ('what these have in common is...').
3. End with something forward-looking, like what teens, parents or schools should do, or a short closing line that ties back to your hook.

Avoid introducing new evidence. Keep it to 3 or 4 sentences. A phrase like 'In conclusion' is fine, but usually unnecessary.

title: Hello, I'm a PhD student in…

question_types: explanation: wants to understand why or how something works
comparison: deciding between two or three specific options
recommendation: asks what they should pick or do in their situation

turns: Hello, I'm a PhD student in computational biology, and I recently ran into a problem where pip install worked in one project but the same package version behaved differently in another. A labmate said it's because of dependency resolution. Could you explain how pip actually decides which versions to install?

Pip's resolver starts from the requirements you give it, then looks at each package's declared dependencies, and tries to find a set of versions that satisfy every constraint at once. Since pip 20.3, it uses a backtracking resolver: if one choice leads to a conflict, it goes back and tries an older version of something.

So the same package can end up at different versions in two projects if the other packages installed alongside have different constraints, or if the environments were created at different times (new releases appear). It also depends on what's already installed. Pinning exact versions in a requirements.txt or lock file is what makes installs repeatable.
That makes sense. So what exactly is a virtual environment doing, and why does it matter here?

A virtual environment is a separate directory with its own Python interpreter link and its own site-packages folder. When you activate it, `python` and `pip` point at that folder, so packages installed there are invisible to other projects.

Without one, everything goes into your global environment, and Project A's need for numpy 1.24 can clash with Project B's need for numpy 2.0. Each project gets its own isolated set of packages with a venv, which is why the same package may resolve differently in each. It's also why you should make one per project and record its dependencies.
Thank you. Is there a way to see why pip picked a specific version, so I can debug the discrepancy?

Yes. A few useful tools:

- `pip install -v somepackage` (or `-vv`) prints the resolution steps, including candidates it rejected and why.
- `pip list` and `pip freeze` in each environment, which you can diff to see exactly where they differ.
- `pip show somepackage` lists what it requires and what requires it.
- `pipdeptree` (install it separately) shows the full dependency tree, including which package pulled in a version.
- `pip install --dry-run` shows what would be installed without changing anything.

Diffing the two `pip freeze` outputs is usually the quickest way to find the cause.

That worked, thanks. Unrelated question: comparing a dutch oven, a baking stone and just a preheated sheet pan for sourdough at home. Which gives the best oven spring and crust for a standard home oven? I've been using a sheet pan with a pan of water and the crust is pale.

A preheated Dutch oven gives the best oven spring and crust. The lid traps the steam your dough releases in the first 20 minutes, so the loaf expands fully and the crust stays soft long enough to rise, then browns when you remove the lid. A baking stone also works well, since it stores heat and gives a strong bottom crust, but you need to create steam separately with a tray of water or ice cubes, and the results are less consistent. A sheet pan with a water tray is the weakest option, which matches your pale crust. Use the Dutch oven if you can, preheated at 500 to 550 F for about 45 minutes, and bake covered for 20 minutes before uncovering.

Hi, I'm working on a research codebase in Python with about 15 dependencies including numpy, scipy, pytorch and a few bioinformatics packages. I need to pick a tool to manage the environment and keep it reproducible for collaborators. Should I use pip with venv, conda, or poetry?

For a scientific project with PyTorch and bioinformatics packages, I'd lean toward conda (or mamba, its faster alternative), because many bioinformatics tools (samtools, bedtools, etc.) and compiled libraries are distributed through conda channels like bioconda and conda-forge, and are difficult to install with pip.

Pip with venv is lighter and works well if all your dependencies are on PyPI. Poetry is great for packaging libraries and locking pure-Python dependencies, but it's less convenient for non-Python tools. If everything you need is on PyPI, I'd consider a pip-based tool; otherwise conda is the safer option.
Most of it is on PyPI but two tools are only on bioconda. Does that change things?

Yes, it points to conda. Mixing is possible (a conda environment with pip install for the PyPI-only packages), but in that setup you should install as much as you can with conda first, then use pip for the rest, because conda doesn't track pip-installed packages and can break things if you alternate.

A practical setup: an `environment.yml` that lists the conda packages (including the bioconda tools) and a `pip:` section for the PyPI-only items. Use mamba or conda with strict channel priority (conda-forge, then bioconda).
How would I make it reproducible for collaborators who might be on Mac and Linux?

Use two levels:

1. `environment.yml` with the main dependencies and loose version pins (e.g. `numpy>=1.26`). Collaborators can recreate it with `conda env create -f environment.yml`.
2. A lock file with exact versions. `conda-lock` generates lock files for multiple platforms (linux-64, osx-64, osx-arm64) from your environment.yml, and anyone can install exactly the same versions.

Also note that some bioconda packages aren't built for Apple Silicon Macs, so test that. For full reproducibility on any machine, you could also publish a Docker image.
Is it worth using Docker too, or is that overkill?

It depends on your goal. For day-to-day collaboration among lab members, conda plus a lock file is usually enough. Docker adds value if you need to run the code on a cluster or cloud, you want a snapshot to go with a paper, or someone's system libraries cause trouble.

Many HPC clusters don't allow Docker but support Apptainer (Singularity), which can run Docker images. I'd start with conda-lock, and build a container later when you reach publication or need to share with people outside your group.
One last thing: where should I commit the lock file, and should I put the venv in git?

Commit the lock file (and environment.yml) to the repository root, as they define the environment. Do not commit the environment itself (the conda env directory or a `.venv` folder). It's large, platform-specific, and can be rebuilt from the lock file.

Add `.venv/`, `__pycache__/` and other generated folders to `.gitignore`. In your README, include the two or three commands to set up the environment, so a new collaborator can get going in a few minutes.

title: giving a toast at my brothers…

question_types: recommendation: asks what they should pick or do in their situation
explanation: wants to understand why or how something works

turns: giving a toast at my brothers wedding in 2 months. he's the quiet type, im the loud one. should i go funny or sentimental

I'd do mostly funny with a sincere ending. Pure sentimental can feel heavy when delivered by someone with your style, and pure funny can feel hollow. A split of about 70/30 usually works best: make people laugh early, then move to something real for the last 30 seconds.

Since he's quiet, you have good material in the contrast between you two. Keep the jokes affectionate and aimed at yourself as much as at him.
he'd hate being the center of attention tho

Then lean the toast toward the couple and his partner rather than a long set of stories about him. You can do jokes about the contrast ('I got the mouth, he got the brains') and then talk about how she brings out a different side of him.

Keep the stories short and make sure none puts him in the spotlight for long. A rule of thumb: if it makes him cringe in the first few seconds, cut it.
should i use notes or memorize it

Use notes, but keep them light. A small card with key phrases or a one-page script in large font is ideal. Memorizing a whole speech is risky since one blank can throw you off, and reading word for word sounds stiff.

Write the full text, practice until you know it well, then reduce it to bullet points on a card. Memorize just the opening line and the ending, so you can look at the room for those parts.
how long
Two to three minutes, which is about 300 to 400 words. Toasts that go past four minutes start to lose the room, especially if people are waiting for dinner. If you're unsure, shorter is better.
do i mention his ex or past stuff? he had a long relationship before

No. Leave out exes and past relationships completely. It can make the bride uncomfortable and it's not a good moment to stir that up, even as a joke.

The same goes for embarrassing stories involving alcohol, money or anything that would make the in-laws wince. If you're not sure whether something is safe, ask your brother's partner or a close friend to listen to it beforehand.
ok random q. why does ^\d+$ match "123\n" in python re.match. thought $ meant end of string

In Python, `$` matches at the end of the string **or just before a trailing newline at the end**. So `"123\n"` matches because `$` is allowed to match right before that final `\n`.

If you want the true end of the string, use `\Z`:

```python
re.match(r'^\d+\Z', '123\n')   # None
```

or use `re.fullmatch(r'\d+', s)`, which requires the entire string to match and doesn't have the newline exception.
wtf why would anyone design it like that

It comes from Perl, and the reasoning was practical: when you read lines from a file, each line ends with `\n`. Being able to write `/foo$/` on `"foo\n"` without stripping first was considered convenient. Python copied Perl's regex semantics, so it inherited this.

Most regex flavors in that family (Perl, PCRE, Python, Java, .NET) behave the same way. JavaScript is the main exception: its `$` without the `m` flag only matches at the very end.
ok and with re.MULTILINE $ matches at every newline?

Yes, with `re.M`, `$` matches before every `\n` (end of each line) plus at the end of the string. Similarly `^` matches at the start of the string and right after every `\n`.

```python
re.findall(r'^\d+$', '12\nab\n34', re.M)  # ['12', '34']
```

`\A` and `\Z` ignore the multiline flag and always mean start and end of the whole string. That's why they're the safer choice for validation.
so for validating input like user ids i should always use fullmatch

Yes, that's the cleanest option in Python 3.4+. `re.fullmatch(pattern, s)` only succeeds if the pattern consumes the whole string, with no newline exception and no need for anchors.

Common bug it avoids:

```python
re.match(r'[a-z0-9_]{3,16}', 'valid_user; DROP TABLE')  # matches the prefix!
re.fullmatch(r'[a-z0-9_]{3,16}', 'valid_user; DROP TABLE')  # None
```

`re.match` only anchors at the start, so forgetting `$` (or using `$` and getting bitten by `\n`) lets garbage through.
also does \d match only 0-9

Not in Python 3 by default. With `str` patterns, `\d` matches any Unicode decimal digit, including things like Arabic-Indic digits (`٣`), Devanagari (`३`), or fullwidth digits (`３`).

```python
re.fullmatch(r'\d+', '١٢٣')  # matches
```

If you only want ASCII 0-9, either:
- use `[0-9]`, or
- pass `re.ASCII` (`re.A`), which makes `\d`, `\w`, `\s` ASCII-only.

For user ids that end up in a DB or URL, `[0-9]` is the safer explicit choice.
lol another trap. \w too then

Yes, same thing. In Python 3, `\w` matches Unicode letters, digits and underscore, so `é`, `ß`, `日`, `ж` all count as word characters.

```python
re.fullmatch(r'\w+', 'héllo')   # matches
re.fullmatch(r'\w+', 'héllo', re.A)  # None
```

So `[a-zA-Z0-9_]` and `\w` with `re.A` are equivalent; plain `\w` is not. For identifiers you validate on the backend, being explicit with character classes avoids surprises, including lookalike characters (homoglyphs) in usernames.
why does .* sometimes eat way more than i want. like <.*> on '<a><b>' gives the whole thing

Because `*` is greedy: it matches as much as possible, then backtracks only if the rest of the pattern fails. `<.*>` on `<a><b>` goes like this:

1. `<` matches the first `<`
2. `.*` grabs everything to the end: `a><b>`
3. `>` fails at end, so it backtracks one char, and `>` matches the final `>`

Result: the whole string.

Two fixes:
- **Lazy quantifier:** `<.*?>` matches as little as possible, giving `<a>` and `<b>` separately.
- **Negated class:** `<[^>]*>` can't go past a `>` at all. Usually faster and more predictable, because it doesn't backtrack.
why is negated class faster

Because it avoids backtracking work.

With `<.*?>`, the engine has to try at each step: 'can `>` match here? no, extend `.*?` by one char, try again'. That's a check per character, plus the lazy-quantifier bookkeeping. On failure cases (no closing `>`), it tries extending repeatedly and can backtrack a lot.

With `<[^>]*>`, `[^>]*` just consumes characters until it hits `>`, with no decisions to revisit. When the next char is `>`, the match continues; if it's missing, the match fails quickly.

The difference is small on short strings, but on large inputs or when combined with other quantifiers, greedy/lazy `.*` patterns can lead to catastrophic backtracking (exponential time). Negated classes make the boundaries explicit, so that's much less likely. Good habit for anything parsing untrusted input.

got it. different thing, have onsite interviews at a mid size company in 3 weeks, senior backend role. 4 rounds: coding, system design, behavioral, and hiring manager. need a prep plan. i can do about 1.5 hrs on weekdays and 4 on weekends

That's about 25 hours total, which is workable. A plan:

**Week 1: Baseline**
- Weekdays: 1 coding problem a day (medium level, in your interview language), review patterns you miss
- Weekend: one system design practice (e.g. design a URL shortener), 2 hours, plus write 5 behavioral stories using STAR

**Week 2: Depth**
- Weekdays: alternate coding and system design reading
- Weekend: a mock coding interview and a design mock with a friend or a platform

**Week 3: Polish**
- Weekdays: light problems, review weak areas, research the company
- Weekend before: a full mock loop, then rest

Want details for each round?
yeah system design first, thats where im weakest

For system design, spend about 40% of your time here. Plan:

1. Learn a framework: clarify requirements, estimate scale, outline the API, data model, high-level design, then deep dive and tradeoffs.
2. Review core building blocks: load balancers, caching, queues, SQL vs NoSQL, sharding, replication, CDN, consistency.
3. Practice 6 classic problems: URL shortener, news feed, chat system, rate limiter, notification service, file storage.
4. For each, talk through it out loud in 35 to 40 minutes, and compare with a reference solution.

Resources: 'Designing Data-Intensive Applications' chapters 1 to 6 for depth, and the System Design Primer on GitHub. Since you're senior, tradeoffs and failure cases matter most.
coding round?

Since you've got the 1.5 hours a day, don't try to grind hundreds of problems. Do about 20 to 25 well-chosen problems over three weeks:

- Cover the main patterns: hash maps, two pointers, sliding window, BFS/DFS, binary search, heaps, intervals, basic DP.
- Take 25 to 30 minutes per problem. If stuck after 20, read the solution, then redo it from scratch the next day.
- Practice speaking your thinking out loud, as interviewers grade communication.
- Use a plain editor or a shared doc occasionally, without autocomplete.

LeetCode's 'Top Interview 150' or the Blind 75 lists are a good source.
behavioral stuff, how many stories do i need

Five to seven strong stories that you can flex to different questions. Pick from your own work:

1. A project you led and delivered
2. A conflict with a teammate or stakeholder
3. A failure or production incident and what you learned
4. A time you mentored someone or raised the bar
5. A time you disagreed with a decision and how it played out
6. A tough tradeoff under a deadline

Write each with Situation, Task, Action, Result, with numbers where you can. For a senior role, emphasize your decisions and your impact on the team, not just the tasks you did. Practice each aloud for about 2 minutes.
and the hiring manager one

That's mostly a fit and motivation conversation. Prepare:

- Why this company and role, with specifics from their product, blog or engineering posts
- Your story: why you're moving and what you want next
- Questions for them: team structure, how success is measured in the first 6 months, what the biggest technical challenge is, on-call load, how decisions get made
- Salary expectations: have a number ready, in case it comes up

Spend a few hours across the weekdays of week 3 on this. Reading recent news and the job description carefully pays off.
ok can u put the week 3 schedule day by day

- **Mon** (1.5h): Redo 2 coding problems you missed earlier; skim system design notes
- **Tue** (1.5h): System design: one new problem timed at 40 min, plus review
- **Wed** (1.5h): Behavioral: run through all stories aloud, tighten each to 2 minutes
- **Thu** (1.5h): Company research and hiring manager questions; write your questions

Sleep well the night before the interview.

title: what do i need to pack…
