turns: what do i need to pack for a week in iceland in january. i dont really know what the weather is like there

January in Iceland is cold, windy and often wet, with temperatures usually around freezing and sometimes below. Pack these:

- A waterproof, windproof outer shell, the most important item
- Warm base layers, merino if you have it
- A warm mid layer, like a fleece or wool sweater
- Insulated waterproof boots with good grip for ice
- Thermal leggings and warm socks, wool is best
- Hat, gloves and a scarf
- Swimsuit if you want the geothermal pools

Wind chill can make it feel much colder than the thermometer, so layering matters more than heavy coats. Check the forecast a few days before you go.
do i need a separate pair of boots or can i just wear sneakers

Sneakers won't cut it for most of Iceland in January. Ice on sidewalks and trails is common, and the snow can get deep, so sneakers will leave your feet wet and cold. You don't need heavy mountaineering boots. Insulated waterproof boots with a deep tread, like a hiking boot or a winter boot, are enough. If you plan to walk on frozen waterfalls or glaciers, you'd need crampons and better boots, but a regular winter boot works for city walks and the Golden Circle.
what about microspikes, are those worth it

Yes, they're worth it if you're walking a lot outside the city. Microspikes are small rubber harnesses with metal spikes that strap onto your boots, and they give you grip on packed snow and ice. They're cheap compared to crampons and easy to pack. You can often rent them in Reykjavik, so you may not need to buy. Get the pair with a good strap system, and try them on at home so you know how they fit before you go.
i think im good then, thanks
Sounds good. Pack light and keep your shell and boots easy to reach, since you'll be putting them on often. Enjoy the trip, and bring a bag for your wet gear on the way back.
need a recall training plan for my dog, hes 5 months and comes maybe 40% of the time. i have 15 min a day and i'd like to see progress in two weeks. steps please

Here's a two week plan with about 15 minutes a day.

Days 1 to 3: Start in the living room with no distractions. Say his name and the recall word once, in a happy voice, and reward every time he comes, even if he took a while. Use high value treats like cooked chicken. Do 5 to 6 repeats per session, and end on a success.

Days 4 to 7: Move to the yard or a quiet hallway. Add a longer distance, a few steps further, and use a light leash so he can't ignore you. Reward first, then let him go back to play.

Days 8 to 11: Add mild distractions like a toy on the floor or a family member sitting nearby. Keep the reward for coming all the way to you, and stop calling if he's clearly not going to come, then go get him calmly.

Days 12 to 14: Practice in a safe fenced area with a longer line, and keep the reward value high. Never call him to punish him or to end fun, or he'll learn to avoid you.
oh also, carry on only or a checked bag for a 10 day trip to japan. i'm trying to decide

Carry on only is doable for 10 days in Japan, and it has real advantages. Trains are easy with a rolling bag, you avoid baggage fees and waiting, and you can switch hotels without repacking hassles. The limits are that you'll need to do laundry or pack light clothes, and you'd need to stay under the carry on size and weight limit on your airline. If you pack a few outfits and plan one laundry stop, carry on is the better choice. If you want a lot of clothes, bulky items or heavy shoes, a checked bag is easier.
what about a 40L backpack vs a 22 inch spinner

A 40L backpack is easier on cobblestones and stairs, and it fits more into an overhead bin and on crowded trains. It's also great if you hike. A 22 inch spinner is easier to roll on smooth train station floors and keeps everything organized, but it's awkward on stairs, which are common in older hotels and ryokan. For Japan, many travelers pick the backpack for the flexibility. If you're staying in traditional inns or walking through older neighborhoods, the backpack is the safer bet. Check your airline's carry on dimensions before buying either one.
why do recruiters spend only like 6 seconds on a resume? is that actually true

It comes from an eye-tracking study by a company called TheLadders in 2012, which found recruiters spent about 6 seconds on the first look. It's a real figure, but it was a small study, and it measured the initial screening scan, not the full review. A resume that passes that scan then gets read more carefully.

The reason it's quick is volume. A popular job posting can get hundreds of applicants, and recruiters need to filter fast to build a shortlist. So the first scan decides whether anyone reads further.
so what are they looking at in those 6 secs

The eye-tracking showed they focus on a few spots: name, current title and company, previous title and company, dates, and education. They're checking whether your background matches the job.

That's why layout matters. Clear headings, consistent formatting, and job titles and dates that are easy to find help. Dense paragraphs and decorative designs make them harder to scan. Keywords from the job description also help, since the recruiter is matching quickly to the requirements.
what about ats, does it actually reject you

Mostly no. Applicant tracking systems like Workday and Greenhouse parse your resume into fields and let recruiters search and filter. Few of them auto-reject on a score. The 'ATS rejects 75% of resumes' claim is mostly a myth.

What can happen is that bad formatting (tables, text in images, odd columns, headers/footers) causes the parser to misread your info, so you don't show up in searches. Also some employers set knockout questions (work authorization, required degree) that filter automatically. Use a clean single-column layout with standard headings and you'll be fine.
why do they say one page for students

Because a student or new grad doesn't have enough experience to fill more than one page without padding, and recruiters are scanning quickly. One page forces you to include only your strongest items, which makes the scan easier.

It isn't a hard rule. Once you have several years of relevant experience, publications, or technical projects, a second page is fine. For a student, though, a second page often means including weak material that hides the good stuff.

title: lower back has been killing me…

question_types: troubleshooting: something is broken or not working and they describe what they see

turns: lower back has been killing me for like 3 weeks. I'm a designer so I'm at my desk 9+ hours. I bought one of those lumbar support cushions off amazon thinking it'd fix it and honestly it's maybe worse? dull ache across the lower back, worse by end of the day, better on weekends

That pattern (worse after long sitting, better on weekends) points strongly to sitting load and posture rather than an injury. Lumbar cushions help some people, but if the cushion is too thick or sits too high, it can push you into an exaggerated arch and make things worse.

Things to try:
- **Cushion position:** it should sit at the small of your back, around belt line, and feel like gentle support, not a push. Try lowering it, or swap for a rolled towel to test.
- **Seat height:** feet flat, knees about level with or slightly below hips.
- **Screen at eye level** so you're not leaning forward.
- **Move every 30-45 minutes.** Even 1-2 minutes of standing or walking helps more than any perfect chair setup.

If you get numbness, tingling down a leg, weakness, or pain at night that doesn't ease, see a doctor.
tried the towel instead, slightly better. but I still feel it by like 4pm. the moving thing is hard when I'm in flow on a project

That's the common problem: the best fix is the one that's hardest to remember when you're focused. Some ways to make movement automatic:

- **Tie it to natural breaks.** Stand up every time you export a file, send a design for review, or join a call.
- **Take calls standing or walking** if you have video off.
- **Set a timer, but make it short.** A 45-minute timer with a 2-minute stretch. Apps like Stretchly or a simple Pomodoro timer work.
- **Water.** Drinking more means more trips to the kitchen and bathroom.

Also worth adding a short routine around 3pm, before it gets bad: a few cat-cows, a standing back extension, and a hip flexor stretch. Tight hip flexors from sitting all day pull on the lower back and are a big contributor to this exact pattern.
did the stretches yesterday and today. hip flexor one felt really tight on the right side. back still achy by evening, not much difference

Two days is too early to expect much change; this kind of ache usually takes 2-4 weeks of consistency to improve. But the tight right hip flexor is a useful clue. An imbalance can tilt your pelvis slightly and load one side of the lower back more.

Some additions:
- **Hip flexor stretch twice a day**, holding 30-45 seconds per side, a bit longer on the right. Squeeze your glute on that side during the stretch, which makes it more effective.
- **Strengthen glutes and core.** Glute bridges (2 sets of 12) and bird dogs (2 sets of 8 per side) daily. Weak glutes from sitting make the lower back work harder.
- **Check how you sit.** Do you cross one leg, lean on one armrest, or have your mouse far to one side? Any of those can explain the right side.
- **Walk daily**, even 20 minutes.

If it isn't noticeably better in 3-4 weeks, a physiotherapist is worth it. They can assess the imbalance properly.
oh I definitely sit with my right leg tucked under me a lot. that's probably it huh

Very possibly a big part of it. Sitting on one leg rotates your pelvis and puts your lower back in a twisted, uneven position for hours. Combined with a tight right hip flexor, that fits your symptoms well.

To break the habit:
- **Make the alternative comfortable.** People often tuck a leg because their feet don't rest well. A footrest or a box under your feet can help.
- **Notice it without forcing it.** You'll catch yourself doing it; just switch back. A sticky note on your monitor helps for the first week.
- **If you need to change positions,** alternate sides or try a short standing break instead.
- **A standing desk converter** is another option to break up sitting time.

Keep the stretches and glute work going. If you stop the leg tuck and keep the routine, I'd expect improvement over the next few weeks.

ok that makes sense, thanks. switching gears: trying to book NYC to Lisbon for a client workshop, Mar 3-10. tried booking on Kiwi because it was cheapest ($480) and it turned out to be two separate tickets with a 9 hour layover in Madrid and no bag. not doing that. now it's between TAP nonstop $720 and United/Lufthansa via Frankfurt $640. which one

Good call skipping Kiwi for a work trip; self-transfer tickets mean no protection if the first flight is late.

For these two, I'd lean TAP nonstop:

- **Time:** JFK/EWR to Lisbon nonstop is about 7 hours. Via Frankfurt you're looking at 12-14+ hours with the connection, and you'd fly past Lisbon and back.
- **Risk:** one flight vs two. A missed connection in Frankfurt could cost you a day before a client workshop.
- **Jet lag:** arriving fresh-ish matters if the workshop is soon after you land.

The $80 difference is real, but for a client trip the nonstop is usually worth it. Check what fare type each is, though; bag and change fees can change the comparison.
TAP $720 is 'Discount' which is carry-on only. checked bag is +$100ish. United fare includes one checked bag. so its like $820 vs $640

That widens the gap to about $180, which makes it a more real choice. Do you actually need a checked bag? For a 7-day trip with workshop materials, maybe.

Options:
- **TAP Classic** (one tier up) usually includes a checked bag and sometimes seat selection. It's often less than Discount + bag fee. Check the price.
- **Carry-on only on TAP.** If you can fit a week in a carry-on and ship heavy workshop materials ahead (or print in Lisbon), the $720 works.
- **United/Lufthansa** if budget matters more than time. It's a reliable connection through a major hub, just longer.

What's in the bag? Samples, equipment, or just clothes?
just clothes and a laptop. workshop stuff is digital. but I hate carry-on only for a week

Then it's really a question of whether 5-6 hours of travel time and the connection risk are worth ~$180 to you.

My take:
- If the client is paying for flights, or you can bill travel, TAP Classic or TAP + bag is easy to justify.
- If it's out of your own pocket and the workshop isn't the day after you land, United/Lufthansa saves real money.

One other thing to check: arrival time. TAP's overnight flights from NYC usually land in Lisbon in the morning. Via Frankfurt you might land in Lisbon around midday or afternoon. If the workshop starts on Mar 4 morning, both work. If it starts Mar 3 afternoon, the nonstop is much safer.
workshop starts mar 4 morning. client's not paying, I am. invoice includes a flat fee

Then the money matters more. Arriving on Mar 3 and starting on Mar 4 morning gives you a full buffer day either way, so the connection risk is lower: even if you miss the Frankfurt connection, there are usually later flights to Lisbon that same day.

In that case I'd lean United/Lufthansa at $640, as long as:
- the connection in Frankfurt is at least 90 minutes (Frankfurt is big, and you'll go through passport control into Schengen there)
- it's all on one ticket, so the airline rebooks you if something goes wrong

If the connection is under an hour, I'd pay more for TAP.
connection is 1h50. ok. but the return on united is via newark with a 55 min connection, from frankfurt. that seems tight

55 minutes on arrival into the US is tight. On a return from Europe, you have to clear US immigration and customs at Newark, recheck your bag, and go through security again before a domestic connection.

Wait, though: if you're flying back to NYC, is Newark your final destination? If the return is Lisbon to Frankfurt to Newark, the 55 minutes might be in Frankfurt, not Newark. A 55-minute connection in Frankfurt is possible but tight: you'd need to go through passport exit control when leaving Schengen.

Which airport is the 55-minute connection in?
sorry yes it's in frankfurt. lisbon -> frankfurt 55min -> newark

Got it. 55 minutes in Frankfurt, leaving Schengen, is legal (Lufthansa sells it as a valid connection) but risky. You have to go through exit passport control, and the walk between gates can take 15-20 minutes. If the Lisbon flight is even 20 minutes late, you could miss it.

The upside of a single ticket: if you miss it, Lufthansa/United rebooks you on the next flight at no cost. The downside is you might arrive in NYC hours later, or the next day.

Options:
- Look for a later Frankfurt-Newark flight on the same fare, which gives you a longer connection. Sometimes it's the same price.
- Book TAP nonstop one-way for the return and United for the outbound, if one-way prices aren't terrible.
- Accept the risk if nothing urgent is waiting for you back home on Mar 10.
found one with a 2h15 connection for $665. outbound is the same

That's a good fix. For $25 more, you get comfortable connections both ways: 1h50 outbound and 2h15 on the return. Compared to TAP at $820 with a bag, you're still saving about $155, and with a buffer day before the workshop the risks are low.

Before booking:
- Make sure the whole trip is on one ticket (one booking reference).
- Check whether the bag is checked through to Lisbon so you don't need to collect it in Frankfurt.
- Note the 24-hour free cancellation rule on bookings from the US, in case something changes.
booked. bag is checked through. how early should I be at JFK

For an international flight from JFK, airlines generally recommend arriving 3 hours before departure. Check-in and bag drop usually close 60 minutes before for international flights, and security at JFK can be slow, especially in the evening rush when most European flights leave.

Practical tips:
- **Check in online** 24 hours before. You'll still need to drop the bag and show your passport, but it's faster.
- **Check which terminal.** United at JFK is in Terminal 7, Lufthansa in Terminal 1 (moving to the new Terminal 1 when it opens). Your booking will say which airline operates the first leg.
- **Have TSA PreCheck or CLEAR** if you fly often; it cuts security time a lot.

2.5 hours is usually fine if you have PreCheck, 3 hours if not.

trying to train a little image classifier to sort my design references into 'minimal', 'brutalist', 'retro' etc. 400 images, used a tutorial with a pretrained ResNet in colab. training accuracy hits 98% but when I test it on new images it's basically guessing, like 35%. I already tried training for more epochs and it got worse. what's going on

That's textbook overfitting: the model memorized your 400 training images instead of learning the style differences. Training longer makes it worse, which is exactly what you saw.

Likely causes and fixes:

1. **Too little data per class.** If you have ~6 classes, that's about 65 images each. Fine-tuning a whole ResNet on that will memorize it. **Freeze the pretrained layers** and only train the final layer first.
2. **Data augmentation.** Add random crops, flips, slight color jitter and rotations, so the model sees variations instead of the same images.
3. **Use a validation set** and stop training when validation accuracy stops improving (early stopping).
4. **Check the classes themselves.** Design styles overlap a lot. If you'd struggle to label some references consistently, the model will too.
5. **Check your test images** look similar in format to training (e.g. not all training images being screenshots while test images are photos).

Start with freezing the backbone and adding augmentation. Those two alone often make a big difference.
froze everything except the last layer and added flips + crops. test accuracy went to 61%. better but still kind of meh

That's a real improvement, and with style classification on ~400 images, 60-70% may be close to what's realistic. A few more things to try:

- **Look at the confusion matrix.** If most errors are between two classes (say 'minimal' vs 'swiss'), the categories may overlap too much. Merging or redefining them can help more than any model change.
- **Try a better feature extractor.** CLIP embeddings are much better at capturing style and aesthetics than ResNet trained on ImageNet objects. Extract CLIP image embeddings and train a simple logistic regression on top. With your dataset size, this is often a big jump.
- **Clean the labels.** Go through each class and remove ambiguous examples.
- **More data.** Even 50 more images per class helps.

I'd try the CLIP approach first; it's a small code change and well suited to this kind of task.

nice, way better. separate thing: applied to 8 in-house design jobs with this cover letter and got nothing back. I'm a freelance brand designer, 6 years. here it is:

"Dear Hiring Manager, I am excited to apply for the Senior Brand Designer position at [Company]. I have 6 years of experience as a freelance designer working with clients across many industries. I am skilled in Figma, Adobe Creative Suite, and brand strategy. I am a creative problem solver who is passionate about design. I would love to bring my skills to your team. Thank you for your consideration."

what's wrong with it

Honestly, it's generic enough that it could be sent by almost any designer to any company, and hiring managers can tell. Specific issues:

- **No specifics about them.** Nothing about the company, its brand or why you want to work there.
- **No specifics about you.** 'Many industries' and 'creative problem solver' don't say what you've actually done. Name a client or project and a result.
- **Tools list.** Figma and Adobe are assumed for a senior brand designer. Listing them wastes space.
- **No answer to the obvious question.** For a freelancer moving in-house, they'll wonder why you want to switch, and whether you can work inside a team. Address it briefly.

A good cover letter for this kind of role is maybe 150-250 words: why them, one or two concrete projects, why in-house now.

ok rewrote it:

"I've been following [Company]'s rebrand since last year and love how you kept the playful tone while making the system more scalable. Over 6 years freelancing, I've built brand identities for 30+ clients, including a full rebrand for a regional coffee chain that grew to 12 locations. I'm looking to go in-house because I want to work on one brand long-term. I'd love to talk about how I could contribute."

Much better. It's specific, it shows you've looked at their work, and the coffee chain example is concrete. A few improvements:

- **The coffee chain line** implies your rebrand caused the growth to 12 locations. If that's not what you mean, rephrase so it's not overclaiming, e.g. 'and supported them through expansion from 3 to 12 locations with packaging, signage and a design system.' That also shows ongoing system work, which is what in-house teams care about.
- **Expand the rebrand compliment** by one sentence with something specific (a typeface choice, the motion work, packaging). 'Love how you kept the playful tone' is good but still slightly generic.
- **The in-house reason** is good. You could add what you'd bring from freelancing, like working fast with lots of stakeholders.

It's about 80 words now, so you have room to add a bit.
the coffee chain grew from 3 to 12 while I worked with them, but obviously not because of me. so your version is right

Then your version of the fact is solid; just make the wording precise. Something like:

"...including a regional coffee chain I've worked with for four years, building their identity and then scaling it across packaging, signage and menus as they grew from 3 to 12 locations."

That sentence does a lot: it shows a long-term client relationship (good for an in-house role), system thinking, and real-world application across formats. It's honest and still impressive.

If you have a link to that case study in your portfolio, reference it right after.
what if I don't know anything specific about the company's brand. some of these are pretty boring b2b companies

Then focus on what you can find, rather than pretending to love the brand:

- **Their product or customers.** 'You help logistics teams track shipments...' shows you understand the business.
- **A visible design problem or opportunity.** E.g. their website and product feel inconsistent, or their LinkedIn graphics don't match the site. Mention it tactfully as something you'd enjoy working on.
- **The job description.** If it mentions building a design system, refreshing the brand, or supporting a product launch, connect directly to your relevant experience.
- **Company news.** A funding round, a new market, a product launch.

B2B brand roles often exist because the brand needs work. Showing you see the opportunity can be more compelling than praising what's there.

ok here's one for a boring B2B company, payroll software:

"[Company] has grown fast, and it shows in the brand: your website, product and sales materials each feel like a slightly different company. I'd love to help bring them together. For the past 4 years I've built and maintained the visual system for a regional coffee chain as they grew from 3 to 12 locations, across packaging, signage and digital. Before going in-house, I wanted to find a company where I could own a brand long-term, and a growing B2B product with a real consistency challenge is exactly that."

This is a strong letter. It shows you looked closely, names a real problem, and connects it to relevant experience.

A few refinements:

- **The opening is a bit blunt.** Pointing out problems is good, but in the first line it could read as critical. Try softening: 'As [Company] has grown, the brand has expanded across website, product and sales materials, and there's a real opportunity to make it feel like one company.'
- **'Before going in-house, I wanted to find'** reads slightly odd. Maybe: 'I'm moving in-house to own one brand long-term, and a growing B2B product with a real consistency challenge is exactly what I'm looking for.'
- **Add one line on how you work with others,** e.g. working with marketing, sales and product. In-house roles rely on that.

At this length, you'll be near 150 words. Good.
this is so much better than what I sent before. ugh. should I resend to the 8 companies

Usually not to the same posting. Most applicant tracking systems flag duplicates, and recruiters rarely re-read a second application for the same role.

What can work instead:
- **If a role is still open and recent,** find the recruiter or hiring manager on LinkedIn and send a short, personal message with your portfolio link and a line or two of your new pitch. That can actually be more effective than the application.
- **Ask someone at the company** for a referral if you have a connection.
- **Re-apply later** if the role is re-posted or a similar role opens.

For new applications, use the new approach. Customizing the first paragraph for each company is the part that matters most; the middle can be reused.
how long should the linkedin message be

Short, 3-5 sentences, under 100 words. Something like:

"Hi [Name], I recently applied for the Senior Brand Designer role. I've spent the past 4 years building the visual system for a regional coffee chain as they grew from 3 to 12 locations, and I'd love to bring that kind of long-term system work to [Company], especially as the brand expands across product and sales. My portfolio is here: [link]. Happy to chat if it's a fit."

Tips:
- Send a connection request with the note, or an InMail if they're not accepting connections.
- Don't ask why you didn't hear back.
- Make the portfolio link go straight to the relevant case study.

I'm building a little web app for my freelance business to track clients, projects and invoices (switching off a messy Notion setup). Tried to design the database myself with a single 'projects' table that has client name, email, invoice amount, paid status etc all in one row. It became a mess quickly (same client typed 3 different ways, multiple invoices per project don't fit). using Supabase (postgres). can you help me plan this properly

That 'everything in one table' problem is exactly what normalization solves. Here's a plan:

**Step 1: Identify the entities** (the things you track):
- clients
- projects
- invoices
- maybe invoice line items, payments

**Step 2: Relationships**
- one client has many projects
- one project has many invoices
- one invoice has many line items (optional)

**Step 3: One table per entity**, with foreign keys linking them.

**Step 4: Migrate data** from Notion, cleaning duplicate client names along the way.

**Step 5: Build the app views** on top.

Before designing tables: do you also need to track hours/time, or only fixed-price projects? And do invoices ever cover multiple projects?
mostly fixed price but sometimes hourly. invoices sometimes cover 2 projects for the same client, like a logo and website billed together

Then invoices shouldn't belong directly to one project. Instead, invoices belong to a client, and line items link to projects. Proposed tables:

```
clients
  id, name, email, company, created_at

projects
  id, client_id -> clients.id, name, status,
  pricing_type ('fixed' | 'hourly'), fixed_price, hourly_rate,
  start_date, end_date

invoices
  id, client_id -> clients.id, invoice_number, issue_date,
  due_date, status ('draft' | 'sent' | 'paid' | 'overdue')

invoice_items
  id, invoice_id -> invoices.id, project_id -> projects.id (nullable),
  description, quantity, unit_price

time_entries (for hourly projects)
  id, project_id -> projects.id, date, hours, note
```

The invoice total is the sum of its items, so you don't store it separately. That avoids totals going out of sync.
wait I don't store the total? that seems annoying, I want to see it in a list

You can still show it in a list, you just calculate it instead of storing it. In Postgres, create a view:

```sql
create view invoice_totals as
select i.*, coalesce(sum(it.quantity * it.unit_price), 0) as total
from invoices i
left join invoice_items it on it.invoice_id = i.id
group by i.id;
```

Then query `invoice_totals` instead of `invoices` in your app, and Supabase treats it like a table.

The reason: if you store the total and later edit a line item, the stored total becomes wrong unless you remember to update it. For a few hundred invoices, the calculation is instant.

One exception: once an invoice is sent, you might want to freeze its total for your records. You can add a `total_at_send` column filled when you mark it sent.
ok makes sense. what about payments, sometimes clients pay in 2 parts

Add a payments table:

```
payments
  id, invoice_id -> invoices.id, amount, paid_on, method, note
```

Then 'paid' becomes something you calculate: an invoice is paid when the sum of payments ≥ its total. You can add `amount_paid` and `balance` to the view:

```sql
... coalesce((select sum(amount) from payments p
            where p.invoice_id = i.id), 0) as amount_paid
```

You could drop 'paid' from the status column and keep only 'draft', 'sent', 'void', with 'paid' and 'partially paid' coming from the numbers. Or keep the status for simplicity and update it when a payment is recorded. The calculated version is more reliable; the manual one is simpler to build. For a solo business, either is fine.
ok let's do calculated. can you put this into an actual plan with order of steps, I want to do it over the next 2 weekends

Here's a 2-weekend plan:

**Weekend 1: database**

*Saturday*
1. Create tables in Supabase in this order (because of foreign keys): `clients`, `projects`, `invoices`, `invoice_items`, `payments`, `time_entries`.
2. Add constraints: `not null` where needed, `check` on status values, unique `invoice_number`.
3. Create the `invoice_totals` view with total, amount_paid and balance.
4. Turn on Row Level Security, with a policy allowing only your user.

*Sunday*
5. Export your Notion data to CSV.
6. Clean client names in a spreadsheet: make one row per real client, with an ID.
7. Import clients, then projects (map client names to IDs), then invoices and items.
8. Spot-check: do invoice totals match what you actually billed?

**Weekend 2: app**

*Saturday*
9. Client list and client detail page (their projects and invoices).
10. Project page with time entries.

*Sunday*
11. Invoice creation: pick client, add items from projects.
12. Record payments, show balance and overdue invoices.
13. Back up: export a database dump.
for step 6 I have like 40 rows and the same client is 'Bloom Studio', 'bloom studio', 'Bloom Studios'. what's the easiest way to clean that

With 40 rows, doing it by hand in a spreadsheet is fastest:

1. Copy the client name column to a new sheet.
2. Sort alphabetically. Similar spellings will end up next to each other.
3. Add a column 'canonical_name' and type the correct name for each row ('Bloom Studio' for all three variants).
4. Remove duplicates of canonical_name to get your clean client list. Add an ID column (1, 2, 3...).
5. In your projects sheet, use VLOOKUP / XLOOKUP from original name to canonical name to ID.

For 40 rows, maybe 20-30 minutes. If you had thousands, tools like OpenRefine can cluster similar names automatically, but it's overkill here.

Once clients have IDs in the database, you'll pick them from a dropdown in your app, so typos can't happen again.
should email be unique on clients? some clients have a few people I email

Then don't make email unique on clients. Better: split contacts out into their own table.

```
contacts
  id, client_id -> clients.id, name, email, role,
  is_billing_contact boolean
```

- A client (Bloom Studio) has many contacts.
- Mark one as the billing contact, so invoices go to the right person.
- You can put a unique constraint on `contacts.email` if each person only belongs to one client.

On your plan, this fits into weekend 1 Saturday: create `contacts` after `clients`. Then on Sunday, import contacts along with clients.

If you only ever email one person per client, you could skip it for now, but since you already have multiple, it's worth doing from the start. Adding it later means migrating data again.

title: why do people get 221(g) after…

question_types: explanation: wants to understand why or how something works
comparison: deciding between two or three specific options
planning: wants help putting together a plan or schedule
comparison: deciding between two or three specific options

turns: why do people get 221(g) after their visa interview. i had mine last week for f1 and the officer just gave me a white slip and kept my passport. am i rejected??

No, a 221(g) isn't a rejection. It's a temporary refusal under section 221(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which means the officer couldn't approve the visa on the spot and needs something more before deciding.

The white slip, usually called a blue, yellow or white slip depending on the case, tells you the reason. Common ones: administrative processing (extra security or background checks), missing documents, or a request for more information. If they kept your passport, it's typically because they plan to issue the visa after the follow-up is done.
what did white slip mean tho, mine says administrative processing

That's the most common reason for an F-1 student. Administrative processing means your case is under additional review, often because of your field of study (certain technical fields are checked for export-control reasons under what's called Technology Alert List), your background, or sometimes a name match or random check. Most of these cases are cleared, but they take time.

The officer doesn't tell you the specific cause. It's usually a few weeks, but it can be a couple of months. You can't speed it up much, but you can check your status on the CEAC website and contact the consulate by email after a reasonable waiting time.
how long do i wait before i email them

Wait at least 30 to 60 days from the interview, unless your program starts sooner, in which case you can write sooner and mention the start date. Many consulates say processing may take up to 180 days. Emailing earlier rarely changes the result and usually gets a template answer.

When you write, include your name, DS-160 confirmation number, passport number, interview date and a short note about your I-20 start date. Also tell your school's international office (DSO), who may be able to give you an updated start date or a deferral if you can't make it on time.
ok and does this affect my chances of getting it eventually?

For most applicants, no. Administrative processing finishes with the visa being issued in the majority of cases. It's not a mark against you in itself, and you aren't banned from reapplying.

What can affect the outcome is answering any follow-up request quickly and accurately, such as sending the documents the slip asks for. If the slip asks for documents, upload or send them as instructed as soon as possible. Keep your I-20 and funds documents ready in case they're requested again.
unrelated, trying to pick between stronglifts 5x5, starting strength and gzclp. i'm 28, been lifting like 6 mo just random stuff, wanna do a real program. whihc is best

All three are linear progression programs for beginners, and they're similar:

- **Starting Strength**: 3 days a week, alternating A/B with squat each day, then bench or press, and deadlift or power clean. Very simple, minimal volume (3x5, one set of deadlift).
- **StrongLifts 5x5**: also 3 days A/B, squats every session, with 5 sets of 5 and barbell rows. More volume, has a popular app.
- **GZCLP**: 3 or 4 days, with tiers: heavy main lifts, then lighter volume work, then accessories. Better for slow progress as it gives you ways to deal with stalls.

For 6 months of random training, GZCLP or StrongLifts would be my pick.
whats the diff between sl and gzclp when you stall

StrongLifts is simple when you stall: if you fail 5x5 at a weight three times in a row, you drop 10% and work back up. It's a single path with no flexibility. Once you stall a lot, usually after a few months, you're expected to move on.

GZCLP builds in the stall: when you fail to get all reps on a T1 lift (5x3+), it changes the rep scheme to 6x2, then 10x1, and then you reset with a lower weight. So it extends your linear progress for longer and also has T2 volume lifts and T3 accessories for arms, back and so on.
is gzclp too complicated for first program

It's slightly more to keep track of, but it's not hard. You have a spreadsheet or an app (there's a free one on Reddit and several in the app store) that handles the numbers. The first couple of sessions feel confusing, but after a week it's routine.

StrongLifts is the easier one to start, with two workouts and one rule. If you like simplicity and want to get going now, choose that. If you want something that lasts longer and includes accessory work, choose GZCLP. Both will do the job.
i only have 3 days tho

That works for either. For GZCLP, the standard layout is 4 days, but there's a 3-day version where you rotate 4 workouts (A1, B1, A2, B2) across the days, so each week the days shift. It's less symmetric, but it works well.

StrongLifts is built for 3 days a week, so there's no adaptation. Since you're limited to 3 days, StrongLifts is the more natural fit, and you can add a couple of accessories (curls, face pulls, calf raises) at the end if you have time.
ok going with sl then. should i start with the empty bar

Yes, that's the usual advice: start with just the 45 lb (20 kg) bar on bench, squat and rows (and 95 lb / 40 kg for deadlift), and add 5 lbs each session. Even if it feels too light, it lets you learn the movements and get used to the schedule while you build a habit.

Since you've trained for 6 months, you might start higher. A good way is to take a weight you could do for 5 reps with several reps in reserve and start there. You'll hit the point of real challenge in a few weeks regardless.

my best friend's wedding is nov 16 and im the best man, need to do a toast. ive known him since we were 12. i literally write code all day and have no idea how to write a speech lol. where do i start, its like 4 weeks away

4 weeks is plenty of time. Rough plan:

**Week 1: collect material**
- Brain-dump stories, inside jokes and things you admire about him. Don't filter yet.
- Ask 2-3 people (his siblings, other friends) for a story or detail.
- Think about the couple: when you met his partner, when you knew it was serious.

**Week 2: draft**
- Pick 1-2 stories, not ten.
- Structure: intro, a story about him, how the couple fits, toast.

**Week 3: edit and practice**
- Read it out loud. Cut anything that's only funny to 3 people.
- Time it. Aim for 3-5 minutes.

**Week 4: rehearse**
- Practice until you can glance at notes instead of reading.

What's his partner's name and how long have they been together?
her name is priya, together 5 yrs. i introduced them actually at my bday party lol

That's great material. You introducing them is basically a built-in structure:

1. **Who you are:** best friend since age 12.
2. **A story about him growing up** that shows what kind of person he is.
3. **Your birthday party,** when they met. What you noticed, what he said the next day.
4. **Them as a couple:** what you've seen over 5 years, how Priya brings out something in him.
5. **Toast.**

The intro story works well if it can be funny on the surface but say something real underneath, like loyalty, how stubborn he is, how he shows up for people.

For this week, write down anything from age 12 onward that fits. Even a few words per memory.

ok brain dump so far: he broke his arm skateboarding at 13 and still came to my bday party in a cast, he drove 6 hrs when my dad was sick, he's super competitive at board games, the night he met priya he told me 'i'm gonna marry her' which i thought was a joke

That's a strong list, and it nearly writes itself.

- **'I'm gonna marry her'** is the best line you have. Save it for the meeting part of the speech. It's the kind of moment a whole room reacts to.
- **The 6-hour drive** shows what kind of friend he is. It's the emotional center. Keep it brief and don't go into detail about your dad if it's hard for you.
- **The cast at your birthday** is a nice parallel: he showed up even then. Could be the funny opening that sets up the loyalty theme.
- **Board games** are a good light moment, maybe tied to Priya (does she beat him?).

A possible arc: he always shows up (cast, the drive), and the night he met Priya at your party, he announced he'd marry her. Then 5 years later, here we are.
lol priya destroys him at catan, he hates it. ok i like that arc. how long should each part be

For a ~4 minute speech (about 500-550 words spoken at a relaxed pace):

- **Intro (20-30 sec / ~60 words):** who you are, how long you've known him, a quick joke.
- **Cast story (40 sec / ~90 words):** funny, sets up 'he always shows up'.
- **The drive (40 sec / ~90 words):** the shift to serious. Brief.
- **Your party + 'I'm gonna marry her' (60 sec / ~130 words):** the heart of it.
- **Them as a couple, Catan (40 sec / ~90 words):** light, but includes what you've seen in them.
- **Toast (20 sec / ~50 words):** raise glasses.

That's a good default. If you go a bit over, that's fine; under 6 minutes is the main thing.
wrote a draft of the first 2 parts, ~170 words. should i send it to you or wait til its all done

Send it now. It's easier to adjust the tone and structure early than after the full thing is written. If the opening works, the rest will follow the same voice.

When you paste it, tell me:
- roughly how many people will be there
- whether the crowd is more family/older relatives or mostly friends

That affects how edgy the jokes can be.

~150 ppl, lots of family incl his grandparents. heres the draft:

'hi everyone, for those who dont know me im dan, ive been Marcus's best friend since we were 12 which means ive seen him at his worst, mostly his hair in 8th grade. when we were 13 marcus broke his arm skateboarding, which honestly wasnt surprising since he was terrible at it. the doctor told him to rest. two days later he showed up at my birthday party in a cast, holding a present he'd wrapped with one hand. it looked like it was wrapped by a raccoon. but he was there. and thats marcus. he shows up.'

That's a really good start. The tone is warm, the jokes are gentle enough for grandparents, and 'he shows up' is a great line to build on. Small edits:

- **Opening:** 'hi everyone' is fine, but you could start with the hair joke straight away for a bigger first laugh: 'For those who don't know me, I'm Dan, Marcus's best friend since we were 12, which means I've seen him at his worst. Mostly his hair in 8th grade.'
- **'He was terrible at it'** is fine but slightly mean-spirited for a first joke about the groom. Consider 'he was not, let's say, a natural.'
- **Raccoon line** is great. Keep it.
- **End of the section:** 'But he was there. And that's Marcus. He shows up.' Pause after it. Short sentences work great spoken.

The 'he shows up' line can come back at the very end, too.
oh calling back 'he shows up' at the end is good. how do i practice it without feeling dumb lol

Everyone feels dumb at first; it goes away after a few run-throughs. Plan for weeks 3-4:

- **Read it out loud alone** 3-4 times. You'll find awkward sentences right away. Rewrite them.
- **Record yourself on your phone** and listen back once. You'll notice where you rush (usually the jokes).
- **Practice standing up**, holding a glass or a phone like you would on the day.
- **Do one run-through for someone,** a partner, sibling or friend not in the wedding party. One trial audience is enough.
- **Make cue cards with bullet points,** not the full text, in week 4. You'll sound more natural.

10 minutes a day for the last two weeks is plenty.
last q, should i drink before lol. one beer?

One drink to take the edge off is fine for most people. Lots of best men do exactly that. Just be strict about it:

- **One, not 'one more'.** At weddings, glasses get refilled fast. Hold off on the rest until after the speech.
- **Eat something** before. Wedding schedules often put speeches before or during dinner.
- **Water before you speak,** so your mouth isn't dry.
- **Know when the toast is.** Ask the planner or the couple where it falls in the schedule.

And you'll have practiced, so the nerves will mostly be in the first 20 seconds. Once you get the first laugh with the hair line, it gets easier.
haha fair. ok totally different topic, im indian citizen going to a conference in florida then 2 weeks vacation. i think i need a b1/b2 visitor visa and not esta since i dont qualify for esta, right

Right. ESTA is only for citizens of countries in the Visa Waiver Program, and India isn't one of them, so you'd need a B1/B2 visitor visa. Combining business and tourism is allowed under a B1/B2 visa, and you can attend the conference and travel afterward, as long as the visa covers your entire trip and the trip is primarily for business or tourism. Apply through the US embassy or consulate in India, complete the DS-160 form, pay the visa fee, and book a visa interview. Bring your passport, the confirmation page, a conference invitation letter, and proof of your ties to India, like a job letter and travel plans. Check the current process on travel.state.gov, since it changes.
how long do the interview wait times usually take

They vary a lot by consulate and by season, and they change often, so the only reliable answer is the current one. The State Department publishes estimated wait times for visa interviews by location, so check that before you choose a consulate. You can sometimes choose a different consulate if the wait is much shorter there, but you usually need to apply in the country you're in. Apply as early as you can, and build in time for your visa to be processed before you book nonrefundable flights.

title: wanna start cooking vegan more, trying…

question_types: comparison: deciding between two or three specific options
feedback: pastes or describes their own draft, numbers or idea and asks for review
troubleshooting: something is broken or not working and they describe what they see

turns: wanna start cooking vegan more, trying to decide between oat milk, soy milk and almond milk for cooking and coffee. which do u think is best

Depends on the use:

- **Soy milk**: closest to dairy milk in protein (about 7g per cup) and it behaves well when heated, so it's good for sauces, baking and custard. It can curdle in very hot coffee, though.
- **Oat milk**: creamy and sweet-ish, the best for coffee (barista editions foam well). It's a bit starchy in savory sauces.
- **Almond milk**: thin and low in calories and protein. Fine for smoothies and cereal but a weak choice for creamy dishes.

I'd get soy for cooking and oat for coffee, if you want one carton, barista oat.
soy curdles in coffee? why

It's the combination of acidity and heat. Coffee is acidic, and when soy milk's proteins meet hot, acidic liquid they clump together. Cheaper soy milks with fewer stabilizers curdle more easily.

Tricks: let the coffee cool for a minute before adding it, pour the milk in first and then the coffee slowly, or use a barista soy milk, which has added stabilizers. Oat milk usually avoids this problem.
what about for baking, cakes and stuff

For baking, soy milk is the safest choice because its protein helps with structure and browning. It also makes a good vegan buttermilk: add a tablespoon of lemon juice or vinegar to a cup of soy milk, wait 5 minutes, and it curdles into something that works with baking soda.

Oat milk also works in cakes and muffins, with a slightly softer result. Almond milk is okay, but you may notice a paler, less rich cake. Use unsweetened versions for savory dishes and baking where you control the sugar.
is homemade worth it or just buy

For soy and oat, buying is usually easier and the store-bought has added calcium and B12. Homemade oat milk is quick (blend oats with cold water for 30 seconds, strain) but can turn slimy if you blend too long or use warm water, and it doesn't keep long, about 3 to 4 days.

Homemade soy milk is fresher and tastes great, but it takes a bit more work: soaking, blending, and boiling beans. It's worth trying if you drink a lot, and cheaper per litre. For occasional use, buying is more convenient.
ok last q, any brand recs? im in the us

Some widely available ones:

- **Soy**: Silk Unsweetened or Westsoy Unsweetened (the latter has just soybeans and water). Trader Joe's organic soy is good value.
- **Oat**: Oatly Barista Edition is the gold standard for coffee, and Califia Farms Barista Blend is a close second. Planet Oat is cheaper.
- **Almond**: Califia or Silk unsweetened.

Store brands (Kirkland, Trader Joe's, Whole Foods 365) are cheaper and often similar. Check the label to see if it's fortified with calcium and B12 if it's your main milk.

so im a PM at a 6 person startup and our devs keep stepping on each other in git, last week someone force pushed to main and we lost like half a day of work. i wrote this proposal for a simple workflow, can u tell me if its reasonable before i bring it to the team? 

1. main is protected, no direct pushes, no force push
2. everyone works on feature branches named like feature/ticket-123-short-desc
3. open a PR when ready, 1 approval required to merge
4. squash merge only
5. delete branch after merge
6. if main changes while ur working, rebase ur branch on main before merging
7. deploy from main automatically

am i missing anything or is anything here dumb

It's a reasonable, standard setup for a team your size, and the first rule alone would have prevented last week's problem. Notes:

- **1 is the big one.** In GitHub, set a branch protection rule (or ruleset) on main: require PRs, block force pushes and deletions. Also apply it to admins, otherwise someone with admin rights can still bypass it.
- **2-5 are good.** Squash merge keeps main history clean, one commit per feature. Enable 'automatically delete head branches' in repo settings so 5 happens on its own.
- **6 is fine, but consider softening it.** Rebasing is where people get confused and reach for force push on their own branch, which is OK on a personal branch but scary for some. Since you squash merge anyway, 'merge main into your branch' works too. Let devs choose either, as long as they never force push to a branch someone else is working on.
- **7 needs one addition:** require CI checks (tests, lint) to pass before merging. Otherwise auto-deploy from main will ship broken code.

Also worth adding: a rule for hotfixes (same process, just faster review), and keeping PRs small so 1 approval is meaningful. Present it as a draft and let the devs tweak it; they'll follow it more if they've had a say.

different q, made a vegan chickpea curry for a team lunch tmrw, used canned chickpeas + coconut milk + curry paste. its super watery and kinda bland, like soup. already simmered it 20 min. how do i save it before tmrw

Very fixable. For watery:

- **Simmer uncovered** on medium for another 15-20 min, stirring. Coconut milk curries thicken a lot when the lid is off.
- **Mash some chickpeas** against the side of the pot, maybe a cup's worth. The starch thickens the sauce fast.
- **Cornstarch slurry** as backup: 1 tbsp cornstarch mixed with 2 tbsp cold water, stir in, simmer 2 min.

For bland:
- **Salt.** Usually the main issue. Add a bit at a time, taste.
- **Acid:** juice of half a lime at the end brightens everything.
- **More curry paste,** but fry it in a little oil in a separate pan first for a minute before stirring it in, so it doesn't taste raw.
- **A bit of sugar or maple syrup** balances the spice if needed.

Also, it'll taste better tomorrow. Curries deepen overnight.
did the mashing + uncovered simmer, way thicker now. added salt and lime, better but still missing something

Usually 'missing something' in a vegan curry is umami or aromatics. Try in small amounts:

- **Soy sauce or tamari:** a teaspoon or two adds depth and saltiness.
- **Garlic and ginger:** if you didn't use fresh, fry a couple of cloves of garlic and a thumb of ginger in oil and stir in.
- **Tomato paste:** a tablespoon, fried briefly first, adds richness.
- **Garam masala** stirred in at the very end (half a teaspoon). Very aromatic.
- **Fresh cilantro** right before serving.

Taste after each addition. If it's a Thai red/yellow paste, soy sauce plus a bit of brown sugar is usually the fix. If more Indian-style, try the garam masala and tomato paste.

title: ok so for my thesis im…

question_types: comparison: deciding between two or three specific options

turns: ok so for my thesis im classifying cell images (about 12k labeled, 5 classes, kinda imbalanced, smallest class is ~600). deciding between fine tuning a resnet50 vs a ViT (vit-base) vs just doing random forest on handcrafted features my lab already computes. which would u pick

With 12k images and decent visual differences between classes, I'd go with fine-tuning ResNet50 as the main approach, and keep the random forest as a baseline.

- **ResNet50:** CNNs fine-tune well on datasets of this size. Strong inductive bias (local features, translation invariance) means it needs less data than a ViT. Reliable and well-understood.
- **ViT-base:** ViTs generally need more data or strong pretraining to beat CNNs. With 12k images, a ViT pretrained on ImageNet-21k can do fine, but it's more sensitive to hyperparameters and often not better than ResNet at this size.
- **Random forest on handcrafted features:** fast, interpretable, and reviewers in biology often like it. Good baseline. But usually lower accuracy than a fine-tuned CNN on raw images.

What do the images look like? Microscopy with multiple channels, or RGB?
fluorescence microscopy, 3 channels but not rgb, like DAPI + 2 markers. does that change anything

Yes, a bit. ImageNet-pretrained models expect natural RGB images, so the pretrained features don't map perfectly onto DAPI + markers. Still, pretraining usually helps compared to training from scratch, because low-level features (edges, textures, blobs) transfer.

Things to consider:
- **Channel mapping:** feed your 3 channels in place of RGB. It works, but normalize per channel using your dataset's stats, not ImageNet's.
- **Domain-specific pretraining:** there are models pretrained on microscopy, e.g. from the Cell Painting / JUMP datasets or models like CellViT-style or DINO trained on cell images. Those can transfer better than ImageNet.
- **CNNs are more forgiving** with a domain shift like this, which is another point for ResNet.

The random forest isn't affected at all, since your lab's features are designed for these channels. That's an argument for keeping it in the comparison.
hm ok. whats the actual reason vits need more data, ive heard it a million times but never really got it

It's about inductive bias, the built-in assumptions of the architecture.

A CNN is built to assume:
- **locality:** nearby pixels relate to each other (small kernels)
- **translation equivariance:** a feature looks the same wherever it appears (shared weights)

These assumptions are true for most images, so the network doesn't have to learn them from data.

A ViT splits the image into patches and uses self-attention, where every patch can attend to every other patch from the first layer. It has almost no built-in idea that nearby patches are related. It has to learn spatial structure from data.

With lots of data, that flexibility pays off, because the ViT can learn patterns a CNN's assumptions would limit. With small data, it means the ViT may overfit or learn worse features. Strong pretraining (on very large datasets) partly solves this, which is why pretrained ViTs can still work on moderate datasets.
makes sense. so for the imbalance, smallest class 600 vs biggest ~4500. weighted loss or oversampling

Both are reasonable; the imbalance (about 7.5:1) isn't extreme.

- **Weighted cross-entropy:** weight each class inversely to its frequency (or by the square root of that, which is gentler). Simple, no change to the data pipeline, every image seen once per epoch.
- **Oversampling** (e.g. PyTorch `WeightedRandomSampler`): rare class images appear more often per epoch. Works well combined with augmentation, so repeated images look different. Risk of overfitting on the small class if augmentation is weak.

In practice, for CNNs, they give similar results. I'd start with weighted loss since it's one line, and try oversampling if the small class recall stays low.

More important: **evaluate with macro F1 or per-class recall**, not overall accuracy. With imbalance, accuracy can look great while the 600-image class is badly classified.
for the random forest, any reason to also try xgboost or is that overkill

Not overkill, it's a cheap addition. On tabular handcrafted features, gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) usually beats random forest by a few points, and it takes maybe an hour to set up with the same features.

Tradeoffs:
- **Random forest:** fewer hyperparameters, hard to badly overfit, robust defaults.
- **XGBoost/LightGBM:** usually more accurate, but needs some tuning (learning rate, depth, number of trees, early stopping).

For a thesis, a comparison table with RF, XGBoost and the CNN is good: it shows whether deep learning actually beats the lab's existing features, and by how much. If the gap is small, that's an interesting finding too, because the handcrafted features are interpretable.
how should i split the data. random 80/20?

Probably not a plain random split, depending on how the images were collected. The key question is whether images are independent.

In microscopy, images usually come in groups: multiple fields of view from the same well, plate, slide, or experiment day. Images from the same group share lighting, staining intensity and cell batch. If you split randomly, the model can learn batch-specific artifacts and look better on the test set than it really is.

Better options:
- **Group split by plate/experiment/day**, so all images from a group are in the same split (sklearn's `GroupKFold` or `GroupShuffleSplit`).
- **Stratify** within that so each split has all 5 classes.
- **Hold out a test set** you only evaluate on once at the end, and do model selection on a validation split.

Apply the same split to all three models so the comparison is fair.
we have 4 experiment batches. so like train on 3 test on 1?

Yes, leave-one-batch-out is a good fit. Even better, do it 4 times, rotating which batch is held out (4-fold cross-validation by batch), and report the mean and spread. With only 4 batches, a single split can be lucky or unlucky.

Caveats:
- Check that every batch has all 5 classes. If one batch is missing the rare class, that fold will be weird.
- Inside the 3 training batches, hold some images out for validation (early stopping, hyperparameters). Ideally, again by batch or at least by well.
- Training a ResNet 4 times takes longer, but it's usually manageable.

This also gives you a nice result for the thesis: how well each model generalizes to a new experiment batch, which is what really matters for the lab.
ok so final: resnet50 main, vit as secondary comparison if time, rf + xgboost baselines on lab features, weighted loss, macro f1, leave-one-batch-out. sound good?

That's a solid plan, well justified for a thesis. A few small additions:

- **Same augmentations for ResNet and ViT,** and similar tuning budgets, so the comparison is fair.
- **Report per-class metrics** too, especially for the 600-image class, along with a confusion matrix.
- **Check for batch effects explicitly:** if performance drops a lot on one held-out batch, look at whether staining or imaging differed. That's worth a paragraph in the discussion.
- **Grad-CAM or similar** on the CNN can show which parts of the cell it relies on. Biologists on your committee will like that.

And log everything (seeds, splits, hyperparameters) from the start, because you'll be re-running experiments when you write up.
