turns: I have two kids (6 and 9), work 9 to 5 and my free time for running is either 5:30am before everyone wakes up or about 8pm after bedtime. I'm training for my first 10k in 10 weeks. Which is better for training, morning or evening runs?

Neither is objectively better for fitness, so consistency and sleep matter more. Compare:

Morning (5:30am):
- Pros: nobody can derail it with plans, work or kid needs; cooler air in summer; sets up the day.
- Cons: stiffer body so you need a longer warm-up; early wake-up can cut sleep if you don't go to bed earlier; harder in winter dark.

Evening (8pm):
- Pros: body is warmed up, performance tends to be slightly better; more relaxed in your day.
- Cons: tiredness after a full day; running late can make it hard to fall asleep; family or work events often cancel it.

For a beginner with kids, I'd pick the slot you'll actually keep 3 times a week. Mornings are usually more reliable.
sleep is already rough. is it worse to cut sleep for the morning run or run late and have trouble falling asleep

For most people, losing sleep is the bigger problem, because sleep is when your body adapts to training. Running at 8pm might delay falling asleep by a bit, but it is usually fine if you finish at least 60-90 minutes before bed and keep the pace easy. Many people actually sleep better after an evening easy run.

A 5:30am wake-up is only fine if you're also asleep earlier, which with kids is often not realistic.

Options: if you currently get 7 hours, evening is probably better. If you already get under 6, avoid cutting more, and consider running only 2-3 times a week, with one longer weekend run when the other parent can cover the kids. Test evening running for 2 weeks and watch how you sleep.
what about a mix, like two evening runs and one weekend morning

That's a good structure for your schedule and training:

- Tuesday 8pm: easy run, 25-30 minutes.
- Thursday 8pm: easy run with a few faster pickups, 25-30 minutes.
- Saturday or Sunday morning: long run, building from 40 to about 70 minutes over the 10 weeks. Mornings on a weekend are warmer, you can have a proper breakfast, and your partner can cover the kids for an hour.

This gives you three runs, with at least a rest day between them, which is a good load for a first 10k. The mix also avoids the early wake-ups on weekdays. If a week gets chaotic, protect the weekend long run and drop one of the weekday sessions.
ok and for the weekend run, should I go before the kids wake up or take my partner's offer to watch them later in the morning

Later in the morning with your partner covering is better on balance. Reasons:

- You get to sleep in a normal amount and eat something before running. Running fasted on a longer run feels worse and recovers worse.
- It's warmer, which suits your body and lets you skip the dark and cold.
- No rush to be home before the kids wake up, so you can do the full distance without watching the clock.

The early option only wins if you want the rest of your weekend free for family plans. If you pick the later slot, set a consistent time like 8:30am so your partner can plan, and take 20 minutes afterwards to eat and stretch. Having a specific agreed window also makes it much less likely to be skipped.
last question, any difference in how I should fuel for the evening vs weekend runs

Yes, a little.

Evening easy runs (25-30 minutes): eat a light snack 60-90 minutes before if dinner was earlier, like a banana or toast with peanut butter. If you eat dinner at 6, you probably don't need anything extra. Keep dinner moderate and avoid heavy, greasy food. Afterward, a small snack with protein, such as yogurt or milk, helps recovery without stuffing you before bed.

Weekend long run (up to 70 minutes): have a proper breakfast 1.5-2 hours earlier: oats, toast with eggs, or a bagel with jam. Drink water before. For runs under 75 minutes you generally don't need gels, just water. After, eat within an hour: carbs plus protein.

Either way, avoid trying anything new close to race day.

Thanks, that helps. Different topic. Background: I cook for four on weeknights and have 40 minutes max. I want to batch cook on Sunday and plan a week of Indian curries and dal. Can you put together a plan for Monday to Friday, with one curry per night and one dal for lunches?

Here's a plan that keeps Sunday to about two hours of cooking, with each curry sharing a base so you're not starting from scratch every night.

Sunday prep:
- Cook a big pot of dal, enough for lunches Monday to Thursday, and cool it quickly.
- Make one onion and tomato base, and split it into two containers to freeze.
- Cook a large pot of rice, and portion it.
- Chop extra onions and ginger-garlic paste for the week.

Weeknights:
- Monday: chickpea curry, using the base plus a tin of chickpeas and spinach.
- Tuesday: chicken curry, with the second base and chicken thighs, about 20 minutes to cook.
- Wednesday: paneer or tofu in a tomato sauce, using leftover base and a splash of cream.
- Thursday: egg curry, which takes about 15 minutes from start to finish.
- Friday: a fresh tray of roasted veg and rice, or a takeaway if you want a break.

Freeze the base you won't use until Thursday, and check the dal on Wednesday, because it keeps for about four days in the fridge.

Great, thanks. Separate question. Background: I'm 36 and haven't run since uni. I can do about 20 minutes of walk-run intervals now and I work full time with two kids. I want to get to a 10k in 12 weeks. How do I set up a training week?

With 12 weeks and a full-time job, three runs a week is a good target, plus one longer session at the weekend.

1. Monday: an easy run-walk session, around 25 to 30 minutes. Run 2 minutes, walk 1 minute, repeat.
2. Wednesday: intervals or a short tempo. For example, 6 to 8 times 1 minute of faster running with 90 seconds easy in between, after a warm-up.
3. Friday or Saturday: your longest session, starting at 25 minutes and building by about 5 minutes every two weeks. Keep it at an easy, conversational pace.
4. Rest or a walk on the other days, and one day of light strength work, like squats and planks, if you have the time.

In the early weeks, if the run-walk feels too hard, make the walk longer. Build up gradually and stop if you get sharp pain, rather than pushing through.

I'm 38 and going back to school part time for an engineering degree, 2 kids and a full time job so I'm doing calc 1 online at night. I just did a homework problem: derivative of f(x) = x^2 * sin(x). I got 2x * cos(x). Is that right? Pretty sure you just take the derivative of each piece and multiply.

Not quite. That's a very common mix-up. The derivative of a product isn't the product of the derivatives. You need the product rule:

(uv)' = u'v + uv'

With u = x^2 and v = sin(x):
- u' = 2x
- v' = cos(x)

So f'(x) = 2x * sin(x) + x^2 * cos(x).

Your answer 2x * cos(x) multiplied the two derivatives together. A quick sanity check: at x = 0, the true derivative is 0 (both terms vanish), which happens to match yours, so that test isn't informative. Try x = pi/2: the correct answer gives 2(pi/2)(1) + 0 = pi, while yours gives 0.
ah ok. then for g(x) = x^3 / cos(x), would it be g'(x) = (3x^2 * cos(x) - x^3 * (-sin(x))) / cos^2(x)? that's the quotient rule right

Yes, that's correct, with the quotient rule (u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v^2.

Here u = x^3, v = cos(x), u' = 3x^2, v' = -sin(x):

g'(x) = (3x^2 cos(x) - x^3(-sin(x))) / cos^2(x)

Simplify the double negative:

g'(x) = (3x^2 cos(x) + x^3 sin(x)) / cos^2(x)

You had it right and just left it in unsimplified form, which is fine unless your instructor wants the simplified version. Another route is to rewrite it as x^3 * sec(x) and use the product rule, which should give the same answer.
next one is a chain rule one: h(x) = sin(x^2 + 1). I said h'(x) = cos(2x). good?

Close but not quite. You differentiated the inner function but dropped something. Chain rule: derivative of the outside function evaluated at the inside, times the derivative of the inside.

- Outside: sin(u), whose derivative is cos(u). Keep the inside unchanged: cos(x^2 + 1).
- Inside: x^2 + 1, whose derivative is 2x.

So h'(x) = cos(x^2 + 1) * 2x = 2x cos(x^2 + 1).

What happened in yours: cos(2x) swapped the inner expression for its derivative, but the inner function x^2 + 1 should stay inside the cosine. A good habit is to write the inside as u first, then compute du/dx separately.
ok last one. integral of 2x * cos(x^2) dx, I got sin(x^2) + C. think that's right because of u sub

Yes, that's right. With u = x^2, du = 2x dx, so the integral becomes the integral of cos(u) du = sin(u) + C = sin(x^2) + C.

You can always check an integral by differentiating your answer. Here, d/dx of sin(x^2) = cos(x^2) * 2x, which matches the original integrand exactly. Notice that this connects to the chain rule problem you just did, since u-substitution is basically the chain rule run backward. If you can do the chain rule confidently, u-sub gets much easier.

title: I've just started meal prepping because…

question_types: feedback: pastes or describes their own draft, numbers or idea and asks for review
quick fact: a short factual question, then a follow-up or two
quick fact: a short factual question, then a follow-up or two
planning: wants help putting together a plan or schedule
planning: wants help putting together a plan or schedule

turns:
I've just started meal prepping because client deadlines keep making me skip lunch or order takeout. Here's my plan for this week, could you tell me if it makes sense?

Sunday: cook 1 kg chicken breast (baked), 600 g brown rice, roast tray of broccoli, peppers and sweet potato, boil 8 eggs
Lunches Mon-Fri: chicken + rice + veg in boxes
Breakfasts: 2 boiled eggs + toast
Dinners: 'whatever' (usually cook fresh or leftovers)
Snacks: almonds, an apple

My worry is it'll get boring and I'll give up by Wednesday.

It's a solid starter plan: protein, carbs and vegetables in each lunch, and breakfast handled. A few points:

**Things that work well**
- Boiled eggs keep about a week in the shell, so breakfast is easy.
- Roasting vegetables on one tray is efficient.

**Things to adjust**
- **Food safety**: cooked chicken and rice are best within 3 to 4 days. Freeze Thursday and Friday's boxes, or cook a second small batch on Wednesday.
- **Boredom**: five identical lunches is exactly what makes people quit. Keep the base, change the flavor. For example, split the chicken into 2 or 3 seasonings before baking.
- **Quantity**: 1 kg chicken across 5 lunches is about 200 g raw per day, which is plenty. 600 g dry brown rice is a lot for 5 lunches, closer to 6 to 8 portions, so you may have extra.

Want ideas for flavor variations?
Yes please, ideally without making three separate dishes.

The trick is one batch of chicken, cut into 3 sections before baking, each with a different seasoning. Same oven, same tray, maybe 5 extra minutes of prep.

Ideas:

- **Mediterranean**: olive oil, lemon, garlic, oregano. Pair with a spoon of hummus or tzatziki at lunch.
- **Mexican-ish**: cumin, smoked paprika, chili, lime. Add salsa and a bit of cheese.
- **Asian-style**: soy sauce, ginger, garlic, a little honey. Add sesame seeds and a drizzle of sriracha.

Then vary the sauces too, which change the whole box. Keep 2 or 3 jars in the fridge: pesto, a peanut sauce, or yogurt with herbs. Adding a sauce at lunch makes it feel like a different meal even with the same base.
That's helpful. For the dinners, should I prep those too or is 'whatever' fine?

Since your main problem is lunch, 'whatever' can work for dinner, but it helps to have a fallback so takeout isn't the default on a tiring evening.

A few low-effort options:

- **Prep one extra component** on Sunday, like a big pot of lentil soup or a chili. Freeze half, and that covers 2 to 3 dinners.
- **Keep 'emergency' ingredients**: eggs, frozen vegetables, a jar of pasta sauce, tortillas, canned beans. Any combo makes a 10 minute dinner.
- **Plan two dinners loosely**, for example 'stir-fry on Tuesday, pasta on Thursday', and leave the rest flexible.

You don't need to over-plan this in week one. Get lunches right first, then adjust dinners if takeout is still sneaking in.

Here's my revised plan. Does this look better?

Sunday: 1 kg chicken in 3 flavors, 400 g brown rice, roast veg tray, 8 eggs, big pot of black bean chili (freeze half)
Lunches: Mon/Tue Mediterranean, Wed Mexican, Thu/Fri Asian (Thu/Fri boxes in freezer)
Dinners: chili Mon and Wed, fresh pasta or eggs other days
Sauces: pesto, tzatziki, sriracha

Much better. It's varied, realistic and handles food safety. Small tweaks:

- **Freezing**: the Asian chicken freezes well. Move Thursday and Friday boxes to the fridge the night before so they're thawed for lunch.
- **Veg in the freezer**: roasted peppers and sweet potato freeze fine, broccoli gets a bit soft. Either accept it or add fresh or frozen broccoli to those boxes.
- **Tzatziki** keeps about 4 to 5 days, so use it early in the week. Pesto and sriracha last longer.
- **Chili**: you'll eat it Monday and Wednesday from the fridge half, then the frozen half becomes next week's dinners.

One optional addition: a bag of salad greens or cucumber to toss into lunch boxes for some crunch. Otherwise this looks good.
How long should Sunday take with all of this? I'm worried it'll eat my whole afternoon.

About 2 hours if you overlap things, including cleanup. Rough order:

1. **0:00** Oven on to 200C. Start rice. Start onion and garlic for the chili.
2. **0:10** Season the chicken in 3 sections on one tray, cut veg onto a second tray.
3. **0:20** Both trays in the oven. Add beans, tomatoes and spices to the chili, leave it simmering.
4. **0:30** Eggs in to boil, 10 minutes, then into cold water.
5. **0:45** Rice done, spread it out to cool. Wash up what you can.
6. **0:50** Chicken out when it's at 74C inside. Veg out once browned.
7. **1:00 to 1:30** Cool everything, slice chicken, assemble 5 boxes, portion and freeze half the chili.
8. **1:30 to 2:00** Final cleanup.

Once you've done it twice, it tends to drop to around 90 minutes.
Is there anything I'm missing nutrition-wise? I want this to actually keep me going through long design sessions.

It's a pretty balanced plan. A few things to consider for energy during long work sessions:

- **Fiber and slow carbs**: brown rice, sweet potato and black beans are good for steady energy. Keep those.
- **Healthy fats**: almonds, olive oil and pesto are there. Maybe add avocado to a few lunches.
- **Fruit and variety**: one apple a day is a start. Adding berries or a banana gives more variety and vitamins.
- **Hydration**: a lot of afternoon slumps are mild dehydration. Keep water at your desk.
- **A mid-afternoon snack with protein**, like yogurt or a boiled egg, can help if you crash around 3 or 4.

If your energy still dips after lunch, a slightly smaller rice portion and more vegetables sometimes helps reduce the post-meal sleepiness.

Okay, one more review. Final plan below, is it good to go?

Sunday (~2 hrs): 1 kg chicken in 3 flavors, 400 g brown rice, roast veg, 8 eggs, black bean chili (freeze half)
Breakfast: 2 eggs + toast + banana
Lunch: chicken/rice/veg boxes with rotating sauces + handful of greens + avocado on Mon/Tue
Snack: almonds, apple, yogurt around 3pm
Dinner: chili Mon/Wed, pasta or eggs otherwise
Thu/Fri boxes frozen, moved to fridge night before

That's good to go. It covers the original problem (skipping lunch or ordering takeout), has enough variety to get past Wednesday, and handles food safety.

Two minor notes:

- **Avocado**: add it on the day rather than at prep, or it'll go brown. Half an avocado sliced at lunch takes a minute.
- **Greens**: add them on the day too, or put them in a separate small container, so they don't wilt against warm food.

After this week, note which flavor you liked least and swap it. Most people settle into a rotation of 4 or 5 favorites within a month.
quick one. im a freelancer in india, not registered for GST, and i earned about 9 lakh this year. some clients deducted TDS. do I still need to file an ITR even though tax was already deducted?

Yes, you should file. The TDS that clients deducted is credited against your total tax liability, but filing is what lets you claim that credit and get any refund. Even if your total tax would be zero after the credit, filing an ITR is still the right step, and it creates a record for future loans and visa applications.

Check your Form 26AS or the AIS on the income tax portal, which shows every TDS deduction made against your PAN. Make sure the amounts match what you received before you file.
ok and if i use presumptive taxation, does it cover all my expenses or is it 50%

Under presumptive taxation for professionals, which is Section 44ADA, you're deemed to earn 50% of your gross receipts as profit, and you pay tax on that amount. You don't need to track individual business expenses, which is the main appeal.

For 9 lakh in receipts, the deemed profit would be 4.5 lakh. You'd still be able to claim deductions like Section 80C and others under the presumptive scheme, so it's worth comparing the result with the normal method if your actual expenses are high. Check that you're eligible, since the rules depend on your profession and receipts.
Got it, thanks. Unrelated quick question, is it normal to ask for a raise before the annual review, or should I wait? I've been at the company 18 months and my manager said things are going well.

It's normal, and it's often a good idea after about a year or more if your role has changed. Waiting for the annual review can mean months of delay, and many companies set budgets months in advance, so the earlier you raise it, the more likely there's room.

Your manager's comment is a good opening. You can say something like: 'You mentioned things are going well, and I'd like to talk about my compensation based on what I've taken on this year.' Bring a short list of what you've delivered, with any numbers you have.
if they say no, what should i ask next, like a timeline?

Ask what would need to change for a yes, and get specifics. Good questions are: what criteria would they use, what has to happen by when, and whether a raise is possible at the next cycle or a review in a set number of months.

Then ask them to put the plan in writing or follow up with an email summarising what you agreed. That gives you something to point to later, and it turns a vague 'not right now' into a timeline you can hold them to.

Thanks. Switching gears, I'm a freelance designer working from home, and I've realized my protein intake is pretty low. I'm 62 kg, I do pilates twice a week and started strength training at home with dumbbells. I tracked for a few days and I'm usually around 50 to 55 g a day. I'd like to get to about 100 g. Could you help me make a plan to get there without completely changing how I eat?

Sure. 100 g is about 1.6 g per kg for you, which is a common target for strength training. Going from 50 to 100 g is a big jump, so it's easier to do it in steps rather than all at once.

**Plan in phases**
- **Weeks 1 and 2**: add about 20 g a day by upgrading breakfast and snacks.
- **Weeks 3 and 4**: add another 15 to 20 g by improving lunch and dinner portions.
- **Week 5 onward**: fill the last gap with a shake or extra snack if needed.

**Daily targets to aim for**
- Breakfast: 25 to 30 g
- Lunch: 25 to 30 g
- Dinner: 30 g
- Snacks: 15 to 20 g

What do you usually eat in a day? That'll help pick the easiest swaps.
Breakfast is usually toast with peanut butter and coffee. Lunch is often a salad or leftovers. Dinner varies, pasta, stir fry, sometimes fish. I snack on crackers and fruit when I'm working.

That's a common pattern for people who work from home. Swaps by meal:

**Breakfast** (currently around 8 to 10 g)
- Add 2 eggs or a cup of Greek yogurt alongside the toast. Brings it to about 20 to 25 g.
- Or a latte with milk instead of black coffee adds about 8 g.

**Lunch** (salad)
- Add a protein topping: canned tuna, chickpeas, feta, tofu, or chicken. A can of tuna adds about 25 g.

**Dinner**
- Pasta: add chicken, shrimp or lentils, or try a lentil or chickpea pasta (about twice the protein).
- Stir-fry: make sure there's a palm-to-hand-sized portion of tofu, chicken or prawns.

**Snacks**
- Swap crackers for cottage cheese, edamame, roasted chickpeas, or cheese with fruit.

Those swaps alone could take you to around 85 to 95 g.
Okay, for weeks 1 and 2 then, what exactly should I change?

Focus on breakfast and snacks only:

**Breakfast (choose one each day)**
- Toast with peanut butter plus 2 eggs (around 22 g)
- Toast with peanut butter plus 170 g Greek yogurt with berries (around 25 g)
- Overnight oats with milk, Greek yogurt and chia (around 25 g)

**Snacks (one a day)**
- 150 g cottage cheese with fruit (around 18 g)
- 1 cup edamame (around 17 g)
- Cheese stick and an apple (around 7 g, the light option)

That should bring you from around 55 to 75 g a day without touching lunch or dinner. Track for 3 days at the end of week 2 to see where you're at.

Tip for working from home: prepare overnight oats or boil eggs in advance so breakfast doesn't depend on how your morning goes.
And for weeks 3 and 4? I'd like the lunches to be quick because I'm usually in the middle of a project.

Quick lunch options, each about 25 to 35 g protein, under 10 minutes:

- **Tuna or salmon salad**: canned fish, greens, cucumber, olive oil and lemon.
- **Chickpea and feta salad**: chickpeas, feta, tomato, red onion, herbs.
- **Wrap**: tortilla with hummus, chicken (store-bought rotisserie or pre-cooked) and vegetables.
- **Leftovers plus**: whatever's left from dinner, plus an extra protein like an egg or some yogurt on the side.
- **Lentil soup** made in a big pot once a week, with a slice of bread.

Prep tip: cook a tray of chicken or tofu on Sunday, or buy a rotisserie chicken. That alone makes most of these lunches faster.

For dinners in weeks 3 and 4, just make sure each one has a palm-sized protein portion. That plus the lunches should take you to around 90 to 100 g.
Should I time protein around my workouts at all?

It matters less than hitting your daily total, but a bit of timing can help:

- **Spread it out**: around 25 to 30 g at each meal tends to work better than most of it at dinner. Your plan already does this.
- **Around workouts**: having a protein-containing meal or snack within a couple of hours before or after training is a reasonable practice. It doesn't need to be immediately after.
- **Pilates**: it's less demanding on muscle, so normal meals are fine around those days.
- **Dumbbell sessions**: if you train mid-afternoon, the cottage cheese or yogurt snack works well after.

If your total is around 100 g and spread across the day, you've covered most of the benefit.
What about protein powder? I'd rather get it from food but I'm open to it.

Food-first is a good approach, and it looks like you can reach around 90 to 100 g with food. Protein powder is optional, but useful in a few situations:

- **On busy days**: when a deadline means you skip lunch or snack, a shake is a quick 20 to 25 g.
- **To close a consistent gap**: if you're stuck around 85 g after week 4.
- **In food**: a scoop in oats, yogurt or a smoothie.

If you try it:

- **Whey** (or whey isolate if dairy bothers you) is the most researched and tastes good.
- **Plant blends** (pea and rice) work if you prefer dairy-free.
- Look for brands with third-party testing, like Informed Sport.

I'd wait until the end of week 4 and see if you actually need it.
Could you summarize the plan so I can pin it above my desk?

Here you go:

**Goal**: 100 g protein a day (from about 55 g)

**Weeks 1 and 2: breakfast and snacks**
- Breakfast: toast with PB plus 2 eggs, or Greek yogurt, or overnight oats
- Snack: cottage cheese, edamame, or cheese and fruit
- Target: about 75 g

**Weeks 3 and 4: lunch and dinner**
- Quick lunches: tuna salad, chickpea feta salad, chicken wrap, lentil soup
- Dinner: palm-sized protein every time, or lentil or chickpea pasta
- Sunday: cook a tray of chicken or tofu
- Target: 90 to 100 g

**Week 5 onward**
- If under 90 g, add a shake on busy days
- Track 3 days a month to check

**Daily rough split**: breakfast 25, lunch 30, dinner 30, snack 15

I'm a freelance UI designer based in Pune and I've been invited to speak at a design conference in San Francisco in the first week of April 2027. I've never applied for a US visa before. I know I'll need a B1/B2, but I'm not sure how to plan it, especially as a freelancer without an employer letter. Could you help me put together a timeline?

Congratulations on the invite. Speaking at a conference generally falls under B1 (business), and most people apply for a combined B1/B2. Since it's late 2026 and appointment wait times in India can be long, start right away.

**Rough timeline**
- **This week**: check current wait times on the US visa appointment website for Mumbai and other Indian consulates. Fill in the DS-160 online form.
- **Next 1 to 2 weeks**: pay the visa fee (check the current amount on the official site, since fees and surcharges have changed recently) and book the earliest biometrics (OFC) and interview slots.
- **While waiting**: collect documents, including financial and work proof as a freelancer.
- **Interview**: be ready to explain your trip and your ties to India.
- **After approval**: passport is usually returned within 1 to 2 weeks.

If Mumbai's wait is very long, you can apply at any Indian consulate (Chennai, Hyderabad, Kolkata, New Delhi), so check all of them.
What should I prepare as a freelancer, since I don't have salary slips or an employer letter?

Freelancers can show a stable income and ties to India in other ways. Useful documents:

**Income and work**
- ITRs for the last 2 to 3 years
- Bank statements for 6 to 12 months showing regular client payments
- GST registration, if you have one
- A few client contracts or invoices
- A portfolio website or Behance profile, and a short professional bio

**Trip purpose**
- The speaker invitation letter from the conference, ideally stating who's covering travel and accommodation
- Conference registration or speaker confirmation
- Rough itinerary with dates

**Ties to India**
- Proof of home (rent agreement or property papers)
- Ongoing client projects you're returning to
- Family ties if relevant

Not all of these will be checked, but bring them organized in a folder.
That's helpful. How should I plan the interview prep part?

B1/B2 interviews are short, often 2 to 3 minutes, and the officer mainly wants to know: why you're going, how it's funded, and that you'll come back. A plan:

**2 to 3 weeks before**
- Write down clear 1 to 2 sentence answers to likely questions:
  - What's the purpose of your trip?
  - What do you do for work, and who are your clients?
  - Who is paying for the trip?
  - How long will you stay?
  - Have you travelled abroad before?

**1 week before**
- Practice saying the answers out loud. Keep them brief and honest.
- Re-read your DS-160 so your answers match exactly.

**Day before**
- Organize your folder, print the appointment confirmation and DS-160 confirmation.

As a freelancer, be ready to explain your work simply, for example: 'I'm a UI designer working with clients in India and abroad, mainly on apps and websites.'
The conference is paying for my hotel but not my flight. Does that matter?

It's fine. Partial sponsorship is common. You just need to show you can cover the rest.

What to have:

- **The invitation letter** stating that they're covering the hotel and for which dates.
- **Bank statements** showing enough funds for flights (Pune or Mumbai to San Francisco round trip, roughly ₹80,000 to ₹1,50,000 depending on timing) plus daily expenses.
- **A rough budget** in your head for the interview, in case they ask.

If asked who's paying, a simple answer works: 'The conference is covering my hotel, and I'm paying for my flights and other expenses.' Don't book non-refundable flights until the visa is approved.
Should I plan for extra days in the US? I'd love to see a bit of California after the conference.

That's completely fine. B1/B2 covers both business and tourism, so you can add a few days of travel.

Planning points:

- **Be clear and consistent** in the DS-160 and interview. For example: 'The conference is April 1 to 3, and I'll stay until April 10 to visit Los Angeles and Yosemite.'
- **Keep it reasonable.** A week or 10 days total looks normal for a first trip. A very long stay could raise questions about your ties to work.
- **Show funds** for the extra days, which your bank statements should cover.
- **Have a rough itinerary**: cities and dates, nothing elaborate.

If you go to the interview with a specific plan and return date, it usually helps rather than hurts.
What if the appointment wait is too long to make April?

A few options if wait times are long:

1. **Check other consulates** in India regularly. Slots often open up when people cancel, so checking several times a week can help.
2. **Request an expedited appointment.** The visa appointment system allows an emergency or expedite request, and attending a business event is sometimes accepted as a reason. Include the invitation letter and conference dates. Approval isn't guaranteed.
3. **Ask the conference organizers** for a supporting letter that mentions your role as a speaker. This helps an expedite request.
4. **Have a backup**: ask if you can present remotely if the visa doesn't come through in time.

Whatever happens, don't book non-refundable travel before the visa is in hand.
Could you put everything into a simple month-by-month plan?

Here's a month-by-month plan for an early April 2027 trip:

**October 2026**
- Fill in the DS-160, pay the fee, book the earliest slots at any Indian consulate
- Ask the conference for a formal invitation letter

**November 2026**
- Collect documents: ITRs, bank statements, contracts, invoices, GST, portfolio link
- Keep checking for earlier slots; submit an expedite request if the wait goes past mid-February

**December 2026 to January 2027**
- Biometrics (OFC) appointment, then interview
- Prepare and practice answers 2 to 3 weeks before the interview

**February 2027**
- Once approved, book flights and post-conference travel
- Confirm hotel dates with the organizers

**March 2027**
- Travel insurance, final itinerary, copies of key documents

**Early April 2027**
- Conference, then a week in California

title: training for a 5k in 6…

question_types: comparison: deciding between two or three specific options

turns: training for a 5k in 6 wks, 2 kids so mornings are tight. treadmill at the gym at 5:45 or outdoors near home at lunch. which one

For a 5k, both work. Quick comparison:

Treadmill at 5:45: consistent, safe in the dark and weather, easy to control pace. Set the incline to 1% to roughly mimic outdoor effort. Downsides: boring, and you need to get the gym time.

Outdoors at lunch: closer to race conditions (wind, surface, hills), and often more enjoyable. But lunch can get cancelled by work, and you need time to change.

If your 5k is outdoors, do most of your key runs outside. I'd say lunch outdoors for the main runs, treadmill on days you can't make it. What days do you plan to run?
3 days. what about doing 2 outside lunch 1 on treadmill

That's a solid split. Make the treadmill session the one that benefits from control: intervals or a steady tempo. For example, 5 x 3 minutes at a faster pace with 2 minutes easy between, where you can set the speed exactly.

The two lunch runs: one easy run, 25-30 minutes, and one slightly longer run (30-40 minutes) as your weekly long one. Do at least one on a similar surface to your race.

Space them out, like Monday, Wednesday, Saturday or Friday, to give a rest day between. If lunch is ever missed, shift it to the treadmill rather than skipping.
does treadmill running count the same as outside

Mostly, yes. The treadmill belt helps move your legs a little, so at the same pace it feels easier than outside, mainly at faster speeds. Setting the incline to 1 percent compensates for that.

Differences: outdoors uses stabilizer muscles more because of uneven ground and wind, and treadmills are softer than pavement, so they are kinder on joints. Pace on a treadmill can be more accurate than a watch, though belts can be miscalibrated.

So treadmill runs count, but don't do only treadmill if your race is outside. Do at least one outdoor run a week so the race itself doesn't feel unfamiliar.
ok ill do that. last thing what pace should the treadmill intervals be

Base it on your current 5k effort. If you don't know your pace, use feel: intervals should be hard but controlled, around an 8 out of 10, where you can say a few words but not a sentence.

If you have a recent 5k time, say 30 minutes (about 9:40 per mile / 6:00 per km), set your intervals at about 20-30 seconds per mile faster than that, and recover at an easy jog or walk.

If you don't have a time, start with 1 mph (1.6 km/h) faster than your comfortable easy pace and adjust after the first interval. Start conservatively; it should feel manageable on the last repeat, not exhausting.

title: I just bombed a technical interview…

question_types: comparison: deciding between two or three specific options
recommendation: asks what they should pick or do in their situation
brainstorming: wants ideas or options to choose from
explanation: wants to understand why or how something works
troubleshooting: something is broken or not working and they describe what they see

turns: I just bombed a technical interview for a summer internship. I had been doing random LeetCode problems for a month (about 60 solved), but when they gave me a medium graph problem I completely froze and couldn't even start. My next interviews are in about 5 weeks. I'm trying to decide between grinding the NeetCode 150 list, continuing random LeetCode, or doing mock interviews on Pramp. Which would actually help?

Sorry about the interview. Freezing on a medium graph problem after 60 random problems is very common, and it usually points to two gaps: pattern recognition and practice under pressure.

How the three options compare:

- **Random LeetCode**: builds some skill, but it's easy to keep solving the types you like and miss whole categories, like graphs.
- **NeetCode 150**: organized by pattern (arrays, two pointers, trees, graphs, DP and so on), with video explanations. Great for filling gaps systematically.
- **Pramp mock interviews**: practice talking through problems with a real person under time pressure. Directly addresses freezing.

With 5 weeks, I'd combine the last two: NeetCode 150 as your main practice, and 1 to 2 mock interviews a week starting around week 2. Drop random LeetCode.
NeetCode 150 in 5 weeks? That's 30 problems a week, I have classes

Right, don't try to finish all 150. Prioritize the patterns that show up most in internship interviews:

1. Arrays and hashing
2. Two pointers and sliding window
3. Stacks
4. Binary search
5. Linked lists
6. Trees
7. Graphs (BFS, DFS)
8. Heaps

Skip or lightly touch DP, tries and advanced graph algorithms for now.

Realistic plan: about 3 to 4 problems on weekdays (one a day, 45 to 60 minutes) plus 3 to 4 on weekends, so around 7 to 10 a week, 40 to 50 in total. Since you've done 60 already, skip ones you've solved and focus on the categories you haven't touched, especially graphs and trees.
I tried Pramp once last year and the other person was really unprepared, it was a waste of time. Is interviewing.io better?

They're different:

- **Pramp**: free, peer to peer. You interview each other. Quality varies a lot, as you saw. Still useful for practicing talking out loud, but inconsistent.
- **interviewing.io**: mock interviews with experienced engineers from real companies. Much better feedback, but paid, usually over $100 a session.
- **Peers you know**: a friend from class doing the same prep. Free, and you can choose someone serious.

Given a student budget, a mix often works best:

- 1 or 2 sessions with a friend each week, swapping roles and using problems from the NeetCode list.
- Retry Pramp a couple of times, since partners vary.
- One paid session near the end, if you can afford it, for honest professional feedback.

Also check your career center. Some universities offer free mock technical interviews.
okay. what do I actually do differently in a mock so I don't freeze again

Use a fixed process so you always have a next step, even if the solution isn't obvious:

1. **Restate the problem** in your own words and confirm with the interviewer.
2. **Ask questions**: input size, edge cases, can there be cycles, is the graph directed.
3. **Work through a small example** by hand on the whiteboard or in comments.
4. **Say a brute force solution** out loud, even if it's slow. It gets you moving.
5. **Look for the pattern**: 'this is about connections between nodes, so BFS or DFS.'
6. **Write code** while explaining.
7. **Test** with your example and an edge case.

Freezing usually happens when you try to jump straight to the optimal answer. Steps 1 to 4 give you something to say and do while your brain catches up.
Should I do mocks with LeetCode problems I've already solved or new ones?

Mostly new ones, but at your current level:

- **Weeks 1 to 2**: mocks with problems you've solved before but not recently. Focus on explaining clearly and following the process, without the stress of the problem itself.
- **Weeks 3 to 5**: new problems from the categories you've studied, ideally medium level. This is closer to the real interview and builds confidence with unseen problems.

When you do mocks with a friend, have them pick the problem so it's actually unseen. A shared list where each of you picks problems for the other works well.

After each mock, write down where you got stuck. Those notes tell you what to practice next.
So final answer is NeetCode by pattern plus mocks with friends, and maybe one paid one?

Yes, that's the plan:

**Practice**: NeetCode 150, prioritizing arrays, two pointers, sliding window, stacks, binary search, linked lists, trees, graphs and heaps. About 7 to 10 problems a week, skipping ones you've done.

**Mocks**: start in week 2. One or two a week with a serious friend, maybe a Pramp session or two, and a paid session (interviewing.io or similar) in week 4 or 5 if you can afford it. Check the career center for free ones.

**Process**: use the 7-step approach in every mock so it becomes automatic.

**Review**: keep a short log of where you got stuck, and use that to choose what to practice next.

Random LeetCode is out. With 5 weeks, structure helps more than volume.

Great. On a different note, I got a 54 on my Calc 2 midterm, almost all the points I lost were on integration techniques (integration by parts, trig substitution, partial fractions). I watched Khan Academy videos for all of them before the exam and felt like I understood them, but on the test I couldn't figure out which technique to use. The final is in 6 weeks. Should I keep using Khan, switch to Professor Leonard, or just grind problems from the Stewart textbook?

The issue you're describing, understanding each technique but not knowing which one to pick, usually comes from watching more than practicing, and from practicing each technique in isolation. Videos feel productive but don't build that decision skill.

My recommendation:

- **Main focus: Stewart problems**, especially the mixed review section at the end of the integration chapter (often titled 'Strategy for Integration'). Those mix all techniques, so you have to decide which to use, exactly like the exam.
- **Professor Leonard** for any technique you're still shaky on. His lectures are long but very thorough, good for trig substitution in particular.
- **Khan Academy** only for quick refreshers.

Aim for something like 70% problem solving, 30% watching.
the mixed problems are where I get stuck though, I just stare at them. how do I even start

Use a checklist and go through it in order, every time:

1. **Simplify first.** Algebra, expand, split the fraction, use a trig identity.
2. **Obvious substitution?** Is there a function and its derivative (up to a constant)? Try u-sub.
3. **Rational function** (polynomial over polynomial)? Partial fractions, after long division if the top's degree is higher or equal.
4. **Product of different types** (polynomial times exp, log, or trig)? Integration by parts.
5. **Square root of a² − x², a² + x², or x² − a²**? Trig substitution.
6. **Powers of sin and cos, or tan and sec**? Trig integral rules.
7. **Still stuck?** Try a different substitution or rewrite.

Write the checklist on a card and use it for every mixed problem. After 30 to 40 problems, you'll start recognizing the type in a few seconds.
ok and how many problems per week is realistic? I have 4 other classes

Something like 20 to 25 integration problems a week is realistic and enough to make a difference over 6 weeks. That's about 3 to 4 problems a day, 30 to 45 minutes.

Suggested split:

- **Weeks 1 and 2**: 15 problems a week on your weak techniques, then 10 mixed. Use Professor Leonard where needed.
- **Weeks 3 and 4**: mostly mixed problems, 20 to 25 a week.
- **Weeks 5 and 6**: old exams or practice finals under timed conditions, plus any other topics on the final (series, probably).

Also check the answers right after each problem, and keep a short 'mistakes list' noting why you got it wrong, such as wrong technique or algebra slip.
the final also covers series which I haven't started. should I split time or finish integration first

Split it, but weighted toward integration early. Series usually comes later in the course, and it uses integration (the integral test, for example), so you'll need both.

Rough split over 6 weeks:

- **Weeks 1 and 2**: 70% integration, 30% series (learn the basics as they're taught).
- **Weeks 3 and 4**: 50/50. Mixed integration practice plus convergence tests.
- **Weeks 5 and 6**: practice exams covering everything.

For series, the same approach as integration works: learn each test (ratio, comparison, alternating, integral, etc.), then do mixed problems where you have to choose which test to use. Professor Leonard and Paul's Online Math Notes are both good for series, and Paul's notes include a strategy section similar to the integration checklist.

For my databases class I need to write a query to find students who have taken ALL the courses in the CS department. Tables are Student(sid, name), Course(cid, dept), Enrolled(sid, cid). I tried joining all three and filtering dept = 'CS' but it returns students who took ANY CS course, not all of them. I've been stuck on this for an hour. What are some ways to approach this?

This is a classic 'relational division' problem, and the join approach can't do it on its own. A few ways to solve it:

**1. Count comparison**
```sql
SELECT e.sid
FROM Enrolled e JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid
WHERE c.dept = 'CS'
GROUP BY e.sid
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT e.cid) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Course WHERE dept = 'CS');
```

**2. Double NOT EXISTS** ("there's no CS course this student hasn't taken")
```sql
SELECT s.sid, s.name FROM Student s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM Course c WHERE c.dept = 'CS'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM Enrolled e WHERE e.sid = s.sid AND e.cid = c.cid
  )
);
```

**3. EXCEPT** per student, which is less common.

The count version is usually easiest to understand. The double NOT EXISTS is the one professors often expect since it maps directly to the relational algebra definition.
the count one worked! but my professor said we need to show 2 approaches. is the double not exists really that different, it's hard to read

It is different, and it's worth understanding since it shows up on exams. Read it inside out:

- The innermost query: 'is there an enrollment for this student in this course?'
- The middle: 'find a CS course where that's NOT true', meaning a CS course the student hasn't taken.
- The outer: 'keep students where no such course exists.'

So: students for whom there's no CS course they haven't taken, which is the same as 'took all CS courses'.

Other options for your second approach, if you want variety:

- **EXCEPT**: for each student, `(SELECT cid FROM Course WHERE dept='CS') EXCEPT (SELECT cid FROM Enrolled WHERE sid = s.sid)` is empty. Wrap it in `NOT EXISTS`.
- **LEFT JOIN with NULL check**: cross join students with CS courses, left join Enrolled, and exclude students with any NULL match.

The double NOT EXISTS is probably the best choice to show, since it's the textbook approach.
one edge case: if there are 0 CS courses, the count version returns nobody but double not exists returns everyone. which is right?

Good catch. Logically, double NOT EXISTS is 'correct' in the mathematical sense. If there are no CS courses, every student has vacuously taken all of them, so everyone qualifies.

The count version behaves differently: `COUNT(*)` is 0, but a student with no CS enrollments never appears in the grouped result at all, so nobody's returned.

Which one is 'right' depends on what the question means in practice:

- In relational algebra terms, division by an empty set returns all tuples, matching NOT EXISTS.
- In real applications, returning everyone is usually not what anyone wants.

For your assignment, it's a nice point to mention in a comment: explain that the two queries differ when the CS department has no courses and which one matches the formal definition. Professors tend to appreciate that kind of observation.

Ok that makes sense. Something completely different: I'm giving a toast at my older sister's wedding in three weeks. I did a practice run for my family last weekend with my draft and it went badly, the jokes got almost no laughs and it felt way too long (about 6 minutes). I had a lot of inside jokes from when we were kids and a long story about a camping trip. Why didn't it work? I thought those were the best parts.

Those parts feel like the best because they're meaningful to you, but they're the most likely to fall flat with an audience. Why:

- **Inside jokes need context.** If people weren't there, they need the backstory explained, and a joke that needs explaining rarely gets a laugh. Even family may not remember the details.
- **Long stories lose people.** A wedding audience is hungry, has been sitting a while, and is often drinking. Attention drops quickly after about 2 minutes on a single story.
- **6 minutes is long.** Most good toasts are 2 to 4 minutes. Beyond that, even good material starts to feel heavy.
- **Practice audiences are tough.** A small family group in a living room laughs less than a wedding crowd. So it may not have been as bad as it felt.

The usual fix: keep one short story, cut the inside jokes, and make sure the toast is about your sister and her partner rather than mostly about your shared childhood.
but how do I make it funny without the inside jokes? the camping story is actually funny

Funny for a wedding crowd usually comes from relatable, specific moments that anyone can picture. Your camping story might work if it's shortened and set up so a stranger gets it.

Why that works:

- **Quick setup.** One or two sentences: 'When she was 12, my sister decided she could lead the family on a hike without a map.'
- **One clear punchline**, instead of a series of moments.
- **A link to who she is now.** 'And that's still her: confident, determined, and occasionally completely lost. Which is why I'm glad she found [partner].' That connection turns a funny story into something meaningful.

Try telling it in under 45 seconds. If it still works at that length, it's a keeper. If it only works at 3 minutes, it's probably better saved for a family dinner.
why does the whole thing need to mention her partner so much? I don't know him that well

Because a wedding toast is about the couple, not just one of them. Guests include his family and friends, who may not know your sister well, and a toast that only talks about her can feel like it's leaving him out. It also comes across as more generous and mature.

You don't need to know him well to mention him meaningfully:

- **Something you've observed**: 'The first time she brought him home, he did the dishes without being asked, and my mom has never forgotten it.'
- **How he affects her**: 'I've never seen her as relaxed and happy as she is with him.'
- **Ask around**: talk to your sister, his friends or his siblings for one small story or quality.

Even two or three sentences about him, plus the final toast to both of them, is enough to make it feel balanced.
okay so if it's 3 minutes, roughly how should it be split up?

A common structure for a 3 minute toast:

- **Opening (about 15 to 20 seconds)**: who you are. 'For those who don't know me, I'm [name], [sister]'s younger brother.' Maybe a light line.
- **Story about your sister (about 45 to 60 seconds)**: the short camping story and what it says about her.
- **About the couple (about 45 to 60 seconds)**: how you saw her change after meeting him, something you've noticed about him, what they're like together.
- **Wishes and toast (about 20 to 30 seconds)**: what you wish for them, then ask everyone to raise their glasses: 'To [sister] and [partner].'

Why this order works: humor early relaxes the room, the middle gives it meaning, and ending on warmth gives people a clear moment to toast. Time yourself when practicing, since nerves make people speed up or ramble.

I've been trying to bulk for about 2 months. I'm 19, 175 cm, started at 63 kg and I'm still at 64 kg. I'm hitting around 130 g protein a day with chicken, eggs and a whey shake, and I lift 4 days a week. My weight has basically not moved for the last 6 weeks. What am I doing wrong?

If your weight isn't moving, the most likely cause is calories, not protein. Protein helps build muscle, but you need a calorie surplus to gain weight, and it's easy to underestimate how much you need, especially at 19 with a lean frame.

Things to check:

- **Are you tracking calories, or only protein?** Many people hit protein targets while total calories stay at maintenance.
- **Your rough maintenance**: for someone your size who lifts 4 days a week, it's probably around 2,500 to 2,800 kcal. A lean bulk usually means about 250 to 500 above that.
- **Activity**: walking a lot around campus burns more than you'd think.
- **Consistency**: eating a lot on some days and little on others can average out to maintenance.

Can you track everything you eat for 3 days, including drinks and snacks, and tell me the calorie totals?
I tracked 3 days. 2,150, 2,400 and 1,900. I thought I was eating so much, I'm always full

That explains it. Averaging about 2,150 kcal is likely at or below your maintenance, so no surplus, no gain.

Feeling full is common when you eat a lot of protein and lean foods like chicken, since they're filling but not very calorie-dense. The fix is adding calories without adding a lot of volume:

- **Liquid calories**: blend your shake with whole milk, a banana, oats and peanut butter. That's about 700 to 800 kcal instead of 120.
- **Calorie-dense foods**: nuts, nut butter, olive oil, cheese, dried fruit, granola.
- **Add fat to meals**: cook with olive oil or butter, add avocado, use full-fat dairy.
- **More carbs**: rice, pasta, bread and potatoes are easier to eat in larger amounts than chicken.

Target about 2,800 kcal a day and see how the scale responds over 2 to 3 weeks.
I tried the big smoothie today but it made me feel sick for like an hour after

That happens, especially if you drink a big, thick smoothie quickly or on an empty stomach. Options:

- **Split it**: half in the morning, half in the afternoon.
- **Sip it slowly** over 20 to 30 minutes instead of chugging.
- **Make it lighter**: less oats or peanut butter, a bit more milk to thin it.
- **Timing**: try it between meals rather than with a meal.
- **Smaller additions throughout the day** instead of one huge shake: a handful of nuts after class, a glass of whole milk with lunch, extra olive oil on pasta.

Some people just do better with food than shakes. Spreading 400 to 600 extra calories across the day in small additions often works better than one big hit.
ok I'll try that. but I still don't get how I can eat 130 g protein and not grow

Protein provides the building material for muscle, but your body needs energy to actually build tissue. If you're at maintenance or slightly below:

- Your body uses a lot of the protein for energy and normal repair, rather than new muscle.
- You might gain a small amount of muscle while losing a little fat, but your weight won't change much. That's called recomposition, and it's slower, especially for someone already lean.

At your stage (young, lean, fairly new to lifting), a calorie surplus speeds up muscle gain a lot. Protein is necessary but not sufficient.

Also, 130 g is plenty. It's around 2 g per kg, so you could even drop slightly to about 110 to 120 g and use those calories for carbs, which are easier to eat and fuel your training.
how fast should the scale go up once I fix this

For a lean bulk at your size, a reasonable rate is about 0.25 to 0.5 kg per week, or roughly 1 to 2 kg a month.

How to check:

- Weigh yourself in the morning, after the bathroom, before eating, at least 3 to 4 times a week.
- Use the **weekly average**, not single days. Daily weight swings of 1 kg are normal because of water and food.
- If the weekly average doesn't increase after 2 weeks, add another 200 to 300 kcal a day.
- If it goes up faster than about 0.5 kg a week for several weeks, you may be gaining more fat than needed, so cut back a little.

Also expect a quick 1 to 2 kg jump in the first week of eating more. That's mostly food and water, not fat or muscle.
I've been doing the snacks thing for 2 weeks now and weekly average went 64.1 to 64.3 to 64.4. too slow?

That's a gain, but slower than you probably want, about 0.15 kg a week. Since you're aiming to build muscle, I'd bump it up a bit:

- **Add about 200 to 300 kcal a day.** For example, a glass of whole milk (150 kcal) and a handful of nuts (170 kcal), or a bigger portion of rice at dinner.
- **Check consistency.** Track another 3 days to make sure weekends or busy days aren't dragging the average down.
- **Recheck in 2 weeks** and aim for around 0.25 to 0.4 kg per week.

Also check your training: make sure you're progressively adding weight or reps on your main lifts. If the gym numbers are going up and weight is creeping up, you're on track.

title: doing some creative coding for a…

question_types: sanity check: already has an answer in mind and wants it confirmed
how-to: wants step-by-step instructions to do something
how-to: wants step-by-step instructions to do something
feedback: pastes or describes their own draft, numbers or idea and asks for review

turns: doing some creative coding for a client project, animating stuff along cubic bezier curves. derivative of B(t) = (1-t)^3 P0 + 3(1-t)^2 t P1 + 3(1-t) t^2 P2 + t^3 P3 is 3(1-t)^2 (P1-P0) + 6(1-t)t(P2-P1) + 3t^2(P3-P2) right

Yes, that's correct. The derivative of a cubic Bézier is a quadratic Bézier built from the differences between consecutive control points, scaled by 3:

B'(t) = 3(1−t)²(P1−P0) + 6(1−t)t(P2−P1) + 3t²(P3−P2)

A quick sanity check: at t = 0 it gives 3(P1−P0), so the curve leaves P0 heading toward P1. At t = 1 it gives 3(P3−P2), so it arrives at P3 coming from the direction of P2. That matches how the handles behave in design tools.
ok so the tangent direction at any point is just normalize(B'(t))

Yes. Normalize B'(t) to get the unit tangent, and use it to rotate whatever's moving along the path, for example with `atan2(dy, dx)` for the angle.

One edge case: if a handle sits exactly on its endpoint (P1 = P0 or P2 = P3), B'(t) is zero at that end and you can't normalize it. Common workarounds are to use B'(t) at a tiny offset like t = 0.001, or fall back to the second derivative direction there.
second derivative would be 6(1-t)(P2 - 2P1 + P0) + 6t(P3 - 2P2 + P1)?

Correct. B''(t) = 6(1−t)(P2 − 2P1 + P0) + 6t(P3 − 2P2 + P1).

It's linear in t, which makes sense: differentiating a cubic twice gives a line. At t = 0 it's 6(P0 − 2P1 + P2), and at t = 1 it's 6(P1 − 2P2 + P3).
for constant speed I'm thinking t isn't the same as distance so moving t at a constant rate wont give constant speed

Right. Speed along the curve is |B'(t)|, which varies with t, so stepping t evenly makes the object speed up and slow down, usually faster in the middle and slower near tightly bent sections or short handles.

For constant speed you need to reparameterize by arc length. The usual approach in practice:

1. Sample the curve at, say, 100 to 200 values of t.
2. Sum the distances between consecutive points to build a table of cumulative length versus t.
3. To move at constant speed, step the distance evenly, then look up (and interpolate) the matching t in the table.
theres no closed form for the arc length right, so the lookup table is basically the standard way

Correct. For a general cubic Bézier, the arc length integral ∫|B'(t)| dt has no closed-form solution in elementary functions, since it involves the square root of a quartic polynomial.

So numerical methods are standard:

- **Lookup table** with linear interpolation, the most common in animation and creative coding.
- **Gaussian quadrature** for more accurate length per segment, often with 5 to 10 points.
- **Newton's method** to invert the length function precisely if you need high accuracy.

For a client animation, a lookup table with 100 to 200 samples is almost always accurate enough that no one can see the difference.
curvature is |B' x B''| / |B'|^3 in 2d yeah

Yes. In 2D, curvature is κ = |x'y'' − y'x''| / (x'² + y'²)^(3/2), which is the same as |B' × B''| / |B'|³ using the 2D cross product (a scalar).

Drop the absolute value if you want signed curvature, which tells you whether the curve is bending left or right. Handy if you want something to lean into turns.
and if I want something to slow down in tight curves I could scale speed by like 1/(1+k*curvature)

That works and is a common trick. A couple of notes:

- **Tune k** to the scale of your coordinates. Curvature has units of 1/length, so in pixel space values can be tiny on gentle curves and large at sharp corners.
- **Smooth it**: curvature can spike sharply near a cusp, which makes speed jump. Clamping curvature or averaging over a few samples helps it feel natural.
- **Combine with the arc length table**: compute your target speed from curvature, then advance distance by speed × dt, and look up t from the table.

That gives smooth, constant-ish motion that eases into tight turns.
cool so basically: arc length table for t lookup, tangent from normalized B', curvature for the slowdown. thats the setup

Yes, that's a solid setup:

1. **Arc length table**: sample B(t), build cumulative distance, interpolate to get t from distance.
2. **Position**: B(t) at that t.
3. **Orientation**: normalized B'(t), with a fallback at endpoints if a handle collapses.
4. **Speed**: base speed scaled by 1/(1 + k·κ), with curvature clamped or smoothed.
5. **Advance**: distance += speed × dt each frame.

If you chain multiple Bézier segments, build one combined table across all segments so motion stays continuous at the joins.
different topic. freelancer here, income all over the place (2k some months 6k others). how do i set up a monthly budget that actually works with that

With variable income, the trick is to budget on your lowest typical month, not the average. Steps:

1. Look at the last 6-12 months and find your low baseline, maybe 2,500.
2. List your fixed essentials: rent, utilities, insurance, minimum debt payments, groceries. This is your floor budget.
3. Open a separate 'buffer' account. When a month brings more than the baseline, the extra goes there.
4. Pay yourself a fixed monthly 'salary' from the buffer or business account, equal to the baseline.
5. In a high month, extra goes to taxes, savings, then debt.

Want help setting up the account structure?
yes. and taxes, i always forget about those

Use separate accounts. A simple three-account setup:

1. Business/income account: all client payments land here.
2. Tax account: every time you get paid, move 25-30 percent here immediately (check your bracket; self-employment tax alone is around 15 percent). Don't touch it except for quarterly estimated payments.
3. Personal checking: your fixed monthly 'salary' gets transferred here on the 1st.

Optional fourth: a savings/buffer account for the extra from good months.

In the US, quarterly estimated payments are due in April, June, September and January. Put those dates in your calendar. A high-yield savings account for the tax money earns some interest while it waits.
what if a month comes in under my baseline

That's what the buffer account is for. If income drops below your baseline salary, pull the difference from the buffer so your personal account still gets the same amount.

Steps for a low month:
1. Still transfer 25-30 percent of whatever you earned to the tax account.
2. Pay yourself the usual salary, using the buffer to cover the gap.
3. Cut flexible spending (eating out, subscriptions) for that month if the buffer is thin.

Target a buffer of 2-3 months of baseline expenses first, then raise to 6 months. Before the buffer exists, use the lower of last month's income and your baseline and adjust. If the buffer keeps running down, your baseline is set too high, so reduce it.
how do i split the personal salary into categories

Try the 50/30/20 split as a starting point, adjusted for your costs:

- 50 percent needs: rent, utilities, groceries, transport, insurance, minimum debt payments.
- 30 percent wants: dining out, entertainment, shopping, travel.
- 20 percent savings and extra debt payments.

On a 2,500 salary that's 1,250 / 750 / 500. If rent is high and takes more than half, shrink wants first.

To set it up: list all fixed bills and total them, then give each variable category a monthly cap. Use a spreadsheet or an app like YNAB, Monarch or a simple Google Sheet. Review at the end of each month and adjust for the next.
any tips for sticking to it

A few that work well:

- Automate: set automatic transfers for the salary, tax money and savings on a fixed date, so you don't decide each time.
- Separate cards or accounts for 'wants' so you can see when the money is gone.
- Check weekly for 5 minutes, not just monthly. Catching overspending early is easier than fixing it at month end.
- Give yourself a small guilt-free spending amount so the budget isn't too strict.
- Review every quarter: update the baseline as your income stabilizes.
- When you land a big payment, resist the urge to treat it as extra spending money. Run it through the same steps: taxes, buffer, then salary.

Expect the first two months to be messy, and adjust the numbers rather than giving up.
ok thanks. btw how do i batch cook for the week without everything going soggy by thursday. i have 4 containers and a freezer, cooking for one

The trick is to cook components separately and keep the wet things apart from the dry ones until you eat.

- Cook one or two proteins, like chicken thighs or lentils, and keep them in one container.
- Roast a tray of vegetables, and store them dry. They keep better if you don't pile sauce on top.
- Make the sauce or dressing separately, and add it when you reheat.
- Cook grains and portion them.
- Freeze anything you won't eat by Wednesday, and move it to the fridge the night before.

Cool everything before it goes in the fridge, and eat cooked food within three or four days. Anything beyond that should go in the freezer.
ok the rice always goes weird. what do i do with it

Rice is the one to be careful with. Cook it, then spread it out to cool quickly rather than leaving it in the pot. Once it's cool, store it in the fridge for no more than about three or four days.

When you reheat it, add a splash of water and heat it until it's steaming hot all the way through. It goes dry and hard if you skip the water. For longer storage, portion it into single servings and freeze it, then reheat from frozen with a little water.

ok got it, thanks. unrelated but: first 10k in 7 weeks, currently can run 5k in about 31 min. heres my plan for this week, too much?

mon rest
tue 5k easy
wed 6k tempo at 5:45/km
thu rest
fri 5k easy
sat 9k long
sun 3k recovery

thats 28k, last week i did 15k

That's too big a jump. Going from 15k to 28k is almost double, and the usual guideline is to increase weekly volume by about 10 to 20% at a time. Injury risk rises a lot with sudden jumps.

Other issues:

- **Tempo pace**: 5:45/km is faster than your current 5k pace (about 6:12/km). A tempo should be a bit slower than 5k pace, maybe around 6:30 to 6:40/km for you.
- **Long run**: 9k is too big a step if your longest so far is 5k. Go to 6 or 7k this week.
- **Back to back**: Saturday long followed by Sunday run adds stress. Fine later, but not this week.

A safer week, about 18k:

- tue 4k easy
- wed 5k with 2k at tempo (6:35/km) in the middle
- fri 3k easy
- sat 6k long, slow
ok but will that get me to 10k in 7 weeks

Yes. With 7 weeks, you have time to build gradually:

- **Week 1**: 18k, long run 6k
- **Week 2**: 20k, long run 7k
- **Week 3**: 22k, long run 8k
- **Week 4**: 18k (lighter week), long run 6k
- **Week 5**: 24k, long run 9k
- **Week 6**: 25k, long run 10k
- **Week 7**: race week, about 12k plus the 10k race

Keep most runs easy (you can talk in full sentences), with one tempo or interval session a week. Running 10k a week or two before the race means race day isn't a step into the unknown. At your current pace, finishing around 64 to 67 minutes is a realistic target.
