Nine weeks from a 15-minute jog to a 10k is very doable if you build gradually. Here's a structure that fits your schedule:

**Running days:** Tue morning, Thu morning, Sat or Sun (longer run). Optional 4th: Mon/Wed/Fri afternoon.

**Weeks 1-2:** run/walk
- Tue/Thu: 5 min walk warmup, then 3 min jog / 1 min walk x 5
- Weekend: 3 min jog / 1 min walk x 6-7

**Weeks 3-4:** longer jogs
- Tue/Thu: 20-25 min continuous easy jog
- Weekend: 30 min, walk breaks fine

**Weeks 5-6:**
- Tue: 30 min easy
- Thu: 30 min with 4-6 x 1 min a bit faster
- Weekend: 40-45 min easy

**Weeks 7-8:**
- Tue: 35 min easy
- Thu: 30-35 min with some faster bits
- Weekend: 50-60 min (~5-6 miles)

**Week 9 (race week):** two easy 20-25 min runs, rest 2 days before.

Easy = you can talk while running. Most people go way too fast at the start.
wait do i need to be able to run the whole 10k before the race

Nope. If you can run 50-60 min (~5-6 miles) comfortably by week 8, race day adrenaline plus tapering usually gets you through 6.2.

Also totally fine to walk some of it on race day. Lots of people do.
how fast should i be going rn

ok did week 1 tue and thu, shins kinda hurt now. normal?

Some shin soreness is common for new runners, but take it seriously so it doesn't turn into shin splints.

Check:
- **Dull ache that fades after warming up / a day later**: usually fine, just adaptation.
- **Sharp pain in one specific spot, or pain that gets worse while running**: stop and rest, could be a stress reaction. See a doctor if it lasts.

What helps:
- run on softer surfaces (track, trail, grass) when you can
- shorter, quicker steps. Overstriding is a big cause
- check your shoes. Old or super worn sneakers make it worse
- calf raises and toe walks, a few sets every other day
- ice for 10-15 min after if sore

If it's just achy, do the weekend run but repeat week 1 instead of moving on.

If you can, get fitted at a running store, they'll watch you jog and suggest a few options. You don't need anything fancy; a basic neutral daily trainer for $80-120 is plenty. Older models on sale are great for students.

After: static stretching is fine here if it feels good. Calves, hamstrings, quads, hips, 20-30 sec each. It won't prevent injury much on its own, but it helps you feel less stiff.

For your shins, calf stretches and calf raises after runs are worth doing.

thanks. other thing, got a physics midterm on newtons laws monday and i have like 8 hrs to study total this weekend. should i spend it doing practice problems or re reading the textbook chapters

Practice problems, by a wide margin. Physics exams test whether you can apply the laws to new situations, not whether you remember the text. Rereading feels productive but tends to give a false sense of mastery.

A plan for 8 hours:
- 1 hour: skim your lecture notes and the chapter summaries and formula list, just to refresh the key ideas (F = ma, free body diagrams, friction, tension, inclined planes).
- 5 hours: problems, starting with homework problems you got wrong, then problems from the end of the chapter.
- 1.5 hours: timed practice from a past exam if your professor shared one.
- 30 min: review mistakes.

Reread the textbook only for specific concepts you get stuck on.
ok what if i get stuck on a problem and cant figure it out? i dont wanna waste time

Set a limit: give yourself about 10 minutes to try. Within that, do these steps in order:

1. Draw a free body diagram with every force.
2. Write down knowns and unknowns.
3. Pick axes and write F = ma for each direction.
4. See if you have enough equations.

If still stuck after 10 minutes, look at the solution, but only for the first step or two. Then close it and try to finish yourself. Afterward, write one line on what you missed (like 'forgot normal force changes on an incline') in a mistakes list.

Then do a similar problem from scratch an hour later to confirm you got it. Stuck problems are your most valuable ones.
should i just memorize the formulas or does that not matter

Know the main ones, but memorizing alone won't carry you. For Newton's laws, there aren't many: F_net = ma, weight = mg, friction f = mu*N, and components on an incline (mg sin(theta) along the slope, mg cos(theta) perpendicular). Check whether your exam provides a formula sheet; if so, don't spend time memorizing and focus on when to use each.

If not, make a one-page cheat list and recite it a few times, but focus on understanding where they come from. Most mistakes on these exams come from drawing the wrong forces or picking wrong signs, not forgetting a formula.

So spend 15 minutes on the formulas and the rest on problems.

Wait times change often and I can't see live data, so check the official Visa Appointment Wait Times tool on travel.state.gov. Bring the confirmation page. It has the barcode and is what the consular officer and the scanners use. The full printed DS-160 form isn't required, though keeping a copy is fine.

Yes, the I-20 needs your signature as well as the DSO's. Sign it in ink in the student section before your interview. Officers check that the student has read and accepted the terms, so an unsigned I-20 can cause problems even if everything else is in order.

If the DSO's signature is already there and you've been given an original copy, just sign your part and keep the copy you'll bring. If you aren't sure whether your school has a different version, ask the international office.
what if the interview isnt in my home country though, can i still go to a different consulate

In most cases you apply at the consulate that covers your country of nationality or the country where you're legally residing. Applying elsewhere is generally not allowed, and consulates can refuse or send you back to the correct post.

There are some exceptions for people who are permanent residents or who can show a valid reason to apply somewhere else. Those rules are set by each post, so check the embassy's website or call the consulate before you change anything. Don't rebook at another location until you've confirmed it's accepted.

ok makes sense. switching topics, made my first dockerfile for my flask app (class project) can u check if its ok

COPY . .

it works but the image is like 1.1gb which seems huge??

It works, but a few changes would make it smaller and better:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 5000
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```

What changed:
- **python:3.12-slim** instead of python:3.12. The full image includes compilers and tons of tools you don't need. This alone usually cuts 800MB+.
- **WORKDIR /app** so you're not dumping files into the root directory.
- **Copy requirements.txt first**, install, then copy the code. Docker caches layers, so editing your code won't reinstall all packages every build.
- **--no-cache-dir** skips storing pip's download cache in the image.
- **CMD in JSON form** so signals (like Ctrl+C / docker stop) reach your app properly.

Also add a `.dockerignore` with things like `venv/`, `__pycache__/`, `.git/`, so they don't get copied in.
omg went down to 180mb. but now it says connection refused when i go to localhost:5000. i ran docker run -p 5000:5000 myapp

Classic one. Flask by default listens on 127.0.0.1, which inside the container means only the container itself can reach it. You need it to listen on all interfaces.

In app.py:

```python
app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000)
```

Rebuild and run again. The slim image isn't the issue here; binding to 0.0.0.0 is almost always the fix for 'connection refused' with Flask in Docker.

If you'd rather not touch the code, `CMD ["flask", "run", "--host=0.0.0.0"]` does the same thing.
that fixed it!! my prof said we shouldnt use the flask dev server for 'deployment' tho. is that a big deal for a class project

For a class demo, honestly not a big deal. But it's easy to do it right and might get you points.

Use gunicorn:

1. Add `gunicorn` to requirements.txt
2. Change the last line of the Dockerfile:

```dockerfile
CMD ["gunicorn", "-w", "2", "-b", "0.0.0.0:5000", "app:app"]
```

`app:app` means 'file app.py, Flask object named app'. If your Flask variable has a different name, change the second part.

With gunicorn you don't need the app.run() line to execute at all, and it handles multiple requests properly.

ok heres the final one, anything else?

```dockerfile

```

Put those right before the CMD line.

**Pin versions** in requirements.txt (e.g. `flask==3.0.3`, `gunicorn==22.0.0`) so the build doesn't break if a new version comes out before your demo.

nice, thanks. random q, just adopted a 2 yr old rescue beagle mix, he pulls like crazy on the leash. how do i teach him to walk nicely, i have a regular flat collar and a 6ft leash

Pulling works for him because he gets where he wants faster, so you need to make pulling not work and walking next to you pay off. Steps:

1. Gear: swap the flat collar for a front-clip harness (e.g. Easy Walk or Ruffwear Front Range). It reduces pulling power. Keep the 6 ft leash, not a retractable.
2. Treats: bring small, tasty treats in a pouch, like chicken or cheese.
3. Start indoors or in the yard. Reward him every time he's by your side.
4. Stop when he pulls: the moment the leash goes tight, stop walking and wait. When it loosens or he looks at you, reward and walk on.
5. Short sessions of 5-10 minutes.
he's a beagle tho so he sniffs everything. do i just not let him sniff?

Don't ban sniffing. Sniffing is how dogs 'read the news', it tires them out mentally, and it's especially strong in beagles. Banning it will frustrate him and make the walk harder.

Instead, give structure:
- Pick walk phases: a 'sniff time' with a cue like 'go sniff', where he's free to explore on a loose leash, and a 'walk time' where he needs to stay by you.
- Use the sniffing as a reward: after he walks nicely for 20 steps, say 'go sniff' and let him investigate a good spot.
- Choose places with fewer distractions at first, and walk when he's a bit tired.

This way you're using his favorite thing to motivate him.
ok what do i do when he sees a squirrel and just goes

Prevention first, since a beagle's drive is strong and a lunge can pull you off balance.

1. Hold the leash firmly with both hands and stand your ground when you spot one first. Don't let him build momentum.
2. Increase distance: when you see a squirrel or other trigger, turn and walk away, or cross the street, before he reacts.
3. Practice 'look at me' or his name: use a high-value treat when he notices the squirrel but before he lunges. Reward him for looking at it and then back at you.
4. Use the 'leave it' cue, practiced at home first with low-value items, then increasing difficulty.
5. Keep a treat at his nose to lure him away if he's about to fixate.

Expect this to take weeks; it's one of the hardest things for a scent hound.
how long till he walks nice on the leash

It varies, but plan on a few weeks for noticeable improvement and a few months for reliable walking, especially with a beagle mix and a dog that's had two years of practice pulling.

Rough timeline:
- Week 1-2: he understands that tight leash means stopping. Walks are still slow and stop-start.
- Week 3-6: he's checking in more often and walking loosely on quiet routes.
- Month 2-4: reliable in most situations, except with strong distractions.

What speeds it up: consistent rules from everyone who walks him, short daily practice sessions, harness use, and regular exercise so he has less pent-up energy. What slows it down: letting him pull sometimes. Every time pulling works, it resets the progress.

A group class or a trainer helps if progress stalls.

title: Some background: I'm a senior accountant,…

question_types: troubleshooting: something is broken or not working and they describe what they see
troubleshooting: something is broken or not working and they describe what they see
feedback: pastes or describes their own draft, numbers or idea and asks for review

turns: Some background: I'm a senior accountant, 9 years experience, two kids under 7. I've been interviewing for controller and accounting manager roles for about three months now. I've had 6 first-round interviews, mostly with HR or recruiters, and only one of them led to a second round. I feel like they go well in the moment, friendly conversation, but then I get the rejection email a few days later. I don't know what I'm doing wrong.

Six first rounds and one second round suggests your resume is opening doors, but something in those screening calls isn't landing. A few common reasons for 'felt good, still rejected' at the recruiter stage:

1. **Salary expectations.** If you're giving a number above their band, or answering vaguely, many recruiters screen out quietly.
2. **Unclear 'why this role'.** For a step up to controller or manager, recruiters listen for whether you can explain why you're ready to lead, not just do the work.
3. **Answers too detailed or too technical.** HR screeners aren't accountants. Long walkthroughs of close processes can lose them.
4. **Not enough leadership evidence.** For manager-level roles, they're often checking a box: has this person managed people or owned a process end to end?
5. **Availability or flexibility.** If schedule constraints come up early (school pickup, no travel), some recruiters filter on that even if they shouldn't.
6. **Friendly but not specific.** Pleasant conversation can mask that you didn't give concrete examples with numbers.

Could you tell me how you usually answer 'tell me about yourself' and 'what salary are you looking for'?

For tell me about yourself I usually go through my career in order, from my first job at a small CPA firm, then my current company, what I do day to day. Probably takes 3-4 minutes. For salary I say I'm flexible and would like to hear their range first.

Both of these are likely part of the problem.

**Tell me about yourself:** 3-4 minutes in chronological order is long, and it buries the point. Recruiters often decide in the first 60 seconds. Try 60-90 seconds, structured as:
- **Present:** 'I'm a senior accountant with 9 years' experience, currently leading month-end close for a $120M manufacturing company.'
- **Highlights:** 2 accomplishments with numbers. 'I cut close from 10 days to 6' or 'I trained and oversee two staff accountants.'
- **Future:** 'I'm looking to move into a controller role where I can own the full close and reporting.'

**Salary:** 'I'm flexible, what's your range' sounds reasonable, but it can backfire. Some recruiters read it as unprepared, or assume you'll be disappointed with their number. A better approach: give a researched range. 'Based on my research for controller roles in this area, I'm targeting $115-130k, but I'm open depending on the full package.' Use a range where the bottom is still a number you'd accept.
I have trained two staff accountants but I don't technically manage them, they report to my manager. Can I still say I lead them?

Be precise rather than inflating it, but don't undersell it either. Recruiters are checking for leadership experience, and 'training and reviewing others' work' is real leadership, even without formal reporting lines.

Good ways to phrase it:
- 'I train and mentor two staff accountants and review their reconciliations and journal entries during close.'
- 'I act as the team lead for month-end close, coordinating work across two staff accountants.'

Avoid 'I manage two people' if that's not true. If it comes up in a reference check or later interview, it costs you trust.

If they ask directly, 'have you managed people?', a strong answer is: 'Not formally, but in practice I've been the lead for close. I train, assign work and review. I'm ready to take on formal management, and that's a big reason I'm applying for this role.' That turns the gap into motivation.

That helps. I tried the shorter intro on a recruiter call yesterday and it went much better, she even said it was a great summary. But then she asked about my availability for the 2-3 days a month the role requires at their other site, and I said I'd need to check with my partner because of the kids. She went a bit quiet after that.

Glad the new intro worked.

That availability answer probably did raise a flag. Not because having kids is a problem, but 'I need to check' at the screening stage sounds like 'maybe no', and recruiters are often told to confirm travel requirements upfront.

For future calls, figure out your real answer before the interview, then give it confidently:
- If you can do it: 'Yes, 2-3 days a month works for me. I'd just appreciate some notice to plan around it.'
- If you can partly do it: 'I can do that with about a week's notice. Are those days usually fixed, or flexible?'
- If you truly can't: better to know now and skip those roles.

For yesterday's call, it might be worth a short follow-up email: 'Thank you for the conversation today. I confirmed at home, and the 2-3 days per month at the other site works well for me.' Recruiters appreciate that, and it removes the doubt before they decide.
I just sent that follow-up email. Is there anything else I should practice before my next screening on Thursday?

Good move on the email. For Thursday, I'd practice these out loud a couple of times (record yourself on your phone if you can):

1. **Your 60-90 second intro**, now that you know it works.
2. **Salary range answer.** Research the specific company and city first so your range fits.
3. **'Why are you leaving your current job?'** Keep it forward-looking: 'I've grown as much as I can in this role and I'm ready to own the close and reporting.' Nothing negative about your employer.
4. **'Tell me about a time you led a project or improved a process.'** Use one story with a clear result, ideally with a number.
5. **Your availability**, already decided, including travel and hours.
6. **Two questions to ask them**, like 'What does success look like in the first 90 days?' or 'What's the biggest challenge facing the team right now?'

Also, at the end of the call, ask about next steps and timing. It shows interest and gives you a date to follow up.

My daughter is in 11th grade physics and I said I'd check her homework because I did engineering in college, but it's been 20 years and now we're both stuck. Problem: a 5 kg block slides down a 30 degree incline, coefficient of kinetic friction 0.2, find the acceleration. We both got 6.6 m/s^2 but the answer key says 3.2. What are we missing?

You've almost certainly added friction instead of subtracting it. Check:

- Gravity component along the incline: g sin30 = 9.8 x 0.5 = 4.9 m/s^2
- Friction: μ g cos30 = 0.2 x 9.8 x 0.866 = 1.70 m/s^2

The block is sliding **down**, so friction acts **up** the slope, opposing motion:

a = g sin30 - μ g cos30 = 4.9 - 1.70 = 3.2 m/s^2

If you add them, 4.9 + 1.70 = 6.6, which is exactly your answer. The mass doesn't matter here; it cancels out because both forces scale with m.

A good habit for her: draw the free body diagram, mark the direction of motion with an arrow, and then put friction pointing the opposite way before writing any equations.

Oh that's exactly it. Part b is where it gets weird though. Same block, same incline, but now it's pushed so it starts sliding UP the incline at 4 m/s. How far up does it go? We used a = 3.2 and got 2.5 m but the key says 1.21 m.

Same issue in reverse. When the block moves **up**, friction now points **down** the slope, the same direction as the gravity component. Both slow it down:

a = g sin30 + μ g cos30 = 4.9 + 1.70 = 6.6 m/s^2 (deceleration)

Then use v^2 = u^2 - 2ad with final speed 0:

0 = 4^2 - 2(6.6)d
d = 16 / 13.2 = 1.21 m

So the 6.6 you got in part a was actually the right number for part b. Friction always opposes the direction of motion, so its sign flips when the direction flips. Gravity's component stays pointing down the slope either way.
She's asking why friction changes direction but gravity doesn't, and honestly I'm not sure how to explain it well.

One way to put it for her:

**Gravity doesn't care what the block is doing.** It always pulls straight down toward the Earth. On a slope, part of that pull always points down the slope. Whether the block is sitting still, sliding up or sliding down, that component is the same.

**Friction is a reaction to motion.** It only exists because the surfaces are rubbing past each other, and it always tries to stop that rubbing. So it points opposite to whichever way the block is sliding. It has no fixed direction of its own.

An everyday picture: push a heavy box across the floor to the left, and you feel resistance to the right. Push it to the right, and the resistance is to the left. Gravity, meanwhile, is pulling the box down the whole time no matter which way you push.

That's why in part b, going up the slope, both forces team up against the block, and it stops quickly.
Makes sense. Last part asks if the block will slide back down after it stops at the top, or stay there. The problem doesn't give a static friction coefficient so we're not sure what to do.

Without μs given, the usual approach is to assume static friction is about the same as kinetic, or to check whether even a generous static friction could hold it.

The test: the block stays put only if the maximum static friction can balance the gravity component, which happens when μs ≥ tan θ.

tan 30° = 0.577

With μ = 0.2, that's way below 0.577. Even if static friction were somewhat higher than kinetic (it usually is, but rarely three times higher on the same surfaces), it wouldn't be enough. So the block slides back down.

On the way down, it accelerates at 3.2 m/s^2, same as part a. If there's a follow-up asking for its speed when it returns to the start, use v^2 = 2ad = 2(3.2)(1.21), which gives v ≈ 2.8 m/s. It comes back slower than the 4 m/s it started with, because friction took energy on both trips.

Thank you, that clears it up. On a completely different note, I'm a marketing manager at a mid-size consumer goods company, and I'm interviewing for a senior marketing manager role at a SaaS company next Tuesday. It's a panel with the VP of Marketing, a product lead and someone from sales. I took 3 years where I worked part-time after my second child, and I'm a little rusty on interviews. Could you look at my answers to the likely questions? Here's the first one, for 'Tell me about a time you failed':

'In 2022 I launched a campaign for our new snack line targeting Gen Z on TikTok. We spent $40k on influencer partnerships but the engagement was low and sales didn't move. I learned that you need to understand your audience better before investing. Since then I always do more research.'

The example is good: it's real, it has a number, and it's honest. But the answer stops right where the panel gets interested. Three things to fix:

**1. What specifically went wrong?** 'Engagement was low' is vague. Was it the wrong influencers, the wrong message, the wrong product fit? Naming the actual cause shows analytical thinking.

**2. What did you do about it at the time?** Did you pull budget, change creative, run a test? A failure answer is really about how you respond.

**3. The lesson is too generic.** 'Do more research' could come from anyone. Make it concrete: what process do you do now that you didn't before?

A stronger version might go:

'...After two weeks, engagement was a third of our benchmark. I dug in and found our influencers' audiences skewed older than we assumed, and the content felt like ads. I paused the remaining $15k, and we ran small tests with micro-creators instead, which performed twice as well. Now I always run a small paid test before committing more than 20% of a budget.'

Adjust to what actually happened, of course.

That's helpful. What actually happened is that we paused the last $12k, and the second round with smaller creators got about 3x the engagement rate, though sales only went up slightly. Should I mention the sales part or leave it out?

Mention it. It makes the story more credible, and the panel will likely ask anyway, especially the sales person.

You can frame it honestly and still end strong:

'...The second round with smaller creators got about three times the engagement rate. Sales only moved slightly, which taught me a second lesson: engagement and conversion are different problems, and I hadn't set up the campaign to measure the path from one to the other.'

Then your lesson becomes:

'Since then, I run a small test before committing more than about a fifth of the budget, and I define the conversion metric up front, not just engagement.'

That's a better answer than one with a perfect ending. It shows you can separate vanity metrics from business results, which is exactly what a SaaS marketing team cares about, since they live and die by pipeline and conversion.

Great. Here's my answer for 'Why do you want to move from consumer goods to SaaS?':

'I've always been interested in technology and I think SaaS is where the most exciting marketing is happening. I'd love to learn about B2B marketing and grow my skills in a new industry.'

This one needs the most work. It's polite, but it focuses on what you'll get, and it sounds like you're starting from zero. A panel hiring a senior manager wants to hear what you bring.

Issues:
- 'Always been interested in technology' is generic. Everyone says it.
- 'I'd love to learn about B2B marketing' flags a gap without bridging it.
- There's no reason why *this* company.

Try this structure:
1. **What transfers:** your CPG skills that matter in SaaS, like audience research, testing, brand positioning, working with sales.
2. **Why now:** something specific that drew you to SaaS, like longer customer relationships, data-driven decisions, product-led growth.
3. **Why them:** one detail about the company.

Example:
'In consumer goods I've spent years doing audience research and testing creative, and what I've enjoyed most is when I could tie marketing to measurable results. SaaS takes that further. You can see the full journey from first touch to renewal. I'm drawn to [company] specifically because [product or market detail], and I think my experience positioning products for crowded markets is directly relevant.'
I don't really know much about their product yet beyond the website. What should I look at before Tuesday so I can fill in that 'why them' part?

In a few hours you can get a decent picture:

1. **Their website and pricing page.** Who is it for (company size, role), what problem does it solve, and how do they price? Pricing tells you a lot about the target customer.
2. **G2 or Capterra reviews.** What customers love and complain about. Great for spotting positioning gaps you could talk about.
3. **Their blog, newsletter and LinkedIn.** What content are they putting out? Is the tone polished, playful, technical?
4. **Competitors.** Look at 2-3 competitors' homepages. How does this company differentiate, or does it?
5. **The panel members on LinkedIn.** What did the VP do before? What has the product lead posted about?
6. **Recent news.** Funding round, new product launch, new markets.
7. **Try the product** if there's a free trial.

Pick one specific observation to use in your answer, like 'your onboarding emails are excellent but your homepage leads with features rather than outcomes'. A thoughtful point beats general praise.

Here's my answer for the weakness question:

'I'm a perfectionist and sometimes spend too long on details.'

I'd replace this one. 'Perfectionist' is one of the most common answers, and interviewers usually hear it as a non-answer.

A better weakness is:
- real, but not central to the role
- something you've actively worked on
- something you can show progress on

Given your background, some honest options:
- **Less experience with B2B pipeline metrics.** Ties in with your transition and you can show what you're doing about it (a course, reading, conversations).
- **Delegating.** If you tend to take things on yourself, especially returning from part-time.
- **Public speaking or presenting to senior leadership**, if that's true.

Example using the first:
'My experience is mostly in consumer marketing, so I haven't worked directly with sales pipeline metrics like MQL-to-SQL conversion. I've been closing that gap: I completed HubSpot's inbound marketing certification and I've been talking to friends in SaaS about how they structure handoff with sales. I'd expect to lean on the sales team early on to get it right.'

It's honest and shows initiative.
I like the B2B one, I actually did the HubSpot course last month. What if someone asks about the part-time years? Do I need to explain them?

Have a short answer ready, but you don't need to bring it up yourself. If they ask, keep it to 2-3 sentences and pivot back to the role:

'After my second child, I went part-time for three years and stayed in my role at [company], focusing on [what you owned]. I'm now back full-time and ready to take on a bigger scope, which is a big reason I'm excited about this position.'

Things that help:
- If you delivered meaningful work while part-time, name it. 'Even at three days a week, I led our relaunch of X' is a strong signal.
- Don't apologize or explain childcare arrangements. That's not something they need, and in most places they can't really ask about it.
- If they ask if you can handle the workload, give a confident yes and a concrete example of a busy period you handled.

Since you stayed in your field and kept a marketing manager title, this is much less of a 'gap' than you might feel it is.
Last one. Is there anything I should prepare specifically because it's a panel with sales and product people in the room, not just marketing?

Yes, it's worth tailoring for each person, because each will be listening for different things.

**For the sales person:**
- How you've worked with sales before (trade marketing, retail buyers, key account teams in CPG count).
- Your view on lead quality vs. volume. Sales teams care that marketing sends leads that actually close.
- A story about resolving a disagreement with sales.

**For the product lead:**
- How you'd learn the product and translate features into customer benefits.
- A launch you've run: how you worked with product or R&D on timing, positioning, messaging.
- Questions about the roadmap and how marketing feeds customer insight back.

**For the VP:**
- Strategy, prioritization, how you measure success, how you'd approach the first 90 days.

Also prepare one question for each panelist. For example, ask the sales person 'What does a great marketing-sourced lead look like to you?' It shows you're thinking about cross-functional work, which is a big part of the senior role.

title: Hi, I'm a college junior with…

question_types: planning: wants help putting together a plan or schedule
quick fact: a short factual question, then a follow-up or two
explanation: wants to understand why or how something works

turns: Hi, I'm a college junior with a summer internship that pays about $4,500 total after taxes. I'd like to start investing some of it in mutual funds through monthly SIPs. Could you help me put together a plan for the next year? I have about $1,500 in savings already and I don't have any debt apart from a small student loan.

Congratulations on the internship. A plan for the next year:

1. Keep an emergency buffer first. As a student, 1,500 is a decent start; I'd keep that in a savings account untouched.
2. From the 4,500, decide on a monthly figure after covering any essentials during school. For example, set aside 3,000 to cover school expenses and put 1,500 into investments, or invest a smaller amount monthly.
3. Choose a low-cost index fund (S&P 500 or total market) and set up an automatic monthly investment, e.g. $100-150.
4. Consider a Roth IRA, since you have earned income: contributions can be withdrawn without penalty and growth is tax-free. Many brokerages allow starting with low minimums.

How much do you expect to need for school expenses over the year?
Probably around $2,500 for the year, books and some rent. The rest I could invest. Should I put it all in at once or do monthly SIPs?

With roughly $2,000 to invest, either approach is reasonable. Statistically, lump sum investing has beaten monthly investing about two-thirds of the time, but the difference for $2,000 is small, and monthly investing builds a habit and reduces the risk of regretting your timing.

A practical option: invest $500 now, and then $125 a month for the next 12 months. Or, if the money isn't needed soon, put it all in a Roth IRA now as a lump sum.

Given your savings are tight, I would favor the monthly option and keep the rest in a high-yield savings account (earning 4 percent or so) while waiting to be invested.
That sounds good. What kind of fund should I look for, and what should I check before choosing?

For a first fund, look for a broad, low-cost index fund. Specifically:

- Type: a total US stock market index fund or S&P 500 index fund, or a target-date fund for your retirement year (such as 2065) if you want a single fund that adjusts over time.
- Expense ratio: under 0.10 percent. Many are 0.03-0.05 percent.
- Minimum investment: some funds require 1,000-3,000 to open. ETFs or fractional-share funds (like Fidelity's no-minimum index funds) can start at 1 dollar.
- No sales loads and no transaction fees.
- Tracking: it should closely match its index.

Examples: Fidelity FSKAX or FXAIX, Vanguard VTSAX/VFIAX, Schwab SWTSX/SWPPX. Pick whichever matches your brokerage.
I've also heard about SIPs being popular in India. Is it the same as what I'd be doing with automatic investments here?

Essentially yes. A SIP (Systematic Investment Plan) is the term used in India for investing a fixed amount in a mutual fund on a fixed date each month. In the US, the equivalent is called an automatic investment plan or recurring investment, and the strategy is called dollar-cost averaging.

Small differences: in India, SIPs are an established product, and you can start with as little as 500 rupees a month through an app or your bank. In the US, you set up automatic investments with your brokerage, typically inside a fund or ETF purchase.

If you're a US taxpayer investing in US funds, the mechanics are the same: money leaves your bank on a schedule and buys fund shares at that day's price.
Great. How will I know if it's working, and when should I adjust things?

Don't judge it by short-term moves. Stocks can fall 10-20 percent in a year and still be on track for the long run. Better ways to check:

- Monthly: confirm the automatic investment ran and the amount is right.
- Quarterly: glance at the balance and your total contributions. Make sure you're adding what you planned.
- Yearly: review the plan. Has your income changed, are the expense ratios still low, and do you want to increase the monthly amount?

When to adjust: you get a raise or a new job (increase contributions), you take on debt or have an emergency (pause temporarily), or your goals change (like saving for a house in five years, which needs a safer allocation).

What not to do: sell in a downturn, or check daily.
Could you summarize the whole plan so I can keep it as a checklist?

Here's a checklist:

BEFORE YOU START
- Keep your $1,500 savings as an emergency fund.
- Set aside $2,500 for school costs from your internship pay.
- Confirm you have earned income to qualify for a Roth IRA.

SETUP
- Open a Roth IRA at Fidelity, Vanguard or Schwab.
- Choose one broad, low-cost index fund (expense ratio under 0.10 percent).
- Invest about $500 initially, then set an automatic $125 a month.
- Keep the rest of the money in a high-yield savings account until it's invested.

OVER THE YEAR
- Monthly: check the investment ran.
- Quarterly: look at the balance briefly.
- Yearly: review, raise contributions with income.

RULES
- Don't sell in a downturn.
- Don't chase hot funds.
- Don't pull the money out unless it's a real emergency.
Quick question on essays: is it ok to use 'I' in an argumentative essay for a college class? My prof said first person is fine in one, but my TA said to avoid it.

It depends on the discipline and the instructor. In many humanities classes, 'I' is fine when you're stating your position, as in 'I argue that...', because it makes the claim clear and owns it. Personal anecdotes need more care, and they should earn their place by supporting the argument.

In science or social science writing, the convention is often to avoid first person. Since your prof and TA disagree, check the assignment rubric or ask which one grades the essay. If the rubric doesn't mention it, a safe middle ground is to use 'I' sparingly, mainly for the thesis.
what about 'we' as in 'we can see that'

I'd avoid it. 'We' can sound like you're speaking for the reader, and it often hides who did the analysis. 'The data show' or 'the text suggests' is more precise. If you want a subject for the action, 'I' works better than 'we' in a single-author essay, since you're the one making the claim.
ok and do i need a works cited for a 1000 word essay with 3 sources

Yes. Any source you quote, paraphrase or draw an idea from needs an in-text citation, and each source goes on the works cited page. Three sources is still three sources, so the list is required even for a short essay.

Check which style your class uses. MLA is common in English and humanities, and APA in psychology and social sciences. The format for each citation differs, so use the rubric or a citation generator and double-check the output against the style guide.
does the works cited page count toward the 1000 words

Usually not. Both MLA and APA exclude the works cited or reference list from the word count, but in-text citations count as part of the text. Title pages and headers are normally excluded too.

Since word limits vary, check whether your instructor specifies what's included. If the assignment just says 1000 words, a good rule is to aim for 1000 words in the body and count the works cited separately.
thanks. one more, is a conclusion supposed to introduce new info or just restate

It should mostly synthesize rather than restate or introduce new evidence. Restating your thesis word for word is weak, so rephrase it in light of what you've shown. Then explain why it matters: what follows from the argument, what it changes, or what question is still open.

Bringing in a brand-new source or example in the conclusion usually makes the argument feel unfinished, so put that material in the body instead. A small new idea that follows logically from your argument is fine if it helps the reader see the bigger picture.

got it, thanks. different question, why does a LEFT JOIN with a WHERE clause on the right table act like an inner join? i ran this and got fewer rows than i expected and i don't get why

SELECT s.name, c.title
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id
LEFT JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id
WHERE c.title = 'Biology'

The LEFT JOIN keeps every student, including students with no enrollments, and fills the course columns with NULL for them. But the WHERE clause runs after the join. For a student with no classes, c.title is NULL, and NULL = 'Biology' evaluates to unknown, not true. So those rows get filtered out, and the result looks like an inner join.

If you want all students and only the Biology enrollments attached to them, move the condition into the ON clause:

```
SELECT s.name, c.title
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id
LEFT JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id AND c.title = 'Biology'
```

Now the condition only decides which course rows get matched. Students who don't match still come through, with NULL in the title column.
so if i put the condition in the on clause it keeps the students with no biology class? what would the nulls look like

Yes. Every student appears at least once. Students with a Biology enrollment show the title, and everyone else shows NULL in that column:

```
name      | title
----------+----------
Alice     | Biology
Ben       | NULL
Chen      | Biology
Dara      | NULL
```

If a student took several courses, they'll appear once per matching row, so you may still see duplicates for students with multiple Biology enrollments. If you only want each student once, use DISTINCT or a subquery that checks for the course, rather than joining the table at all.
